THE RILEY

"Certain characteristics, as original as they are concisely practical, have caused the Riley '9' to be regarded as the most advanced design of British built small cars on the market. Now the makers have completed the task of giving the '9' a larger brother and are placing on the market a five seater of similar characteristics, but with a six-cylinder engine." – Autocar.

Clothed in stylish bodywork by Stanley Riley, the Coventry marque's pre-war offerings were among the world's finest small-capacity sporting cars. Percy Riley's 9hp, 1,087cc, twin-camshaft four was an outstanding engine design by any standards, various versions powering Rileys from 1926 to 1957. The twin-cam Riley engine was one of the most advanced of its day, so it can have caused little surprise when the Coventry manufacturer created its first six by, in effect, adding a pair of cylinders to the existing design. Hailed as 'The Wonder Car Plus Two', the first 14hp, 1.6-liter six-cylinder models duly appeared in 1929 followed by 12hp, 1.5-liter versions in 1933. Riley's 1,633cc, 13.5hp engine was also offered in this chassis.

In 1935 Riley introduced the new 1.7-liter 15/6, which incorporated many features of the contemporary 12/4, including an X-braced box-section chassis with over-axle tubular members at the rear. This frame employed the standard 112½" wheelbase at first and a 116½ wheelbase from 1937. The pre-selector gearbox was the only transmission on offer. The 15/6 was available with bodies in five different styles: Stelvio, Kestrel, Falcon and Adelphi saloons, plus the Lynx tourer.


THE CAR OFFERED

Riley's have been renowned the world over for their extreme capability in almost any motoring circumstance. Their diminutive, overhead cam, 6-cylinder jewel of an engine has propelled many a racer to victory. Aside from the factory-built Imps and Brooklands cars, many a Riley have found themselves prepared as turnkey "winners". This Riley is no exception. Having been derived from a 12/6, this special was the initial beneficiary of a fabulous conversion to the general car presented here. Having already been upgraded to 15/6 cam along with new rotating assembly the Riley leaves little to be desired in the way of power.

The "boat-tail" coachwork is very of-the-period racer. Completed in aluminum, it has a craftsman's eye for execution and proportion. Additionally, with period racing appointments such as Brooklands screens, reproduction Micheline tires, color-matched wire wheels with knock off spinners, twin aluminum 'LeMans' style fuel fillers, and twin Andre Hartford shock absorbers to iron out any road imperfections, the "look" but also the functionality of this car really is brought to the forefront.

After the Riley's initial completion, its current owner, a rallyist of the highest order, took the car to a stratospheric level. Now accompanied with stacks and stacks of receipts from marque specialists, in the near $40,000 range, from names such as Blue Diamond and K. Pointing, the Riley has been actively campaigned both in the US and abroad on numerous events, including multiple Great Race and Europe distance tours. No expense was spared on both larger parts down to the trivial £2.00 part, each was fitted with a similar attention to detail. This Riley was prepped for any and all classic motoring events, both long and short distance and most recently completed the Colorado Grand this past September. Also having been accepted to the VSCC, it's sure to be a weapon on both the street and the track. Truly an exciting opportunity for any motoring enthusiast to truly dive in and understand what sets these jewel-like cars apart. A Blue Diamond, perfectly faceted, this Riley is not an experience to be missed.

LAMBORGHINI MURCIÉLAGO

Successor to the Diablo and Lamborghini's flagship model, the Murciélago 'hypercar' was introduced in 2001 for the 2002 model year, and like its forebears was named after a famous fighting bull. The Murciélago was Lamborghini's first new design for 11 years and the Italian company's first since its acquisition by the Volkswagen Group's Audi division in 1998. Audi's input ensured that build quality was of the highest, while the manufacturing time was cut from the Diablo's 500 hours to a much more profitable 300. Features identified as key to the Lamborghini brand were retained, so the Murciélago came with a mid-mounted V12 engine, cab-forward layout, scissor-action doors, and all-wheel drive.

Styled by Lamborghini's head of design Luc Donckerwolke, the angular coupé was very low, boasting a roof height of just under 47.2 inches, and featured distinctive doors that swung upwards and forwards when opened. A combination of carbon fiber, steel and aluminum was used for the chassis/body, while the suspension featured the supercar-standard double wishbones all round. The Murciélago's power unit was a longitudinally mounted 6.2-liter V12, an engine that could trace its ancestry back to the very first Lamborghini of 1964. As installed in the Murciélago, this formidable power unit produced 572bhp, which was delivered to the ground via a six-speed manual gearbox and four-wheel drive, while an active rear wing and active air intakes, deployed automatically when required, helped keep the Murciélago stable at its circa 200mph top speed.

To demonstrate that that all-important top speed claim was no idle boast, Lamborghini test driver Giorgio Sanna set a number of class records at the Nardo test track in Italy, covering 100 miles at an average speed of 320.254km/h (198.996mph) despite less than ideal weather conditions. Autocar's Stephen Sutcliffe declared that the Murciélago's arrival "makes the Diablo seem old and slow".


THE CAR OFFERED

This 2003 Lamborghini Murcielago Coupe is one of just 424 examples produced with a 'gated' 6-speed manual transmission. Originally delivered to Symbolic Motor Company of La Jolla, California, showing just over 9K miles, this Murcielago has only had 2x owners since new.

Finished in Nero Pegaso (Black Metallic) over Nero Perseus (Black) Leather with Red Contrast Stitching, the cabin offers both performance focus and premium comfort. Amenities include hydraulic front lift, automatic climate control, and a CD Changer.

Paint protection film covers the front bumper, hood, fenders, side skirts, and rear quarters, complemented by sport catalytic converters, a titanium exhaust system, and 18-inch Speedline multi-piece wheels framing black-painted Lamborghini-script brake calipers.

The vehicle includes multiple keys, tools, car cover, seat covers, owners' manuals, original window sticker, and battery tender.

With 9,269 miles since new, this 'Gated' 6-Speed Manual Lamborghini Murcielago is destined to be a future-classic for enthusiasts and collectors.

THE 911 GT3 TOURING

The Porsche 911 GT3 Touring stands as a paragon of motorsport-derived purity infused with gentlemanly sophistication, echoing the enduring legacy of the 911 lineage. Tracing its performance roots to the prodigious GT3 models developed by Porsche's Motorsport division, the Touring Package brings a distinct ethos—less ostentation, more soul—by eschewing the brawny aerodynamics for a stealthier approach to street dynamics. Where winged aggression gives way to sleek subtlety, the GT3 Touring recalls classic 911 traditions, yet advances them for the modern enthusiast seeking mechanical engagement without theatrical flourish.

Introduced with the 991 generation in 2017 and further evolved for the 992 platform, the GT3 Touring has been revered among collectors and purists alike as the enthusiast's choice for daily thrill and long-haul adventure. By pairing the same naturally-aspirated, high-revving 4.0-liter flat-six as its track-bred sibling with a mandatory manual transmission, the Touring channels Porsche's storied history of analog driving pleasure. The intrepid GT department in Weissach engineered the GT3's heart to spin to 9,000rpm, producing crystalline power while delivering aural poetry—an engine that balances breathtaking velocity with daily usability.

Visually, the Touring distinguishes itself with restrained elegance. It forgoes the GT3's signature fixed rear wing in favor of a more traditional and automatically deploying decklid spoiler, while unique badging, bespoke trim, and subtle detail changes further emphasize its under-the-radar bearing. Inside, the ambiance is equally bespoke, offering options through Exclusive Manufaktur that harken to Porsche's craftsman roots—fine hides, distinctive stitching, and tailored finishes available only to the most discerning clients.

Acclaimed by road testers and coveted by collectors, the GT3 Touring is not just a spirited grand tourer; it represents a spiritual return to the soul of Porsche, before turbocharging and electronic intervention remade the sports car landscape. Its purist recipe—manual gearbox, rear-drive, naturally aspirated power—epitomizes tactile engagement and the enduring allure of mechanical artistry.

Each Touring, especially those specified with rare colorways and advanced options, is celebrated for its scarcity, timeless design, and collectability. Sentiments among Porsche cognoscenti place the Touring firmly among the most desired "driver's 911s," transcending mere performance numbers with its blend of balanced dynamics and old-world charm. In today's market, the specification and provenance of individual examples matters more than ever, with delivery-mile, highly optioned cars commanding top collector interest.

Above all, the GT3 Touring is an exercise in restraint: a high-water mark for driving purity, perfectly channeling the spirit of the original 911S and Carrera RS, while providing modern comfort, technology, and reliability. Its ability to stand equally at home on both city streets and alpine passes ensures its enduring legacy as one of the definitive sports cars of the 21st century.


THE CAR OFFERED

Delivered new to Porsche Fort Myers and constructed at Zuffenhausen, VIN. WP0AC2A93TS287668 is an extraordinary illustration of Porsche's ability to fuse performance mastery with bespoke luxury—a true collector's dream and, arguably, the most desirable specification of the breed.

This example is distinguished by its Slate Grey Neo exterior finish, a color that nods to Porsche's heritage while showcasing contemporary depth and subtlety. Inside, the Exclusive Manufaktur program has been exercised to striking effect, specifying the interior in sumptuous Guards Red leather—a bold yet classic choice complemented by Neo Exclusive Manufaktur accents. The resultant combination is both visually arresting and deeply evocative, a nod to vintage era sports cars and a celebration of Porsche's modern palette.

True to the Touring ethos, this GT3 is fitted with the enthusiast-preferred 6-speed manual transmission. Rarely seen, rear seats have been optioned, broadening the car's practicality while remaining cohesive with its luxurious and bespoke cabin.

Among its significant options, this GT3 boasts a suite of performance and aesthetic enhancements. Porsche Ceramic Composite Brakes (PCCB) provide exceptional fade resistance and confidence, with calipers finished in high-gloss black. The sought-after front axle lift system ensures that driveways and steep aprons are navigated with ease and grace. An exclusive design taillight and carefully curated detail touches further enhance its individual character.

As a highly optioned, extremely low-mileage 2026 Porsche 911 GT3 Touring, this example exemplifies everything that defines the GT3 legend—track-derived performance, timeless style, and the immersive reward of an unfiltered driving experience. Whether destined for a curated collection or reserved for a connoisseur's open road enjoyment, this rare Slate Grey Neo over Guards Red Exclusive Manufaktur GT3 Touring embodies the very best of Porsche's modern era.

historical_significance: Iconic status in American sports car racing
description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1958 DESCRIPTION:
• Delivered new in the USA
• Restored extensively 2015-2017 (bills available)
• Rare factory hardtop included
• Tastefully modified for Historic rallies
• Long-term ownership since 1999

In 1952 Porsche constructed a trial batch of 15 roadsters at the behest of US importer Max Hoffman, who had persuaded the German manufacturer of the potential for a 'cut-price' entry-level model that would appeal to the North American market. The roadsters' successful reception in the USA led to the introduction of the Speedster model in 1954; in effect, an 'economy' model intended to compete with the cheaper British sports cars.

Stripped of all unnecessary amenities - even the heater was optional - the Speedster established a formidable presence on both the road and in the burgeoning American sports car racing scene. Its combination of style, performance and value for money made the Speedster deservedly popular, and today this most handsome of the 356 variants enjoys iconic status.

Chassis number '84070' was delivered new to the USA and first registered on 1st July 1958. The car was comprehensively restored during 2015-2017 and comes with invoices totalling approximately €120,000, testifying to the rebuild's extensive scope.

When purchased by the current owner in 1999, the car had an older restoration and was used frequently for rallies across Europe. In 2015 to facilitate its restoration the body was mounted on a straightening jig to make subsequent work easier and ensure exact gap dimensions. The body was then immersed in a KTL sealing bath.

A recent third party test protocol states that the engine has been comprehensively overhauled and that it starts easily and runs well, while the gearbox has been exchanged for a reconditioned unit and reportedly shifts smoothly.

Additionally, the car is equipped with a roll-bar and a twin-pipe exhaust system. An OMP fire extinguisher is installed in the space provided for the rear seat, and OMP seatbelts are installed.

Further to emphasise the Speedster's sporty character, the bumpers were removed, the headlights fitted with protective grilles, and fog lights installed. The speedometer and rev counter are highlighted in green. In addition, an oil temperature gauge is installed beneath the dashboard, and a daily odometer on the right-hand side. The steering wheel is a three-spoke wooden item.

The current owner has attended various historic rallies with the Speedster, which has been used sparingly since 2017. The car comes with German registration documents; a third party condition report by Franc Gourge at KFZ-Sachverständige; a rare factory hardtop; and the aforementioned restoration invoices.

Now recognised as representing a 'Golden Age' for Chevrolet's Corvette sports car, the Sting Ray version was manufactured from 1963 to 1967 and has since gone on to become a highly collectible modern classic. The first 'Split Window' model lasted for only one year, a single-piece rear screen becoming the norm thereafter, and is considered one of the most desirable of Corvette variants. A little over 21,000 Sting Rays were made in 1963, the production split being roughly 50/50 coupé/convertible. And, as is the case with most American cars of this period, the Corvette buyer could choose from a host of factory options with the result that seldom are two cars exactly alike.

The current owner imported this 'Split Window' model from the USA into Sweden in 2013, since when he has installed air conditioning and serviced the driveshaft, brakes and rear axle. Finished in light blue metallic with black interior, the Corvette is described by the private vendor as in generally good condition, though there is some slight damage visible in the right front wheelarch. There are some documents with the car, but nothing that states it has been restored; according to our vendor, the paint has not been measured but could possibly be original. The car is registered in Sweden and comes with Swedish registration documents.

historical_significance: One of the world's most exclusive automobiles
description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1953 DESCRIPTION:
• Very rare and beautiful example
• Matching engine
• Restored in 2020

More expensive than the 300 SL sports car and almost double the price of the contemporary top-of-the-range Cadillac, the Mercedes-Benz 300S was one of the world's most exclusive automobiles. Elegantly styled in the pre-war manner yet technologically bang up to date, the 300S was built to the Stuttgart firm's uncompromising quality standards. Inevitably, production was limited, only 760 examples of the 300S/Sc (560/200) leaving the factory between 1951 and 1958.

The 300S (Super) was a short-wheelbase derivative of the 300 saloon, one of Mercedes-Benz's first all-new designs of the post-war era, which had debuted at the Frankfurt Auto Show in 1951. The 300's arrival re-established Mercedes-Benz in the front rank of prestige car manufacturers, marking as it did a return to the marque's tradition of building high-performance luxury automobiles of the finest quality.

The 300's cross-braced, oval-tube chassis followed the lines of the 170S and 220, boasting independent suspension all round, but incorporated the added refinements of hypoid bevel final drive, dynamically balanced wheels, and remote control of the rear suspension ride height. Initially developing 115bhp, the 3.0-litre, overhead-camshaft, six-cylinder engine was also used in fuel-injected form in the 300 SL sports car. Custom built by Mercedes-Benz's most experienced craftsmen, the Mercedes-Benz 300 was luxuriously appointed and trimmed with materials of the highest quality.

Introduced at the Paris Salon in October 1951 and built in coupé and cabriolet forms on a shortened 300 saloon chassis, the 300S succeeded in recapturing all the elegance of the pre-war 540K. Today the 300S is among the most sought after of post-war Mercedes-Benz automobiles.

This 300S Cabriolet was restored in 2020 and comes with numerous photographs relating to the rebuild. Finished in blue with a beige leather interior, this Mercedes breaths elegance and style. The engine runs very smooth and the bodywork and interior are in a nice and good condition. Accompanying documentation consists of history files (dating back 30 years), an old-style logbook and a 'daten karte'. The car also comes with a tool kit and a Dutch registration.

Aston Martin's periodic revival of the Lagonda name saw it applied to a stretched, four-door AM V8 in the mid 1970s: the Series 1, a mere handful of which was constructed. When the concept re-emerged it was the sensation of the 1976 London Motor Show. Clothed in striking 'razor edge' bodywork by William Towns, the new Lagonda Series 2 saloon used the same long-wheelbase V8 chassis as its immediate predecessor while breaking new ground in terms of electronic instrumentation and switchgear. Problems with the latter would delay production until April 1978, by which time a less radical design had been adopted. The interior though, was every bit as luxurious as the exterior was futuristic, featuring selected Connolly hides, Wilton carpeting and walnut veneer, all hand-finished by skilled craftsmen in the Aston Martin tradition. Manufacture ceased in 1989 after 645 production cars had been built.

This left-hand drive Lagonda has been owned by the same family for over 25 years. Regularly serviced and presented in good overall cosmetic condition (the digital instrumentation is working), the engine starts and the gears are shifting smoothly. Finished in dark red with cream leather interior (in good condition), it comes with a Lagonda owner's handbook, expired French contrôle technique, French carte grise and a file of invoices for maintenance work.

provenance: Umberto Martinozzi, Giorgio Marcella, Maurizio Rometti
description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1966 DESCRIPTION:
• Delivered new to Rome, Italy
• One of 460 Series II cars
• Highly original and unrestored
• Matching numbers (chassis & engine)

Introduced in January 1964, the 330 GT 2+2 was the second of Ferrari's four-seater road cars, following the 250 GTE 2+2. Pininfarina was once again entrusted with the styling, adopting a four-headlamp frontal treatment that reflected the tastes of Ferrari's most important export market, the USA. The 330 GT's tubular chassis was 50mm longer in the wheelbase than before, which made conditions less cramped for the rear passengers, while improvements to the discs-all-round braking system saw separate hydraulic circuits adopted for front and rear.

Displacing 3,967cc, the single-overhead-camshaft, all-alloy V12 engine was good for 300-plus horsepower, an output sufficient to propel the 330 GT to a maximum velocity of 152mph (245km/h) making it, when introduced, the fastest road-going Ferrari. Equipped at first with a four-speeds-plus-overdrive gearbox, the 330 GT gained a five-speed transmission mid-1965 and later that year had its four-headlight front end replaced by a two-lamp arrangement, these later cars being known as the 'Series II'. By the time production ceased in 1967, Ferrari had built 1,088 330 GTs, of which 460 were to Series II specification.

This desirable two-headlamp Series II was delivered new in Rome, Italy on 12th February 1966 and registered to one Umberto Martinozzi, as recorded in the accompanying Carta di Circolazione and Foglio Complementare. On 12th May 1967 the Ferrari was sold to Giorgio Marcella in Rome, and at the end of 1968 was acquired by another Roman resident, Maurizio Rometti. The car's subsequent ownership history is not known prior to the current owner's acquisition two years ago. A highly original example, unusual in so far as it has never been restored, '8023' retains its matching engine, original metallic grey paintwork, and original light blue leather interior.

In addition to the aforementioned documents, the Ferrari also comes with its old Roman license plates. The car is not currently registered and is sold without a technical inspection. A wonderful opportunity to acquire a highly original example of this landmark Ferrari Gran Turismo, delivered new to Rome, which undoubtedly forms the basis of a beautiful restoration project.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1966 DESCRIPTION:
• One of only ca. 27 DS 21 'Majesty' models built by Henri Chapron
• Rare internal division
• Directly commissioned from Henri Chapron by Simone Fournier
• Long-standing ownership within the Chapron family
• No-expense-spared restoration

"Perhaps France's most prolific coachbuilders, Henri Chapron's label epitomized the classic style of body design through several generations, evolving at the same pace as popular taste – often in the vanguard, but careful never to be ahead of his time." - The Beaulieu Encyclopedia of the Automobile – Coachbuilding.

Today, the name of Henri Chapron is forever associated with his sublime soft-tops on the Citroën DS platform. Chapron's interpretations of the Citroën DS and ID were quite different from the regular production versions. Chapron added fins to the rear wing tops of Citroëns as early as 1965 and launched his own version of an upmarket DS at the Porte de Versailles Salon de l'Auto in October 1964 using the name 'Majesty'. Its purpose was to satisfy the few customers who considered the upmarket DS Prestige insufficiently exclusive, although that too was built by Chapron for Citroën. The Majesty featured a higher and more angular roofline compared to the factory DS, similar to the 'Concorde' coach, affording increased headroom for the rear passengers and greater interior space. This limited edition model was produced up to 1969, with only 27 examples being built in total.

A masterpiece of French automotive craftsmanship, this 1966 Citroën DS 21 Majesty saloon is one of the ca. 27 meticulously handcrafted by the legendary Parisian coachbuilder, Henri Chapron. Commissioned in July 1966 by Madame Simone Fournier directly from her son-in-law, Henri Chapron, the car was delivered on 10th November 1966 and first registered in Paris on 15th November 1966, with the license plate '6535 TM 75'. The Chapron family owned this car for many years, underscoring its exceptional provenance.

This Majesty boasts an elegant blue paint finish and a stylish interior trimmed in beige leather and fabric, while the partition separating the chauffeur's compartment is both rare and particularly desirable. The car has undergone a compprehensive restoration, carried out at huge expense and with uncompromising attention to detail. It is reported that all major mechanical components have been overhauled for maximum reliability.

With only four owners since delivery and a Certificate of Authenticity issued by Madame Noëlle Chapron, this Majesty represents a unique opportunity to acquire a Chapron masterpiece with a direct connection to the renowned French coachbuilder. French registered and offered with extensive documentation, this one-of-a-kind car affords an unparalleled combination of exclusivity, design heritage and historical significance: a rare opportunity for discerning collectors of French automotive art.

André Citroën's brainchild, the 'Traction Avant' broke new ground in almost every aspect of automobile engineering on its launch in 1934. Unitary construction of the body/chassis; front-wheel drive; all-independent suspension sprung by torsion bars; hydraulic brakes; synchromesh gears; and a four-cylinder, overhead-valve, wet-liner engine were all incorporated in the newcomer at a time when most of its rivals employed a separate chassis, cart springs, sidevalve engines, and mechanical brakes.

Fervent admirer of the model, having owned several, Pierre Strinati purchased this Traction Avant on 17th October 1961 for CHF900 (receipt on file). On 6th March 1972 a major service was undertaken costing CHF1,260.95, during which the electrical system was checked and the valve timing adjusted. Later that same month, repairs were made to the right rear door and wing; the repaired areas were repainted, as were the sills and wheels, while the bumpers were sent away to be re-chromed.

We believe that the 89,692 kilometres odometer reading could very well be correct as the car is in a remarkable state of preservation and retains its original interior. It comes with its original radiator shield and grilles for winter driving, together with some original instruction manuals, service books, old insurance cards, tax receipts, sundry bills, old Swiss registration papers, and a copy of Citroën Traction Avant Gold Portfolio. Recommissioning will be required following a lengthy period of inactivity.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 2006 DESCRIPTION:
• One-off colour, rare and exclusive Dutch supercar
• The very first built customer right-hand drive C8 Spyder
• Only 73 miles recorded from new
• Audi S8 engine instead of A8
• Recent fuel tank and timing belt services (bills available)
• German title

The Spijker company started out as coachbuilders in Amsterdam before constructing its first automobile in 1898. Spijker was technologically adventurous, introducing the first six-cylinder car with four-wheel drive and all-round brakes in 1903, by which time the name had changed to the more internationally acceptable 'Spyker'.
Despite a reputation for quality and the achievement of some notable competition successes, the original Spyker company disappeared in 1925. Its name and reputation for producing well-engineered, high-performance motor cars had not been forgotten though, and an entirely new Spyker possessing the same goals emerged with the Spyker C8, which debuted at the Birmingham International Motor Show in October 2000.

An advanced, mid-engined, two-seat barchetta, the C8 Spyder was powered by a 4.2-litre Audi V8 engine producing approximately 400bhp, and had a top speed of around 300km/h (186mph). Despite its 'new kid on the block' status, Spyker succeeded in establishing a strong presence in the supercar market. Indeed, the C8 won instant acclaim, receiving the Institute of Vehicle Engineers Design Award soon after its introduction. In 2002 the first competition version, the C8 Double12R endurance racer, was entered by the Spyker Squadron factory racing team at Le Mans. On 14th July 2005, it was announced that the C8 was approved for sale on the United States market.

Finished in striking one-off Lamborghini Balloon White with Ruby Red leather interior, this Spyker C8 Spyder was registered new in the Netherlands by Spyker Factory and retained by them until it was acquired in 2023 by Jasper den Dopper, a well-known Spyker specialist and marque authority. The car has since formed part of his private collection, where it has been preserved with exceptional care and attention to originality.

The very first built customer right-hand drive C8 Spyder, this car is understood to be the lowest-mileage RHD example in existence, having covered a trifling 73 miles from new. Boasting the more powerful Audi S8 V8 engine rather than the A8 power unit, it also features a number of desirable factory upgrades, including 19" wheels, quilted leather upholstery, and the distinctive 'propeller' steering wheel.

Importantly, the car has recently been inspected and prepared by Jasper den Dopper himself, ensuring that it meets the exacting standards expected of such a rare and significant Spyker. As one would expect of a little-used and carefully maintained example, the Spyder can be described as pristine and almost perfect, with engine and transmission described as 'like new'. It also benefits from a recent fuel tank service and timing belt service, with related bills available.

Offered with a Certificate of Conformity and German title, this remarkable Spyker C8 Spyder represents a unique opportunity to acquire an ultra-low mileage, early right-hand drive example with outstanding provenance, specialist care, and unquestionable collector appeal—ready to be enjoyed on the road or admired as part of a world-class private collection.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1952 DESCRIPTION:
• One of only five long-wheelbase models produced
• Original SS-specification engine with three Carburettors
• Factory-correct colour combination
• Sold in the USA
• Well documented ownership history
• Correspondence from Carlo Felice Bianchi Anderloni on file
• Carefully restored by marque specialists in the 2000s

According to 1989 correspondence on file from Carlo Felice Bianchi Anderloni, former CEO of Touring Superleggera, this 'Experimental Sport Series Type IV, triple-carburettor touring (long) chassis 918100' was completed on 15th April 1952 finished in grey with a blue leather interior and matching convertible top. This car is one of only five long-wheelbase 6C 2500 models produced, of which only two or three survive. Alfa Romeo Classiche's Certificato di Origine is on file.

Shortly after completion, the car was purchased new by James Omar Radford of Abilene, Texas. A millionaire heir to a thriving wholesale grocery and real estate business, Radford spent most of his time in Hollywood working as a film producer. A few years later, this remarkable Alfa Romeo Cabriolet passed to the famous American architect, William Kesling.

The next recorded owner (from 1972) was L H 'Bud' Von Nordheim of National City, California. Records indicate that Von Nordheim carefully maintained the Alfa until August 1979. The car was then left on his property in a state of partial restoration until it was rescued in 1987 by Alfa Romeo enthusiast David Skora of Escondido, California. Photographs on file show that the car had been repainted several times since 1952 while retaining much of its original interior under a light-coloured top. A set of Borrani wire wheels had been fitted (preserved by subsequent owners to the present day).

Bruce Robertson of Lake Forest, Illinois found this 6C 2500 Cabriolet in 1997 in the middle of a restoration commissioned by Skora. Robertson ensured that it was returned to the factory-correct colour combination and completed to the highest standards by Eric Roseneau. The car left Roseneau in 2003 and immediately claimed awards for 'Best Alfa Romeo' and 'Best of Show' at the Detroit Concorso d'Italia. Robertson later exhibited this beautiful car at the Amelia Island Concours d'Elegance and various local events near Chicago, before selling it to Oscar Davis in 2008.

With superbly elegant lines, this is undoubtedly one of the most desirable variants of the Alfa Romeo 6C 2500 with exclusive coachwork by Touring. It even comes with correspondence with the great Sig. Anderloni himself and will surely to be welcomed at the world's most prestigious concours events. The car is offered with a history file and comes with a US-title. All EU-taxes have been paid.

historical_significance: Represents a rare and fascinating chapter in the sporting history of the Prancing Horse in the United States.
description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1990 DESCRIPTION:
• A genuine racing prototype built around the Ferrari V8 engine
• Highly original and extremely competitive
• Constructed by the late and renowned Joe Huffaker
• Originally commissioned by Paul Newman's racing associate, Bill Freeman
• Campaigned by its current owner in the Ultimate Cup Series in 2020 and 2021
• Approximately 390 bhp at 9,200 rpm for a weight of around 900 kg

Joe Huffaker (1927–2022) began building racing cars as early as the 1940s, before launching his professional career through a partnership with BMC following the competition success of his Austin-Healey 'Huffaker Special'. He subsequently produced a series of Genie sports cars powered by American V8 engines. In 1963, Huffaker entered the Indianapolis 500 under the MG banner.

The 1970s and 1980s proved particularly successful for Huffaker-prepared MG, Austin-Healey, Jaguar and Triumph models, with victories across the Can-Am, IMSA, SCCA and Trans-Am championships. Most notably, the Huffaker-prepared Pontiac Fieros achieved outstanding results in IMSA GTU, with Bob Earl securing ten victories and sixteen pole positions during the 1985 season alone.

Although the Ferrari 308 GTB was never conceived as a competition car, its inherent qualities were undeniable and quickly attracted the attention of independent constructors, most famously Michelotto. His Group 4 version enjoyed considerable success in rallying throughout Europe.

In the United States, Bill Freeman—close friend and racing associate of Paul Newman—identified the potential of the 308 and entered it into IMSA competition in the GTU category. Accordingly, in 1990, three cars were commissioned from Huffaker Motorsport by Newman Freeman Racing and CEO for the 1991 season. Built on tubular chassis derived from IndyCar technology, these 308s featured inboard pushrod suspension, Alcon brake calipers acting on 13-inch discs supplied by Coleman Racing Products, and 16-inch centre-lock BBS wheels. Pneumatic jacks enabled rapid lifting during pit stops.

Mechanically, the 3.0-litre quad-cam V8 was extensively reworked by Bill Pound Automotive, with the front of the block shortened to allow longitudinal rear mounting. The water pump was relocated, while the timing system was redesigned to accept Testarossa belts and adjustable pulleys. Custom-made camshafts were fitted, along with strengthened forged pistons and connecting rods. The 16 valves were optimised for both intake and exhaust, with titanium valve seats. Fuel injection was supplied by Hilborn components, managed by an EFI Technology control unit that also governed ignition for maximum efficiency. Lubrication was provided by a Weaver Bros dry-sump system. Producing approximately 390 bhp at 9,600 rpm, the engine was mated to a rear-mounted Hewland DGB five-speed gearbox.

The car was clothed in a composite body by Italian Design and Racing, echoing the styling cues of the Ferrari 288 GTO.

Unfortunately, changes to IMSA GTU regulations in 1991 prematurely ended the competitive career of the 308 GTB Huffaker. Built in just three examples, it saw only limited competition thereafter in SCCA GT2.

Chassis 003 arrived in France in 2008 after appearing at the Cavallino Classic in Monterey. Acquired by its current owner in 2017, it underwent a comprehensive overhaul in 2019 at Sébastien Darnand Moteur, including replacement of all four wheel bearings, fluid services and timing belts, as well as the installation of an automatic fire-extinguishing system. Since then, it has been driven by its owner at the 2019 Classic Days at Le Mans and in the Ultimate Cup Series at Dijon (2020) and Magny-Cours (2021).

Today, remarkably authentic and spared the excesses of prolonged competition, this Huffaker-Ferrari 308 GTB IMSA GTU represents a rare and fascinating chapter in the sporting history of the Prancing Horse in the United States. It would stand out in any marque-focused collection and is equally well suited to historic racing events or track days.

As a race car, it will be sold without a title but with accompanying invoices.

That a major US manufacturer could come up with such an exciting concept car was startling enough, but Chrysler's decision to put the Viper into production was nothing short of astonishing. Inspired, as its name suggests, by the legendary Cobra, Tom Gale's design study made its auto-show debut in 1989, its appearance triggering an avalanche of deposit cheques. Without doubt, a large part of the Viper's 'back to basics' appeal stemmed from its unique selling point: a massively powerful 8.0-litre V10 engine. Despite being relatively 'low-tech', the Lamborghini-developed pushrod V10 churned out 400bhp and a brutal 450lb/ft of torque, good enough for a 0-100 km/h time of 4.7 seconds and a top speed of 265 km/h. Early Vipers lack modern driver aids such as traction control and anti-lock brakes. Early cars also have the rear antenna mounted visible.

This Dodge Viper RT/10 is one of 285 produced for the 1992 model year. Formerly registered in Florida, it was imported into the EU in 2025 and currently displays a total of only 9,000 miles on the odometer. No accidents or other damage are mentioned in the Carfax report, and the car also comes with US title/registration documents and proof of EU duty paid. Reportedly, the brake pads, battery and fuel pump were replaced in 2024, and it should be noted that the car comes freshly serviced in 2026.

Introduced at the Frankfurt Auto Show in April 1951, the Mercedes-Benz 220 was in effect a six-cylinder cousin to the four-cylinder 170S on the same 2,845mm-wheelbase chassis. Although closely based on the 170S, the 220 featured more modern styling with headlamps integrated into the wings. With 80bhp on tap courtesy of its 2.2-litre overhead-camshaft engine, delivered via a four-speed manual gearbox, the 220 saloon was good for a top speed of around 140km/h (87mph) - as was the Cabriolet B - with 145km/h (90mph) attainable by the Cabriolet A drophead coupé. In the best Mercedes-Benz tradition, both of these convertible models were exceptionally well equipped. Combined Cabriolet A/B production amounted to only 2,360 units in five years, 997 of which were the Cabriolet B version, as seen here. Today these exclusive models are both rare and highly sought after.

This particular Mercedes-Benz Cabriolet B was purchased by the current owner at a French auction in November 1994. The Mercedes has been serviced regularly by local specialists in France. Presented in nice condition both inside and out, the car comes with invoices for works and maintenance; the 1994 bill of sale; a French Carte Grise; an up-to-date Contrôle Technique; and an expertise report.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1971 DESCRIPTION:
• Matching numbers chassis and engine
• One of 500 built
• An interesting recommissioning project

A rare model with a short career that formed the joint between the 365 GT 2+2 and the 365 GT4 2+2, the 365 GTC/4 was unveiled at the Geneva Motor Show in 1971. Contemporary to the revered "Daytona", the 365 GTC /4 used an identical chassis and a wet-sump version of the 4,390cc four-overhead-cam V12 of this one with slightly lower power – 320bhp – mated to a conventional five-speed gearbox, instead. of the "Daytona" transaxle. The cylinder head had been modified to accommodate horizontal carburettors and had enabled coachbuilder Pininfarina to achieve an elegant and low bonnet line. "Discreet, sober and elegant as a whole, with subtleties that can be appreciated by contemplating it attentively. You could say this is a Ferrari dedicated to the discerning enthusiast," wrote Road & Track.

Overall more civilized and easier to drive than the heavy Daytona, the speedy 365 GTC/4 received ZF power steering and power-assisted brakes as standard, optional air conditioning and a particularly luxurious interior, equipped with individual folding seats in the front and booster seats in the rear. Despite increased refinement, the 365 GTC/4 was no match for its competitors in terms of performance, beating the 400m from a standing start in under 16 seconds with a top speed of over 240 km/h. When the model was discontinued in October 1972, production totaled only 500 examples, making it a particularly desirable model today.

Chassis 14545 left the factory on September 29, 1971 and was delivered new by the French importer Charles Pozzi on November 2 of the same year. Painted in Argento Auteuil Metalizzato and fitted with a black leather and gray plaid interior, this elegant 365 was maintained during its first years by the Levallois workshop. It later spent part of its life in Alsace, maintained by Internationale Automobile S.A. In 2002, 14545 was acquired by Thor Johannessen, near Cahors and thus integrated one of the most important French collections of the 2000s. It was in 2011 that its last private owner acquired it.

Since then, it was exhibited in its owner's private museum, this 365 GTC/4 is largely in original condition. Of course, it retains its original engine number 00026 corresponding to the Ferrari Pozzi identification plate. Its Weber carburettors also display serial numbers close to each other. The passenger compartment has a pleasant patina typical of the leathers used by Ferrari in the early 1970s.

Following several years of static display, this 365 GTC/4 represents an interesting project. Recommissioning will therefore be required, as the car has not been driven since 2023. In particular, bodywork repairs will be necessary to the underbody areas, as time and oxidation have affected certain sections of the chassis.

Sold with its French registration document as well as its user manual and spare parts catalogue, this 365 represents a rare opportunity to acquire one of the least produced road-going Ferraris.

Please note that Bonhams has an ownership interest in this Lot.

YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1961 DESCRIPTION:
• One of only 217 cars built
• In an Italian private collection 2009-2021

To fully exploit the Giulietta's competition potential, Alfa Romeo knew that lighter and more aerodynamic bodywork would be necessary, a requirement which resulted in the ultimate Giuliettas: Bertone's Sprint Special and the Sprint Zagato, both built on the short-wheelbase Spider platform and powered by the 100bhp version of Alfa's classic, 1,290cc, twin-cam four. Conceived as an out-and-out competition car, the Sprint Zagato coupé employed lightweight aluminium-alloy coachwork and demonstrated its designer's commitment to weight saving in every detail, tipping the scales at an astonishing 770kg. With a top speed of around 200km/h the SZ was easily the fastest of the Giuliettas, and even today there are few 1.3-litre cars capable of matching this level of performance. The SZ's inherent stability and instantaneous response to steering input made it a driver's car par excellence. On the racetrack it proved virtually unbeatable, and the Sprint Zagato remains a major force to be reckoned with in Historic motor sport, being eligible for a wide variety of prestigious events.

Two series of Sprint Zagato were produced between 1959 and 1962, the second series (SZ2) cars being distinguishable by a redesigned, larger and more aerodynamically efficient body incorporating a 'sawn off' Kamm-type tail, a feature which gave rise to the model's Coda Tronca sobriquet (the first series became known as the Coda Tonda – Round Tail). Under the skin the new SZ remained much as before apart from the welcome incorporation of Girling front disc brakes. SZ chassis numbers ran from '001' to '217', a total of 217 cars, an estimated 44 of which were the later SZ2 Coda Tronca version.

The Alfa Romeo factory records indicate that the car was produced on 29 March 1961 in the colour "Bianco Gardenia" (the same as today), and according to The Italian Car Registry by John de Boer, this delightful SZ Coda Tonda was delivered new on 10 April 1961 to Alfa Romeo in Lugano, Switzerland. In 2009 it was purchased by a very well-known collector in Italy and remained in his private collection until 2021 when it was purchased for his private collection by our vendor, another noted collector based near Milan. Only recently the car benefited from restoration of the bodywork and paint, while the interior showcases the roll bar and lovely Zagato seats in black vinyl. The car will be offered for sale with Italian registration documents and a valid Italian Revisione (roadworthiness certificate).

A very rare Alfa Romeo with the lively Giulietta twin-cam engine and lightweight coachwork by Zagato, this little sports car ticks all the right boxes and is eligible for numerous events worldwide.

This Jowett Jupiter was registered new in the UK as 'JAK 592' on 1st December 1952, at which time it was painted British Racing Green. The Jupiter was first registered to the Jowett Car Co and then to one Leonard Chambers of Surrey in January 1953. From June 1961 it was owned by one J Batt of London, and from 24th October 1962 by Richard Hamlett of Reading, Berkshire. On 3rd October 1966 Mr Hamlett sold the Jowett to Mr Strinati, who imported it into Switzerland. Mr Strinati paid CHF 3,000 (purchase receipt on file). Mr Strinati had owned a new 1951 Jupiter with unique Ghia coachwork, given to him by his father. Information on how to maintain those cars was scarce, so he sold the Jupiter but later regretted it, hence his acquisition of this example (the unique Ghia was undoubtedly destroyed).

The Jowett sat unused until December 1993 when Mr Strinati had it restored by Geneva BMW specialists Pius Buch SA. The engine was rebuilt and the bodywork and hood were redone. The car has rarely been used since the restoration and still appears quite fresh. Nevertheless, recommissioning will be required following a period of inactivity. The car comes with various instruction manuals and plentiful correspondence with the Jowett Car Club. One of the all-time great sports cars, the 356 was the work of Ferry Porsche, who had been inspired by the FIAT-based Cisitalias of Piero Dusio. Ferry's 356 was based on the Volkswagen designed by his father, and like the immortal 'Beetle' employed a platform-type chassis with rear-mounted air-cooled engine and all-independent torsion-bar suspension. Introduced in 1948, the Porsche 356 set a new standard for small sports cars and proved adaptable to all forms of motor sport including circuit racing and rallying. In 1951 a works car finished first in the 1,100cc class at the Le Mans 24-Hour Race, thus beginning the marque's long and illustrious association with La Sarthe.

Cabriolets had been manufactured right from the start of 356 production, but the first open Porsche to make a significant impact was the Speedster, introduced in 1954 following the successful reception in the USA of a batch of 15 special roadsters. The Reutter-bodied Speedster was dropped in 1958 and replaced by the more civilised Convertible D, which differed principally by virtue of its larger windscreen and winding side windows. Porsche sub-contracted soft-top body construction to a number of different coachbuilders, predominantly Glaser and Reutter in the early years, while production of the Convertible D (now renamed 'Roadster') was undertaken by Drauz of Heilbronn and later d'Ieteren of Brussels. Reutter was predominantly responsible for the Coupé and Cabriolet.

By the time the 356B arrived in September 1959, the car had gained a one-piece rounded windscreen and 15"-diameter wheels, and the newcomer's introduction brought with it further styling revisions. The engine, now standardised at 1,600cc, was available in three different stages of tune, the most powerful - apart from the four-cam Carrera - being the 90bhp unit of the Super 90. The 356B represents significant advances in drive-ability and comfort over earlier 356 models and is a pleasingly quick way to enjoy the traditional Porsche values of quality, reliability and mechanical robustness.

According to the accompanying Porsche Certificate of Authenticity (issued by Porsche Spain), this beautifully presented 356B Cabriolet was delivered new in October 1961 to the historic Porsche dealer Max Moritz in Reutlingen (the first Porsche dealer in the world). The original colour combination was Champagne with a green leather interior. Other options listed are additional rear springs, a telescopic aerial, two loudspeakers and a self-dimming rear view mirror.

Since 2009 this car has formed part of a private collection in Spain and presents very well indeed. During restoration the car's colours were changed to the period-correct and equally beautiful silver metallic with a red leather interior and black hood. Accompanying paperwork includes copies of the Spanish registration papers; current German registration papers; the aforementioned Porsche CoA; and an expert's report confirming the car's generally very good condition.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1940 DESCRIPTION:
Exceptional autograph album containing more than 70 signatures from Formula 1 drivers and leading figures of European and international endurance racing from the 1940s to the 1960s. This unique document stands as a rare testament to the golden age of motor racing and the birth of the Formula 1 World Championship, at a time when drivers could still be met informally in the paddock.

Among the identified signatures are:

Belgian drivers:
Johnny Claes, Émile Cornet (winner of the 1949 Grand Prix des Frontières and Formula 1 driver), André Pilette, Charles de Tornaco, Adrien Scheid, Georges Berger, André Milhoux.

World Champions and Formula 1 legends:
Alberto Ascari (World Champion 1952 and 1953), Giuseppe Farina (the first Formula 1 World Champion), Juan Manuel Fangio (World Champion 1951, 1954–1957), Mike Hawthorn (the first British Formula 1 World Champion), Sir Stirling Moss (16 Grand Prix victories), Peter Collins.

Ferrari and Maserati drivers:
Luigi Villoresi, Franco Cortese, Maurice Trintignant, Harry Schell, Jean Behra, Peter Walker, Roy Salvadori.

24 Hours of Le Mans competitors:
Paul Frère, Alan Rippon, John Laurence, Richard von Frankenberg, Alain de Changy.

Other notable drivers:
Roberto Vallone, Amédée Gordini, Roger Laurent, Louis Rosier, José Froilán González, Jack Fairman, Dan Gurney, Hugh Mackay Fraser, John Fitch, Alan Brown, Lex Beels, Horace Gould, Guy Gale, Ivor Bueb, and many others.

Several pages also feature handwritten notes or local inscriptions, making this album far more than a collector's item: a vivid historical record of European motor racing.

The autographs are contained in a dedicated oblong leather-bound album.
Dimensions: 14 × 9 cm.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1962 DESCRIPTION:
• Two owners from new
• Delivered new in France
• 6.2-litre Chrysler V8 engine
• Desirable manual gearbox
• Very important history file
• Valid French Contrôle Technique

"The HK500 was the most interesting car we ever made but the Facel II was the best. It was totally elegant." – Jean Daninos.

During its short existence, Facel built nearly 2,900 cars, all assembled by hand and all intended for a select clientele, including Tony Curtis, Ringo Starr, Ava Gardner, Stirling Moss and Maurice Trintignant.

Facel, founded in December 1939 as a subsidiary of Bronzavia (a supplier grisof military aeronautical equipment), merged with Métallon after the Second World War and began producing bodywork for Panhard, Simca and Ford before becoming an independent car manufacturer. After the war, despite regulations that had caused the last French luxury car manufacturers to disappear, Jean Daninos decided to pursue his project to build a luxury saloon car in France: the Vega. Unable to find a suitable engine in France, Daninos turned to the United States and retained this option for all his models. The first improvements to the FV were not long in coming, and the FV1 launched in March 1955 featured a longer wheelbase and a 4.8-litre Chrysler V8 engine. In 1957, an improved model appeared, the HK 500, equipped with the latest version of the 5.9-litre Chrysler V8, capable of reaching 225 km/h, reaching 100 km/h in less than 9 seconds and delivering 360 horsepower.

Launched in 1961, the Facel II was to be the last model with a V8 engine. During a test drive in 1962, Autocar wrote: 'The large Facel, a striking combination of French, American and British components, covers the miles at high speed without any mechanical problems.' But following an unsuccessful attempt to produce the Facellia's engines in-house, which bankrupted the company, production ceased in 1964 after around 180 Facel IIs had been produced. The Facel II, the direct successor to the HK500, although more refined, lighter and more sophisticated, also embodies French luxury and elegance: Connolly leather, precious woods, instrumentation by Parisian watchmaker Jaeger, etc. Today, these rare Franco-American GTs are among the most sought-after post-war classics.

This magnificent Facel II was purchased new in November 1962 from Pierre Savoye Automobile in Paris by its first owner, Mr Bernard Delbreil-Berges (original invoice, financing contract, Facel order form, Pierre Savoye Automobile order form and correspondence between Mr Delbreil-Berges and Pierre Savoye Automobile included in the file). The car was ordered from Facel with the following options: manual gearbox, black leather dashboard, tinted windows, power steering, air conditioning, seat belts and headrests for the front right seat.

Thanks to the archives accompanying the car, we learn that in early 1963, Mr Delbreil-Berges had a collision on the road between Cahors and Toulouse, the car was sent to Facel in Paris to have the right side of the bodywork restored and to be completely repainted in its original colour, Gregio Glacé (the file contains the bailiff's report, the expert's report, Facel's restoration invoices and all the original correspondence between the various parties involved). The correspondence between Mr Delbreil-Berges and Facel, included in the car's file, tells us that the engine was changed in the summer of 1963 by Facel, as the car's first owner was dissatisfied with its performance. The car was thus fitted with a 6.2-litre Chrysler V8 with twin carburettors. In another letter from 1964, sent by the first owner to Facel regarding an upcoming tyre change, we discover that with this new engine, Mr Delbreil-Berges enjoyed driving at very high speeds, admitting to regularly driving between 150km/h and 200km/h!

Before selling the car to its current owner (the second) in May 2005, its first owner had various repairs carried out at ALS in Beauzelle for a total of over €15,000 (corresponding invoices in the file). Since then, the car has been serviced by the current owner's mechanic.

The car comes with an extensive history file, contained in a 100-page binder containing the original documents (invoices, correspondence, expert reports, etc.) compiled by the two owners. The file contains extensive correspondence between the first owner, Facel Vega and Pierre Savoye Automobile, the original purchase invoice, the corresponding financing contract, various maintenance and repair invoices (from both owners), the current owner's purchase invoice, a 2013 expert report, various maintenance invoices, the owner's workshop manual, technical documents, a valid French MOT certificate and a French registration document.

This is undoubtedly a unique opportunity to acquire what was considered at the time to be the fastest four-seater of its era, having had only two owners and coming with a very important historical file.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1986 DESCRIPTION:
• Rare and sought-after factory-built 'Flat Nose' model
• Delivered new to Sweden
• Finished in Grand Prix White
• Special-order Can Can Red extended leather interior
• Limited-slip differential, electrically heated sports seats, air conditioning, sunroof
• Comprehensively stamped service booklet

Group 4 homologation rules, which required 400 road cars to be built, spurred the development of 'Project 930' - the legendary 911 Turbo. In production from April 1975, the 930 Turbo married a KKK turbocharger to the 3.0-litre RSR engine, in road trim a combination that delivered 260bhp for a top speed of 153mph (246km/h). For 1978 the Turbo's engine was enlarged to 3.3 litres, gaining an inter-cooler in the process; power increased to 300bhp and the top speed of what was the fastest-accelerating road car of its day went up to 160mph (257km/h).

The 911 Turbo's raison d'être - the racing 935 - had pioneered what would become known as the 'flat nose' (flachbau) or 'slant nose' (a more aerodynamically efficient front end) and this new look was soon in demand from 911 customers. Kremer Racing offered a conversion and this service as later taken up by the factory's own Customer Department to special order (Sunderwunschen) from 1981, only becoming an official option in 1986. The front wings were steel, incorporating cooling vents and pop-up headlamps (early examples had them in the air dam) while the rears had extra cooling intakes. There were different sills and, along with the body modifications, came an even more luxurious interior.

More refined than hitherto yet retaining its high-performance edge, the Porsche 911 Turbo sold in the thousands, becoming the definitive sports car of its age. When Porsche revealed that the original 911 would be replaced by the new Type 964, dealer stocks of the existing Turbo model sold out overnight. Production of the Type 930 ceased in September 1989, and there would not be another 911 Turbo until the Type 964 version was launched in September 1990.

Finished in its factory-correct colour combination of Grand Prix White with special-order Can Can Red extended leather interior, the 1986 model-year 911 Turbo 'Flat Nose' we offer is one of an estimated 948 built new with that distinctive feature. Other notable options include a sunroof, air conditioning, electrically heated sports seats, a limited-slip differential, and white centres to the deep-dish Fuchs wheels. This 911 was delivered new to Sweden and is believed to have remained in Scandinavia for its entire life. The current odometer reading is 169,902 kilometres, and the car presents well following sympathetic refurbishment. This most desirable Porsche rarity comes complete with a comprehensively stamped service booklet; a leather tool roll; and a Porsche folio containing instruction manuals.

"Performance, controllability and comfort have been combined in the Aston Martin DB4 to make it a highly desirable car: one in which long journeys can be completed very quickly indeed with the minimum of risk or discomfort and the maximum of pleasure." - The Motor.

Classically proportioned and instantly recognisable from the moment of its introduction in 1958, the Touring-styled Aston Martin DB4 established a look that would survive, with only minor revisions, until 1970. Designed by Tadek Marek and already proven in racing, the DB4's new twin-cam six-cylinder engine displaced 3,670cc while the gearbox was a new David Brown four-speed all-synchromesh unit. An immensely strong platform-type chassis, designed by Harold Beach, replaced the preceding DB2/4's multi-tubular spaceframe, the latter being considered incompatible with Touring's Superleggera body construction. The DB2/4's trailing-link independent front suspension gave way to unequal-length wishbones while at the rear the DB4 sported a live axle located by a Watts linkage instead of its predecessor's Panhard rod. Boasting disc brakes all round and with 240bhp on tap, the DB4 was the first production car capable of accelerating from a standing start to 100mph and back to rest again in under 30 seconds. At a time when few family saloons were capable of exceeding 70mph and took an age to get there, this staggering performance made the DB4 just about the fastest thing on the road, easily the equal of its Italian rivals.

Manufactured between October 1958 and June 1963, the DB4 developed through no fewer than five series. However, it should be made clear that the cars were not thus designated by the factory, this nomenclature having been suggested subsequently by the Aston Martin Owners Club to aid identification as the model evolved. The first series had already undergone several improvements, including the fitting of heavy-duty bumpers after the first 50 cars, before the second series arrived in January 1960. A front-hinged bonnet, bigger brake callipers, and an enlarged sump were the major changes made on the Series II, while the third series featured separate rear lights, two bonnet stays, and a host of improvements to the interior fittings. The fourth series was readily distinguishable by its new grille (with seven vertical bars), shallower bonnet intake, and recessed rear lights, while the final (fifth) series manufactured between September 1962 and June 1963 was 3.5" longer (allowing for increased leg room and a larger boot) and gained 15" wheels, an electric radiator fan, and the DB4GT-type instrument panel.

One of the most notable developments had arrived with the introduction of the 'Series IV' in September 1961, when a 'Special Series' (SS) engine became available as an option. The 'SS' unit boasted a 9.0:1 compression ratio; larger valves and inner valve springs from the DB4GT; and triple SU HD8 carburettors with a black-painted cold-air box, producing 266bhp at 5,750rpm, a gain of 26 horsepower over the standard unit. Optional on the regular model, an oil cooler was standard on the cars coming with the SS engine. Almost all DB4 Vantages were built with the faired-in headlights of the DB4GT, making the example we offer something of a rarity.

The Series V is one of the rarest and most desirable of the DB range with only 50 cars built in this final incarnation of the DB4. Indeed, the original 'James Bond' car used in the filming of Goldfinger was a DB4 Series V, as they look virtually identical to the DB5, which at that time was not quite ready.

Chassis number '1001/L' is one of an estimated 19 Series V examples built with the Special Series (SS) engine, only six of which were of left-hand drive configuration like this car. Shipped to Aston Martin's French agent Garage Mirabeau on 4th October 1962, '1001/L' is a matching numbers example retaining its original engine, chassis, body, gearbox, exterior colour (Aegean Blue), and tan Connolly interior trim (VM 3280). The DB4 was delivered new on 27th October 1962 to its first owner, Mr Pierre Zannettacci, a French gentleman resident in the 16th District of Paris. Remarkably, the Aston has had only two owners since 1962, has belonged to the current vendor for more than 50 years, and has always remained Parisian since its arrival in France.

Some 10 years ago the engine was extensively refurbished; the gearbox synchros and clutch replaced; and the rear brake calipers rebuilt. The DB4 has been serviced regularly at Cecil Cars, and during a recent test drive, the engine started immediately and ran smoothly, revving without difficulties, performing well at low and high speeds, shifting gears smoothly.

Listed in James Taylor's book Factory-Original Aston Martin DB4/5/6, '1001/L' comes with sundry invoices; Garage Mirabeau's delivery note; the original purchase invoice; 2015 Expertise report; a valid French Carte Grise; and an up-to-date Contrôle Technique. A wonderful opportunity to acquire a highly original and well maintained Aston Martin DB4 Series V with Special Series engine - the first 'SS' Series V built - offered from long-term enthusiast ownership.

A proposed Group 5 'Silhouette Formula' for production-based cars triggered the M1 programme in the mid-1970s, a mid-engined concept car designed in-house at BMW by Paul Bracq providing the basis. Head of BMW's newly formed Motorsport Division, former racing driver Jochen Neerpasch was responsible for masterminding this ambitious project, whose aims included taking on rivals Porsche in the World Sportscar Championship and, ultimately, victory at Le Mans.

M1 development was contracted first to Lamborghini and then to Giorgetto Giugiaro's Ital Design, although almost all cars ended up being built by BMW in Germany. Giugiaro's compact coupé bodywork in glassfibre was wrapped around a multi-tubular spaceframe chassis, while a twin-overhead-cam, four-valves-per-cylinder version of BMW's 3.5-litre inline six, driving via a ZF five-speed transaxle, provided the motive power.

The M1's wedge-shaped coachwork proved highly efficient aerodynamically, needing very little in the way of additional spoilers and wings in race configuration. Lamborghini's Gianpaolo Dallara had been responsible for developing the suspension, which followed racing practice by using unequal-length wishbones at front and rear. Soberly trimmed in black and grey, the M1's interior was exceptionally well equipped for a sports car, featuring Recaro seats, air conditioning, electric windows, remotely operated door mirrors and a heated rear screen.

First shown at the Paris Motor Show in 1978, the road-going version came with 273bhp and a top speed of 165mph (265km/h). Only ever intended as a limited-edition model, the M1 ceased production after a little over 450 examples had been built, just exceeding the minimum of 400 required for Group 4 homologation, which would have preceded homologation for Group 5. In the event, the abandonment of the Group 5 Silhouette Formula robbed the car of its raison d'être, though the one-make Procar BMW M1 Championship series run at Formula 1 Grand Prix races in 1979 and '80 provided BMW Motorsport with a valuable showcase by way of consolation. The series ran for only those two years, Nicki Lauda winning the 1979 championship and Nelson Piquet the 1980 one. A new M1 road car was awarded to each winner.

Delivered new to its first owner in Berlin, Germany in the stunning colour combination of Inka Orange with black interior, this M1 is believed to have been enjoyed by the first owner's family from new until very recently, when it was purchased by our vendor. The car had been carefully enjoyed by its Berlin-based owner, who always had it meticulously serviced, mostly at the main BMW concessionaire in Berlin. By 1996 it had already covered some 105,000 kilometres, as evidenced by entries in the accompanying original service book, which has been stamped on no fewer than 19 occasions. At the time of cataloguing the odometer reading was 141,000 kilometres, a testament to BMW reliability and the fact that the M1 has always been, and still is, a very useable supercar.

A new clutch was installed in 2017, while more recent works include services in 2023 and October 2024, when new Pirelli tyres were fitted (P7 to the front, PZero Asimmetrico to the rear) and the oil and brake fluid changed. Since acquisition by our vendor, the central cooling water pipes (which are located in the central tunnel in the chassis and are a notorious M1 weakness) were replaced with original BMW items and the surrounding area thoroughly cleaned and sealed. Charmingly, the interior boasts a period Clarion sound system including radio, cassette player and amplifier as well as sportier Recaro bucket seats, trimmed in black leather.

An important landmark in BMW's history, and in particular of its involvement with motor sport in the post-war era, the M1 is already highly collectible and is surely destined to become increasingly sought after by discerning aficionados of the marque. Offered with German registration documents, its original service book and owner's manual, and various invoices, this BMW M1 ticks all the boxes: Giugiaro styling, superb and reliable BMW engine, beautiful colour combination and long-term enthusiastic ownership.

auction_title: Michelin House Stained Glass Windows – London – Bibendum
description_block:
Set of two large-scale reproductions of the stained glass windows that once adorned the Michelin House in London, created after the famous posters "Le Coup de semelle" and "Pneu Vélo Michelin." These compositions feature the character Bibendum, created in 1898 by O'Galop (Marius Rossillon, 1867–1946).

One panel depicts the Michelin Bibendum, cigar in mouth, presenting his studded sole; the other shows him riding a bicycle while smoking a cigar. Produced by an Italian workshop, these works stand out for their vivid colours and exceptional quality of execution. Each stained glass panel is protected by a front glass pane and housed within a reinforced metal frame.

The Michelin House, inaugurated on 20 January 1911, served as the first British headquarters and tyre depot of Michelin Tyre Company Ltd. During the Second World War, due to the bombing of London, the original stained glass windows were dismantled in the 1940s and were never recovered after the war.

Michelin vacated the building in 1985, when it was acquired and converted into the Bibendum Restaurant & Oyster Bar.

On the occasion of the building's centenary in 2011, the event was celebrated by the occupants at the time—the Bibendum Restaurant and The Conran Shop—as well as by Michelin, the former owner. In this context, Michelin renewed efforts to locate the original stained glass windows, establishing a dedicated website and telephone line, highlighting the importance of these works to the company's heritage.

Dimensions: height 208 cm; 148 × 50 cm.

Introduced as long ago as 1979, the Mercedes-Benz G-Class 'Geländewagen' (cross-country vehicle) was the result of a joint venture with Steyr-Daimler-Puch of Austria, a firm with considerable experience in developing four-wheel-drive systems for off-road vehicles. Its purposeful appearance – fundamentally unchanged throughout its life – and engineering excellence has secured the G-Wagen cult status and earned it a reputation as one of the most coveted of classic 4x4s.

For 1991 an extensively revised (W463) chassis was introduced, incorporating the very latest in off-road traction technology in the form of three electronically engaged differentials in addition to anti-lock brakes. The W463 moved the G-Class from spartan and utilitarian to a luxury model able to compete with the rival Range Rover.

There have been countless updates to the W463 since then and a host of special variants. One of the final models released before production of the W463 ceased in 2018, the G63 was powered by AMG's 5.5-litre twin-turbocharged V8 engine developing 571PS, which was delivered to the ground via AMG's Speedshift Plus 7G-tronic automatic transmission. Boasting high ground clearance and long-travel suspension, the AMG G63 offered greater off-road capability than most customers would ever need in an immensely stylish conveyance with not inconsiderable on-the-road presence. Like the entire model series, the G63 AMG was produced in Graz, primarily in the factory's hand-finishing section.

Representing possibly a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to own one of these rare and super-exclusive luxury 4x4s, this stunning example of the fabulous Mercedes-AMG G63 was dispatched from the factory in Graz, Austria on 21st February 2018. Highlights of the options list include Designo Mystic White 2 Bright paintwork; Exclusive two-tone leather interior; brake calipers painted red; Harman Kardon sound system with Smartphone Integration and Carplay; electric sunroof; 21" AMG wheels; and the Design Exclusive package to name but a few.

The Mercedes was delivered new in Germany and first registered to a company but scarcely used, which explains the current odometer reading of just over 120 kilometres. As a result, this is as close to a new Mercedes-AMG G63 as one can buy; indeed, the interior still features the original protective plastic covering in some places. With only one registered owner from new, this highly desirable 'low mileage' G63 comes with Euro 6 emissions compliance; German registration documents, a copy of the Manufacturer's Certificate of Conformity; and its original books.

"The most luxurious BMW from the pre-war period was the BMW 335, which was the last BMW to go into series production before the war broke out in 1939. The body was essentially a 326 body extended by 23 cm. The increased weight required more powerful brakes and wider tyres. The 3.5 litre inline six-cylinder engine was completely new with a maximum output of 90 hp. The luxurious interior and the top speed of 145 km/h made the BMW 335 a comfortable yet fast touring car and enabled BMW to enter the segment for luxury cars." - BMW.

The success of the Type 326 and its derivatives prompted BMW to build a larger car to take on the likes of Mercedes-Benz and Horch. That first upmarket model was the 335. Three versions were offered: a four-door saloon and two- and four-door cabriolets. Only some 410-420 had been made up to 1941 when production ceased.

One of the very last manufactured, this ultra-rare BMW 335 two-door cabriolet is finished in two-tone grey/green with grey interior. Mr Strinati purchased the car on 30th August 1963 (Swiss taxes had been paid in January 1947). Unfortunately, very little is known about its earlier history, but as with most of the cars in the Collection, we believe it was never restored. YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1966 DESCRIPTION:
• Delivered new in Germany

Few sports cars have proved as versatile as Porsche's perennial 911, a model that, for the last 60-plus years, has proved equally capable as a Grand Tourer, circuit racer, or rally car. A 'modern classic' if ever there was one, the 911 first appeared at the 1963 Frankfurt Show as the '901', but shortly after production proper commenced in 1964 had become the '911' following Peugeot's complaints about the use of '0' model numbers. The preceding Type 356's rear-engined layout was retained, but the 911 switched to unitary construction for the chassis/body and dropped the 356's VW-based suspension in favour of a more modern McPherson strut and trailing arm arrangement. In its first incarnation, Porsche's single-overhead-camshaft, air-cooled flat six engine displaced 1,991cc and produced 130bhp; progressively enlarged and developed, it would eventually grow to more than 3.0 litres and, in turbo-charged form, put out well over 300 horsepower.

This Porsche 911 offered here, chassis number '304 449', is one of the early, short-wheelbase cars of the type much favoured by the historic rallying fraternity, a situation that has led to original examples such as this one becoming a great rarity and consequently much in demand. It is a 1966 model year car, and belongs to the '0-Programme' series built from the start of production in August 1964 up to the introduction of the 'A-Programme' model in August 1967, and thus represents the Porsche 911 in its earliest and purest form.

This car was delivered new on 13th May 1966 to company owner Fritz Fuss through the Max Moritz Porsche dealership in Reutlingen, Germany. In 1998, following restoration at Porsche costing over 50,000 DM (invoice on file), its registration status was changed from commercial to private use. At the end of 2004 the 911's ownership was transferred to the owner's son-in-law. It currently has a German registration.

The car comes with its original folder containing all documents (owner's manual, service books, sunroof manual, etc); a Porsche Certificate of Authenticity; and its first, second and third German titles, which had to be updated over the decades due to new regulations imposed by the German government. Indeed, this is a good documented early 911, that is a rare 'full-matching-numbers' example with a 87,990 kilometres recorded. Understood to have never been raced or rallied, it appears to be in very good condition throughout, retaining its original interior and fitted with a radio in the glove compartment (easily removed).

This exceptional short-wheelbase Porsche 911 is the perfect car for historic rallies, being both fast and competitive.

The Lancia Aurelia was launched at the Turin Motor Show in 1950. It was the result of a close collaboration between designer Felice Mario Boano of Ghia, Carrozzeria Pininfarina and an engineering team led by Vittorio Jano, a former Alfa Romeo engineer and a leading figure in automotive engineering at the time. With its pioneering monocoque design, it was the first production car to be equipped with a V6 engine. The B20 of the third series and subsequent series, launched in 1953, were equipped with a 2,451 cc pushrod V6 engine developing 118 hp.

The chassis B20-3271 was completed on 23 September 1954 before being first registered on 23 November 1954 in the name of Lancia GB, in Alperton, England and delivered new on 1 December 1954 to A B Blanch & Co, in England. It is believed to be one of only six Aurelia B20 Series IVs delivered to the UK. It then belonged to Blanch Lely, in Wiltshire (from 11 January 1964), and then successively to A. McArthur, Beacon Motors, David Hayne, John Glen and Austin Watts, all in the Bristol area. In 1986, the Lancia was purchased by David Sankey, who undertook a complete and documented restoration, with Tim Burrett (an Aurelia specialist) rebuilding the engine with high-lift Nardi camshafts. On 1 December 2003, the Aurelia was purchased by Catherine Janssens, at a Bonhams sale. Maintenance and servicing continued to be carried out by Tim Burrett. In October 2010, the car was sold at auction in London, UK, to Brian Classick & Co, before being sold again in 2011. In 2013, the Lancia was repainted in the original Lancia colour, amaranto, by the Haslams restorers in Bolton, UK. The car was serviced by brand specialists, R&D Automotive Limited of Manchester, with parts supplied by Omicron Engineering Limited (including an MSD ignition conversion to aid starting and the fitting of a battery isolator).

Purchased by its current owner at our Goodwood Revival sale on 17 September 2022, it has since only covered a few hundred miles, always maintained with care and stored dry as advised by its owner. The car comes with an FCA Heritage Classiche certification (issued in July 2018), a FIVA passport, a FIA Historic Regularity documentation and English registration documents (logged as exported). The following items also come with the car: folder and plaque, documented historical folder, original 'bench-seating' frame, jack bag and embroidered Lancia interior car cover.
