historical_significance: One of only 18 W29 coupés built, significant pre-war supercar.
description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1934 DESCRIPTION:
Engine block serial no. 102401.59
Vanvooren body no. 2933

• One-off, matching numbers
• One of only 18 W29 coupés built
• One of only a handful of W29 built with French coachwork
• Delivered new to Paris, France
• Present ownership since 1959
• Formerly on display in the Musée de l'Automobile Jean Tua, Geneva
• Outstandingly original

Sensation of the 1934 Berlin Auto Show, Mercedes-Benz's legendary pre-war 500K supercar cost a small fortune when new and today commands a king's ransom, such is its rarity. The 1930s decade was a period of unprecedented fertility in motor car styling, of which the sublime 500K represented the very pinnacle of excellence. Its timeless appeal endures to this day (the original name of the model, 'Typ 500 mit Kompressor', was later shortened to '500K').

Beneath its seemingly endless bonnet, the 500K's eight-cylinder engine developed 100bhp un-supercharged or 160bhp with the compressor engaged. The car had a top speed approaching 110mph (177km/h). After testing a 500K cabriolet in 1936, The Autocar declared: "This is a master car, for the very few. The sheer insolence of its great power affords an experience on its own."

The Mercedes-Benz 500K and its successor, the 540K, are among the most iconic models of the classic era. A total of 761 chassis of the two W29 models—the 500K and 540K—were produced at the Stuttgart-Untertürkheim plant between February 1934 and November 1939: 342 with a 5-litre engine and 419 with a 5.4-litre engine. Of these, 691 units were fitted with bodies by the "Sonderwagenbau" department at the Sindelfingen plant, while only 70 chassis were delivered to external coachbuilders for bodywork. The most popular model was the Cabriolet B, with 296 units produced, while the exclusive and dignified Special Roadster achieved a total production run of around 50 units. The various coupé variants amounted to only 12 cars, and just 6 examples of the Autobahn Kurier were built.

The chassis of the 500K and 540K had a wheelbase of 3,290 mm and was available in two versions. In addition to the standard configuration, there was a variant in which the radiator, engine-gearbox unit, steering gear and seats were moved rearwards by just over 10 cm. Roadsters, Special Roadsters, Cabriolet A and Autobahn Kurier models were built on this rearward-engine chassis, while all other body variants were constructed on the standard chassis.

According to Mercedes-Benz Classic in Stuttgart, the delivery of chassis no. U105.394 to the Paris branch was recorded in the commission book on 29 November 1934, shortly after the model's first presentation at the Paris Salon in October. Unfortunately, there is no mention of either the customer or the coachbuilder. (According to a letter from DaimlerChrysler Schweiz AG dated 27 November 2006, this car—chassis number "U105394"—was delivered new to Germany; this information has since been proven to be incorrect.)

The number 102401.59 stamped on the engine block provides the following information:
10 for the Untertürkheim plant
24 for the new M24 engine type
01 for the series
59 for the 59th engine of the first series

This corresponds with the total production of 105 units in 1934 and, together with the original engine plate no. U105.394, confirms that this car is matching numbers.

Although sales opportunities for Mercedes-Benz on the French market were limited by exorbitant import duties of 45%, the company maintained a showroom on the Champs-Élysées and regularly exhibited its latest models at the Paris Salon in October. Internal documents from the Mercedes-Benz board of directors show that attendance at the Salon was considered a "must" in order to present the brand to international customers. One way to partially circumvent import duties was to deliver bare chassis—a strategy that proved successful, as the 500K/540K chassis attracted the interest of the most prestigious coachbuilders of the time.

This particular example features a fixed-head coupé body by Vanvooren, one of the most renowned and successful French luxury-car coachbuilders of the 1930s. Carrosserie Vanvooren, based in Courbevoie in north-west Paris, bodied the majority of Hispano-Suiza chassis during this period and also designed and built numerous bodies for Bugatti, Delage, Rolls-Royce, Bentley, Packard and Cadillac. These automotive gems are among the most exclusive one-off creations and can be found today in the world's most prestigious collections.
As confirmed during a thorough inspection by Vanvooren specialist Martin Waltz in December 2025, the Vanvooren body number 2933 appears in several locations on the vehicle and dates from August 1938. What happened to the chassis during the three years following its delivery from Stuttgart to Paris remains unknown. It is possible that it remained unsold during this period, but it may also have received an initial body that was later replaced in 1938. Among the Parisian elite of the 1930s, it was common practice either to purchase new cars at short intervals or to have existing ones modernised. There are countless examples of this trend, often driven by the regularly held Concours d'Élégance, which demanded the very best. Alternatively, it may simply have been a matter of a new owner with new tastes.

As was customary, Vanvooren prepared a design proposal for the customer, illustrated in Jan Melin and Sven Hernström's book Mercedes-Benz 8: The Supercharged 8-Cylinder Cars of the 1930s, Volume 2 (copies of the relevant pages on file). In addition to the spectacular front wings and the rearward-mounted engine/radiator unit, the use of a design feature introduced two years earlier by the coachbuilder Letourneur & Marchand is particularly striking: the pillarless, overlapping front and rear side windows with a rearward-sloping line. Vanvooren employed this feature on several other bodies as well. It is not known with certainty whether the car's first paintwork was dark green, as it is today; however, there is much to suggest this was the case, as the largely original all-green interior—with leather-covered dashboard and window surrounds—corresponds perfectly with Vanvooren's preference for single-colour paintwork and interiors.

It can be assumed that the Mercedes remained in France until 1947, when it first appeared in Geneva, Switzerland. That year, the Vanvooren-bodied Mercedes caught the attention of 18-year-old schoolboy Pierre Strinati. Carrying Swiss dealer plates "GE 2325," it was parked on the curb in front of Garage Verolet at 107 Boulevard de la Cluse (see pictures). Immediately fascinated, Strinati found the courage to enquire about the extraordinary vehicle, despite not yet having a driving licence. The green car was offered for sale at CHF 3,500. He photographed it and cherished the images from that moment on, never expecting to see the Mercedes again (handwritten notes and photographs by Mr Strinati are on file).

The 500K was photographed once more, this time in front of the Eaux-Vives Garage owned by Blanc & Paiches, now without a number plate (the photographer is unknown). Together with Strinati's images, these are the earliest known photographs of the car. Official importation from France to Switzerland followed the next year, as evidenced by the customs clearance certificate dated 31 July 1948 (document on file).
Eleven years later, during a visit to Montreux on the opposite side of Lake Geneva, Pierre Strinati was unexpectedly reacquainted with his dream car. Now painted black, it was driving slowly through town. He ran after it and, when it stopped in front of the "Le Pavillon" tea house, approached the driver, Kaspar Schmid—who was also the proprietor of the establishment. When Strinati asked whether he might consider selling the car, Schmid replied in the affirmative, much to his surprise. Thus, on 29 January 1959—67 years ago to the day—the Mercedes changed hands for the final time, for CHF 10,000.

This Mercedes became the first car in what would grow into one of the most remarkable private collections in the world. Strinati, the only son of a wealthy textile manufacturer, had been cultivating his passion for automotive design since the mid-1950s and, by the mid-1960s, had assembled in his private garage nearly every marque now considered a blue-chip classic. The collection included outstanding examples from Bugatti, Delage, Delahaye, Talbot, Voisin, Ferrari, Lancia, Alfa Romeo, Horch, Maybach, Mercedes-Benz, BMW, Lagonda, Jaguar, Aston Martin and Pegaso. Although he sold several cars during the 1980s and 1990s, he never parted with the Mercedes-Benz 500K Vanvooren, his personal favourite.

Following its purchase, Mr Strinati commissioned Carrosserie Roland Bodi to adjust the bonnet, repair the radiator, re-chrome the bumpers, repair the seats (likely referring to elements of the door panels, as the seats themselves appear completely original), and repaint the car in green—the colour it had when he first encountered it. The related quotation dated 25 February 1960 and the invoice for CHF 2,415 dated 26 April 1960 are on file. Strinati registered the Mercedes on 31 May 1960 under the number "GE 33961" and used it almost daily, often accompanied by his mother, who shared his deep affection for the car. In the 1970s, the 500K was taken out of service and placed into storage. In 1993, it was briefly exhibited at the Musée de l'Automobile Jean Tua in Geneva before being stored on axle stands in a purpose-built garage for the next 30 years.

In 2015, Martin Waltz—then researching a book on Vanvooren—wrote to Mr Strinati and inspected the 500K (documentation on file). More recently, he authored an article on the car in German, also on file.
A high-quality 1:43-scale collector's model of the car presented here is included in the sale. Released in 2014 by EMC/B&G in a limited edition of 150 examples, it is of outstanding quality—thanks in part to the support of Mr Strinati (correspondence on file).

This exceptional automobile, a unique fusion of German engineering and French design, is accompanied by an extensive archive of correspondence, period photographs, brochures, invoices and letters. Despite having been resprayed, in the 1960s, it remains in an outstanding state of originality and preservation, with the sumptuous green leather interior believed to be largely original. In recent years, the rarity, elegance and performance of these large, supercharged Mercedes models have made them among the most sought-after classic cars whenever they appear on the open market. This exceptionally well-documented example, hidden from public view for decades, is worthy of the closest inspection.

Bonhams|Cars wishes to thank Martin Waltz for his help in the redaction of this description.

YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1931 DESCRIPTION:
• Original left-hand drive example
• Restored and re-bodied as a tourer in the 1970s
• Mentioned in John Webb de Campi's book, Rolls-Royce in America

Chassis number '271-AJS' is one of approximately 100 built in the UK with left-hand drive. It is believed to be matching numbers, but this is as yet unconfirmed. Originally bodied in the USA by Huntington as a limousine, the Phantom was delivered new on 27th February 1932 to Mr C T Newberry of Irvington on Hudson, New York City. The car remained with the same family until 1971 when it returned to the UK for restoration and re-bodying by renowned coachbuilders FLM Panelcraft, as confirmed by stamps in the body panels. They named the bodywork 'Derby Tourer' after the Phantom I Derby Speedster, which was considered one of the finest bodies of its time (this car is mentioned in John Webb de Campi's book, Rolls-Royce in America).After restoration the Phantom returned to the USA where our vendor purchased it in 2000 from well known collector S Prestley Blake of Springfield, Massachusetts.

The vendor took the Rolls-Royce to his summer home in Cape Coral, Florida where it was used for rallies and concours events. In 2018 he decided to export the car to Sweden where it is currently registered for road use. The car is described as 100% correct mechanically, and according to the vendor is running well; it has not been driven much recently and would benefit from a repaint.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1923 DESCRIPTION:
• The most desirable, sporting Springfield Silver Ghost
• Original chassis, engine, and coachwork
• An older restoration
• Same family ownership since 2000
• Engine professionally rebuilt circa 2005
• Registered in Sweden

In December 1919 the newly created Rolls-Royce of America Incorporated purchased the American Wire Wheel Company's plant in Springfield, Massachusetts, from which the first US-built Silver Ghost emerged in January 1921. Unlike its British-built counterpart, the American 'Ghost could be ordered with 'factory' bodywork, usually by Brewster, the latter company being taken over by Rolls-Royce in December 1925. Right-hand drive remained the norm for US-built cars until early in 1925, the penultimate year of Silver Ghost production, when the switch was made to left-hand drive. The model was replaced by the New Phantom (retrospectively Phantom I) in 1926.

Prior to its acquisition of Brewster, Rolls-Royce of America Inc had set up the Rolls-Royce Custom Coach Works (RRCCW) program to organise the supply of 'factory' bodywork, commencing with the Silver Ghost and continuing on its New Phantom successor. Various established coachbuilders supplied bodies badged as 'RRCCW', including Massachusetts-based Merrimac, whose sporting Piccadilly Roadster was deservedly popular, some 70 being completed.

Retaining its original Piccadilly coachwork, this Springfield Silver Ghost was delivered new on 18th September 1923 to Mr Charles E F Clarke of 40 Wall Street. New York City. The car is finished in Old English White with beige leather interior, and is an early Springfield Ghost with right-hand drive and the four-speed gearbox (the model was only delivered in this configuration for the first two years). The car is believed to have been owned at one time by the well-known Campbell family in the USA. The current owner purchased the Rolls-Royce from S. Prestley Blake in the spring of year 2000 and it has been in their family's possession ever since.

The 'Ghost is an older restoration believed carried out in the 1970s-1980s. Around 2005 the engine underwent a comprehensive overhaul by renowned Rolls-Royce expert in Sweden, Kjell Lind, who has been helping the current owners with starting and running the car in recent years. The Ghost is today described as in good original condition. It is currently registered in Sweden and comes with Swedish registration documents, a folder of invoices, copies of the first US title, and other historic documents. As one would expect, this car is mentioned in the book Rolls Royce in America by John Webb de Campi.

Some ten years after the original's introduction it was felt that the time had come to update the Land Rover's somewhat primitive slab-sided styling. The result was the Series II, which featured more rounded sides. Introduced in 1958, the Series II was available with either the 2,286cc petrol engine or the newly developed 2,052cc diesel first seen in 1956 on what became known retrospectively as the 'Series I'. By this time the original permanent four-wheel drive freewheel transmission had been superseded by the more conventional selectable two- or four-wheel drive arrangement, with a set of low ratios available with the latter option selected. The chief development on the Series IIA was a much improved diesel engine.

This Series IIA 'Landie' was first registered on 22nd June 1966, and it is believed that Mr Strinati bought it new to use on his exploration and caving expeditions. Boasting the rare 'safari' roof, it was stored with all his speleological equipment in the rear, ready to embark on another tour. We believe that this car too is exceptionally original, most probably retaining its original paint. With its association with a world-renowned caving expert, this Land Rover is worthy of the closest inspection (unfortunately no folder has yet been discovered to further support the above). Again, recommissioning will be required prior to use and it should be noted that the aforementioned speleological equipment is not included in the sale.

auction_title: Scuderia Ferrari F1 – 1950 to 2019 - Over one hundred driver autographs – Collection of 136 models at 1/43 scale
description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1950 DESCRIPTION:
An exceptional collection of 136 Ferrari Formula 1 models at 1/43 scale, each accompanied by a standing driver figure wearing full racing suit and helmet.
Each model originally derives from a high-quality kit, predominantly in white metal (such as BBR, Tameo, and others), and has been assembled by professional model makers.
Almost all models are accompanied by the autograph of the driver represented.
This collection traces the evolution of Scuderia Ferrari Formula 1 cars from 1950 to 2019.
Each car is presented with a plaque indicating the Grand Prix, model type, race number, and the signature of the model maker.
Beside each car stands its driver in full racing attire, with a separate plaque at his feet bearing his autograph.
The collection includes signatures from many legendary drivers, among them:
Fangio, Hawthorn, Hill, Ickx, Amon, Andretti, Lauda, Villeneuve, Prost, Barrichello, Massa, Alonso, Räikkönen, Schumacher, Irvine, Brooks, Mairesse, Vettel, Berger, Pironi, Regazzoni, and many others.
Also featured are autographs of drivers tragically killed during races:
Ascari (1955), Castellotti (1957), Collins (1958), Hawthorn (1959), von Trips (1961).
The ensemble represents an average of two models per year.
This lifetime collection was made possible only through privileged personal contact with the drivers and their representatives.
The majority of the autographs are executed in black felt-tip pen, applied to metal plaques protected by a transparent film.

The years 1969 and 1983 are not represented, as the kits available at the time were deemed insufficient in quality by the collector.
The collection is housed in two red display cabinets, supplied with the lot
(dimensions: 80 × 50 × 200 cm each).

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1955 DESCRIPTION:
• Matching chassis, engine and body
• Delivered new to the USA
• Returned to Europe in 1980
• High-quality restoration in the 1990s
• Present ownership since 2011
• Meticulous maintenance by the French specialist in 300 SLs
• Originally equipped with the rare long axle ratio option (1:3.42) allowing speeds in excess of 160mph

"When it was first announced by Mercedes-Benz, the production 300 SL Coupé was a startling car built to the German concern's customarily startling standards, but above all what left the general public most open-mouthed about the new car was its upward-opening Gullwing doors...!" - Motors, 1963.Post-war, Mercedes-Benz had returned to competition in 1952, fielding two of its new 300 SL (W194) sports cars in the Mille Miglia. The pair finishing a creditable 2nd and 4th overall in this most difficult of events, and this promising start was followed up by a win in the challenging Carrera Panamericana. The works first raced the 300 SL (Sport Leicht) in open form, but for the Le Mans 24-Hour Race in June a trio of 'gullwing'-doored coupés was entered. High sills were a feature of the multi-tubular spaceframe chassis, and while access was not a problem of the open car, the enclosed coupé bodywork required innovative thinking - hence the gullwing doors. Karl Kling and Hans Klenk duly brought their 'Silver Arrow' home in 1st place at Le Mans and the 300 SL was on its way to becoming part of motor sporting legend.

Launched in 1954, the production 300 SL road car retained the spaceframe chassis and lightweight aluminium-alloy bodywork of the W194 racer, while its mechanical underpinnings, like the latter's, owed much to the contemporary Mercedes-Benz 300 luxury saloon. A 2,996cc overhead-camshaft inline six, the 300 SL's engine was canted over at 45 degrees to achieve a low bonnet line and produced 215bhp (DIN) at 5,800rpm using Bosch mechanical fuel injection. A four-speed, all-synchromesh manual gearbox transmitted power to the hypoid bevel rear axle. Suspension was independent all round: by wishbones and coil springs at the front, with swing axles and coil springs at the rear.

A production 300 SL (W198) was tested by Road & Track magazine in 1955, accelerating from 0-60mph in 7.4 seconds on its way to a top speed of 140mph (225km/h). Half expecting the long-awaited 300 SL to provide an anti-climax, R&T were delighted to find the new car, "far beyond our wildest expectations. In fact, we can state unequivocally that in our opinion the 300 SL coupé is the ultimate in an all-round sportscar. It combines more desirable features in one streamlined package than we ever imagined or hoped would be possible. Performance? It accelerates from a dead start to 100mph in just over 17 seconds. Dual purpose? A production model 300 SL can make a very acceptable showing in any type of sportscar competition. Yet the car is extremely tractable and easy to drive in traffic. Comfort? The fully enclosed 300 SL is the most comfortable (and safe) high-speed 'cross-country' car built today".

A 300 SL roadster featuring conventional doors was first exhibited at the Geneva Salon in May 1957 and, although built in greater numbers, has never matched the immortal Gullwing for desirability. Its racing parentage notwithstanding, the 300 SL remains a thoroughly practical car, as civilised in city traffic as it is exhilarating on the Autostrada. By the time 300 SL Gullwing Coupé production ceased in 1957, some 1,400 examples had found customers. Today the model is both rare and most sought after by connoisseurs of fine automobiles.

This magnificent Mercedes-Benz 300 SL Gullwing is a desirable matching numbers example, retaining its original chassis, body and engine. Recorded in Eric Le Moine's 300 SL Register, this car left the factory on 9th August 1955 and was delivered new on 25th August 1955 in New York City via Mercedes-Benz Distributors, Inc. Originally finished in Silver Gray Mettalic with blue leatherette and tartan cloth upholstery, the car has been repainted in black and the interior retrimmed in red leather. It is worth noting that this car is equipped with a very rare option on the 300 SL: a long axle ratio (1 : 3.42) allowing it to exceed 260 km/h, which explains the speedometer graduation up to 180 mp/h. This option was chosen by the first owner when ordering the car. In general, 300 SL Gullwing have a gear ratio of 1 : 3.64 and a speedometer graduated only up to 160mph

The Gullwing enjoyed four owners in the USA before coming to the UK in 1980 where it was extensively restored towards the end of that decade. The car belonged to two owners in the UK before passing to the French vendor, a Parisian collector, in 2011. The current owner sent the car to MB Classic at Stains for a full overhaul, which included having the injection pump rebuilt; new injectors fitted; all hoses replaced; brakes completely rebuilt; water and oil radiators rebuilt; starter motor rebuilt; alternator rebuilt; general vehicle inspection, etc, etc. There are related invoices totalling in excess of €60,000 on file. The car has been serviced regularly by MB Classic at Stains and GFB Classic-Auto.

During a recent test drive we have noted that the engine started immediately and ran smoothly, revving without difficulties, performing well at low and high speeds, shifting gears smoothly and with brakes working correctly.

Also on file is an Expertise valuation report noting that the car is in "excellent overall running order" and "visible parts of the underbody and chassis are in very good condition, with no visible signs of accident damage or rust going through the metal". A fine example of one of the 20th Century's most coveted classics, this beautiful Mercedes-Benz 300 SL Gullwing comes complete with fitted luggage; sundry invoices for maintenance and repairs; the aforementioned Expertise report; a valid French Carte Grise; and an up-to-date Contrôle Technique.

Some ten years after the original's introduction it was felt that the time had come to update the Land Rover's somewhat primitive slab-sided styling. The result was the Series II, which featured more rounded sides. Introduced in 1958, the Series II was available with either the 2,286cc petrol engine or the newly developed 2,052cc diesel first seen in 1956 on what became known retrospectively as the 'Series I'. By this time the original permanent four-wheel drive freewheel transmission had been superseded by the more conventional selectable two- or four-wheel drive arrangement, with a set of low ratios available with the latter option selected. The chief development on the Series IIA was a much improved diesel engine.

This Series IIA 'Landie' was first registered on 22nd June 1966, and it is believed that Mr Strinati bought it new to use on his exploration and caving expeditions. Boasting the rare 'safari' roof, it was stored with all his speleological equipment in the rear, ready to embark on another tour. We believe that this car too is exceptionally original, most probably retaining its original paint. With its association with a world-renowned caving expert, this Land Rover is worthy of the closest inspection (unfortunately no folder has yet been discovered to further support the above). Again, recommissioning will be required prior to use and it should be noted that the aforementioned speleological equipment is not included in the sale.

YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1971 DESCRIPTION:
• Matching numbers chassis and engine
• One of 500 built
• An interesting recommissioning project

A rare model with a short career that formed the joint between the 365 GT 2+2 and the 365 GT4 2+2, the 365 GTC/4 was unveiled at the Geneva Motor Show in 1971. Contemporary to the revered "Daytona", the 365 GTC /4 used an identical chassis and a wet-sump version of the 4,390cc four-overhead-cam V12 of this one with slightly lower power – 320bhp – mated to a conventional five-speed gearbox, instead. of the "Daytona" transaxle. The cylinder head had been modified to accommodate horizontal carburettors and had enabled coachbuilder Pininfarina to achieve an elegant and low bonnet line. "Discreet, sober and elegant as a whole, with subtleties that can be appreciated by contemplating it attentively. You could say this is a Ferrari dedicated to the discerning enthusiast," wrote Road & Track.

Overall more civilized and easier to drive than the heavy Daytona, the speedy 365 GTC/4 received ZF power steering and power-assisted brakes as standard, optional air conditioning and a particularly luxurious interior, equipped with individual folding seats in the front and booster seats in the rear. Despite increased refinement, the 365 GTC/4 was no match for its competitors in terms of performance, beating the 400m from a standing start in under 16 seconds with a top speed of over 240 km/h. When the model was discontinued in October 1972, production totaled only 500 examples, making it a particularly desirable model today.

Chassis 14545 left the factory on September 29, 1971 and was delivered new by the French importer Charles Pozzi on November 2 of the same year. Painted in Argento Auteuil Metalizzato and fitted with a black leather and gray plaid interior, this elegant 365 was maintained during its first years by the Levallois workshop. It later spent part of its life in Alsace, maintained by Internationale Automobile S.A. In 2002, 14545 was acquired by Thor Johannessen, near Cahors and thus integrated one of the most important French collections of the 2000s. It was in 2011 that its last private owner acquired it.

Since then, it was exhibited in its owner's private museum, this 365 GTC/4 is largely in original condition. Of course, it retains its original engine number 00026 corresponding to the Ferrari Pozzi identification plate. Its Weber carburettors also display serial numbers close to each other. The passenger compartment has a pleasant patina typical of the leathers used by Ferrari in the early 1970s.

Following several years of static display, this 365 GTC/4 represents an interesting project. Recommissioning will therefore be required, as the car has not been driven since 2023. In particular, bodywork repairs will be necessary to the underbody areas, as time and oxidation have affected certain sections of the chassis.

Sold with its French registration document as well as its user manual and spare parts catalogue, this 365 represents a rare opportunity to acquire one of the least produced road-going Ferraris.

Please note that Bonhams has an ownership interest in this Lot.

YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1964 DESCRIPTION:
• Delivered new in Germany
• Only 108,550 kilometres recorded
• Desirable manual transmission
• Highly original and unrestored
• Original leather interior

In 1959 Mercedes-Benz debuted four new models at the Frankfurt Show - the 220 SEb (W111) among them. Two-door Coupé and Convertible models appeared in 1960 and 1961 respectively, minus the already dated-looking tail fins of the saloon. More modern in style, the luxurious, hand-built 220 SEb Coupé and Convertible were better appointed too, being equipped as standard with a rev counter, leather upholstery and four-speed automatic transmission. Front disc brakes were fitted from the start of production. These top-of-the-range two-door models simply oozed quality in every department, and it is not surprising that they quickly became favourites among celebrities, royalty and industrialists, often seen in the most glamorous destinations worldwide.

Delivered new in Singen, Germany, this beautiful Mercedes-Benz 220 SEb Convertible has the rare four-speed manual transmission and matching numbers (chassis and engine). Carefully preserved and well maintained throughout its lifetime, the car has had two or possibly three owners in Germany plus one in the Netherlands. According to our vendor, the car has covered only 108,550 kilometres and is still highly original and in good condition. It is finished in the timelessly beautiful colour combination of Dunkelgrün (dark green) with a gorgeous brown leather interior and a brown convertible top. The body looks magnificent and has clearly been well cared for; it has been resprayed only once (for cosmetic reasons) and still looks good. The convertible top is easy to operate and fits nicely, and the car sits on its original steel wheels. Beautifully patinated, the interior seems completely original and appears just as well cared for as the rest of the car, while the seats are as comfortable as one would expect in a top-of-the-range Mercedes.

The car is powered by the 2.2-litre version of Mercedes-Benz's dependable M127 inline six producing 120bhp (DIN). Perfectly complemented by the four-speed manual transmission, the engine is said to be wonderfully smooth and to run beautifully. The chassis and brakes are also very well suited to their task and contribute to the comfortable driving experience; indeed, its relaxed road manners make the 220 SEb Convertible ideal for top-down, cross-country touring.

The car underwent extensive maintenance in 2022 and was serviced in 2023, 2024, and 2025. Well documented, it comes with the original data card; original Fahrzeugbrief; and its original wallet and all books (including the stamped service booklet). It currently has a Dutch registration. It is exceedingly rare to find an unrestored and unmolested Mercedes-Benz 220 SEb in such great condition as this one.

cultural_reference: Featured in the story of Steve McQueen
description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1970 DESCRIPTION:
• Delivered new in the USA
• Imported into Germany from California in 2005
• Comprehensively restored in 2005 (full details on file)
• Test-report rated as 'Condition 1'

Announced at the 1968 Geneva Salon, the Mercedes-Benz 300 SEL 6.3 was the ultimate wolf in sheep's clothing. Visually, the car was practically identical to other W109 models, but - thanks to the 600 limousine's fuel-injected 6,332cc V8 - offered stupendous performance. Air suspension, a limited-slip differential, and four-wheel disc brakes came as standard. Capable of sprinting to 100km/h in 6.5 seconds and reaching 220km/h (136mph), the '6.3' could outrun almost anything else on the road, sports cars included. Enthusiastic owners included Hollywood icon Steve McQueen, who famously ordered one after his Porsche 911 was blown away by a '6.3' on the German Autobahn.

One of only 6,526 produced, the example offered here was first delivered in California in June 1970. In 2005 it was brought to Germany and the previous owner started a comprehensive restoration process that took 1,550 hours. Finished in Silver Grey Metallic with black leather interior, this magnificent Mercedes-Benz is in beautifully preserved condition, having travelled only 15,000 kilometres since restoration. A recent third-party report from Franc Gourge at KFZ-Sachverständige declares that the car is in overall good condition both mechanically and cosmetically, and grades it as 'Condition 1', the top of the scale.

The car comes with German registration documents; the aforementioned condition report; and a file of 1,000-plus restoration photographs.

YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1972 DESCRIPTION:
• Delivered new as a van to the Ministero dell'Interno in Rome, Italy
• Frame-off restoration by the expert vendor (photographs available)
• Accommodation for eight (including the driver)
• Roadworthiness certificate valid until June 2027

According to information supplied by the Centro Documentazione Alfa Romeo, this charming Minibus was completed on 4th July 1972 and sold on 21st December that same year to the Ministero dell'Interno (Ministry of the Interior or Home Office) in Rome. It was delivered new as an unfurnished van powered by the trusted 1.3-litre Giulietta twin-cam engine with single carburettor.

As official vehicles in Italy have different numberplates, a new numberplate was assigned (it is assumed) when the car finished its ministerial career in 1982; consequently, that is the date of first registration on the Italian libretto. Importantly, the libretto states the permitted number of passengers (including the driver) is eight. It is noted on the accompanying Certificato d'Origine that the van had some accident damage earlier in its life, and the minibus also comes with a fresh revisione (roadworthiness certificate) valid until June 2027.

Benefiting from a frame-off restoration by our vendor, who specializes in these beautiful vehicles, the result can only be described as stunning: the two-tone paint elegantly divided by a red coachline and the eight-seat interior tastefully trimmed in brown vinyl with wood panelling. (There are restoration photographs on file showing the chassis and body separated.) We cannot think of a cooler way of taking your friends and family to any motoring event!

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1934 DESCRIPTION:
Body No. 18
• One of only 41 examples built, with an estimated dozen surviving
• Recently restored by its current owner
• Accompanied by its Laugier report
• Delivered new to Marseille

The Bugatti Type 57 was unveiled at the Paris Motor Show in October 1933 as a pillarless four-door saloon named "Galibier". Following the construction of three prototypes built for the presentation, 38 production cars were released in 1934 before Bugatti's own coachbuilding department ceased manufacture of this model. A second, very limited production run of just four bodies in 1935, followed by nine more in 1936, constitutes the second series of Bugatti-built Galibiers, of which only three of the thirteen are known to survive today. Production of the Galibier body by the Molsheim factory then ceased until 1938, when the second series entered production with a more aerodynamic design.

Bugatti Type 57 Galibier chassis no. 57140, corresponding to production number 35, was the 18th example of its kind to leave the Molsheim factory, as confirmed by the number "18" stamped on various wooden and aluminium body components. It is the first of four "C-I" (Conduite Intérieure) bodies built at Molsheim in June 1934, with the coachwork completed on 7 June 1934. Bugatti factory ledgers record that chassis 57140 was invoiced on 1 June 1934 for 61,695 francs to the "Société Marseillaise", run by Gaston Decollas, located at 42 Avenue du Prado in Marseille.

The completed car was dispatched by rail on 8 June 1934 and delivered to its first owner, Monsieur Jean-Michel Storione, at 11 Rue Saint-Jacques in Marseille, registered as 1034 CA 7. The Storione family, originally from Italy, had enjoyed considerable success in Marseille since the late 19th century in the bakery business and were also the founders of the famous Francine brand. Jean-Michel Storione, also known as Jean Storione, was a true connoisseur of mechanical engineering, with a passion for aviation as well as automobiles. Prior to becoming a valued client of the Molsheim marque, he owned several Delage cars. While his Bugattis were purchased through Gaston Decollas, they were maintained twice monthly by Mr Meronni. His Bugatti ownership included a Brescia in 1921, a Type 44 Torpedo in 1929, a Type 55 Roadster in 1933, a Type 49 in 1933, this Type 57 Galibier in 1934, an Atalante in 1938 and finally a Type 57C Stelvio in 1939.

Chassis 57140 also appears in the Bugatti factory mechanical repair archives. On 20 October 1934, when the car was just four months old, its engine was returned to the factory under warranty due to malfunctions. The repair record states: "Overhaul of engine No. 35: the crankcase, cylinder block and one connecting rod were damaged. Piston No. 1 was seized. Rectification required for connecting rods Nos. 4 and 8."

Jean Storione retained his Galibier until 1936, when he sold it—almost certainly through Decollas—to Dr Gustave Cousin, of 27 Boulevard Montricher in Marseille, one of the city's most prominent physicians. Dr Cousin kept the car for many years, registering it under the new registration system on 24 December 1954 as 7983 AQ 13, by then residing at 7 Cours F. Roosevelt (formerly 7 Cours Devilliers). In 1966, Dr Cousin sold chassis 57140 to Jean Brignone, of 47 Rue Monte Cristo, Marseille.

In 1967, the car was acquired by renowned Bugatti hunter Antoine Raffaelli, who recalled his first encounter with 57140: "I went to see the car at the Paragalo garage, 268 Boulevard Baille in Marseille, around 1960. The car was in for servicing for Cousin, and the mechanic was fitting special brake linings for improved braking. He had also cut the cam boxes to make the engine resemble that of an Alfa Romeo 8C! The car was black with blue sides...".

Raffaelli sold the car in the spring of 1967 to Parisian architect Daniel Guidot, then registered as 71 GU 78 and located at 5 Allée du Colombier, Le Pecq. Shortly thereafter, Guidot participated in the Paris–Nice Rally with 57140. Born in 1922, Daniel Guidot had served in the French Resistance during the war as a navigator for the Royal Air Force. A devoted Bugatti enthusiast, he also owned a Type 46 Vanvooren coachbuilt car and a Type 35A.

In 1974, chassis 57140 was sold to Jean Vilette, a member of the Club Bugatti France. Although based in Paris, Vilette worked near the German border, and by the mid-1980s the car was listed by the German Bugatti Club in 1989 as belonging to Walter Metz of Moosbrunn.

Later acquired by Feierabend Klassic Technik, the Bugatti was offered for sale at the 40th Essen Classic Show in 2007. It was subsequently sold to Roland d'Ieteren and intended as the basis for a Type 57S project for Jean-Jacques Strubb. Sadly, Strubb's fatal accident at the wheel of his Type 51 in April 2010 brought the project to an end, and chassis 57140 was not sold again until 2013, when it was acquired by noted marque enthusiast José Piger. The car remained untouched until its sale in 2019 to a Danish owner, at which time it largely retained its 1960s condition.

Acquired by the current owner in 2024, chassis 57140 has since undergone a comprehensive restoration carried out largely by the owner's own specialist workshops. The body was restored with particular attention to the wooden frame and metal panels before being repainted in its original colour scheme, as evidenced by a photograph dating from 1966. At the same time, the interior was restored to its original patterns, trimmed in an elegant red hue that harmonises beautifully with the woodwork and beige carpets.

The car retains its original crankcase stamped "35 – 57140" and still features its Jaeger black-faced instruments on the dashboard. Several body components retain the stamped number "18", confirming its position as the 18th Galibier produced by Bugatti's coachbuilding department. The original identification plate remains affixed to the bulkhead. The chassis frame is stamped 33 which seems consistent with the factory numbering sequence

Offered with its Laugier report, Danish registration document and a comprehensive history file containing period photographs and documentation of the recent restoration, this Bugatti Type 57 Galibier is regarded as "one of the most authentic surviving examples of this first design by Joseph Walter, created in 1932 for the new Type 57 chassis."

For 1978 the Porsche 911 Type 930 Turbo's air-cooled flat-six engine was enlarged to 3.3 litres, gaining an inter-cooler in the process; power increased to 300bhp and the top speed of what was the fastest-accelerating road car of its day went up to 160mph (257km/h). Refined over the years while retaining its high performance edge, the 930 Turbo sold in the thousands, becoming the definitive sports car of its age. When Porsche revealed that the original Type 930 would be replaced by the new Type 964 in 1990, dealer stocks of the existing Turbo model sold out overnight.

Finished in Marine Blue Metallic with a full leather interior in white, the latter in good condition, this late 930 Turbo is car is well equipped and comes with, among other thing : black-painted Fuchs wheels; rear windscreen wiper; electric seats; electric windows; leather dashboard; central locking; and air conditioning. Delivered new in April 1988 to its first owner by the Porsche Simoni dealership in Turin and purchased by the current owner nearly 20 years ago. model: DB4 'SS Engine' Series V Sports Saloon
restoration_history: Engine refurbished 10 years ago; gearbox synchros and clutch replaced; rear brake calipers rebuilt.
provenance: Mr Pierre Zannettacci, current vendor for over 50 years.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1962 DESCRIPTION:
• One of only six left-hand drive Series V cars with the Special Series engine
• Delivered new to France
• In the present ownership for over 50 years
• Matching numbers
• Original colour combination
• Engine refurbished 10 years ago

"Performance, controllability and comfort have been combined in the Aston Martin DB4 to make it a highly desirable car: one in which long journeys can be completed very quickly indeed with the minimum of risk or discomfort and the maximum of pleasure." - The Motor.

Classically proportioned and instantly recognisable from the moment of its introduction in 1958, the Touring-styled Aston Martin DB4 established a look that would survive, with only minor revisions, until 1970. Designed by Tadek Marek and already proven in racing, the DB4's new twin-cam six-cylinder engine displaced 3,670cc while the gearbox was a new David Brown four-speed all-synchromesh unit. An immensely strong platform-type chassis, designed by Harold Beach, replaced the preceding DB2/4's multi-tubular spaceframe, the latter being considered incompatible with Touring's Superleggera body construction. The DB2/4's trailing-link independent front suspension gave way to unequal-length wishbones while at the rear the DB4 sported a live axle located by a Watts linkage instead of its predecessor's Panhard rod. Boasting disc brakes all round and with 240bhp on tap, the DB4 was the first production car capable of accelerating from a standing start to 100mph and back to rest again in under 30 seconds. At a time when few family saloons were capable of exceeding 70mph and took an age to get there, this staggering performance made the DB4 just about the fastest thing on the road, easily the equal of its Italian rivals.

Manufactured between October 1958 and June 1963, the DB4 developed through no fewer than five series. However, it should be made clear that the cars were not thus designated by the factory, this nomenclature having been suggested subsequently by the Aston Martin Owners Club to aid identification as the model evolved. The first series had already undergone several improvements, including the fitting of heavy-duty bumpers after the first 50 cars, before the second series arrived in January 1960. A front-hinged bonnet, bigger brake callipers, and an enlarged sump were the major changes made on the Series II, while the third series featured separate rear lights, two bonnet stays, and a host of improvements to the interior fittings. The fourth series was readily distinguishable by its new grille (with seven vertical bars), shallower bonnet intake, and recessed rear lights, while the final (fifth) series manufactured between September 1962 and June 1963 was 3.5" longer (allowing for increased leg room and a larger boot) and gained 15" wheels, an electric radiator fan, and the DB4GT-type instrument panel.

One of the most notable developments had arrived with the introduction of the 'Series IV' in September 1961, when a 'Special Series' (SS) engine became available as an option. The 'SS' unit boasted a 9.0:1 compression ratio; larger valves and inner valve springs from the DB4GT; and triple SU HD8 carburettors with a black-painted cold-air box, producing 266bhp at 5,750rpm, a gain of 26 horsepower over the standard unit. Optional on the regular model, an oil cooler was standard on the cars coming with the SS engine. Almost all DB4 Vantages were built with the faired-in headlights of the DB4GT, making the example we offer something of a rarity.

The Series V is one of the rarest and most desirable of the DB range with only 50 cars built in this final incarnation of the DB4. Indeed, the original 'James Bond' car used in the filming of Goldfinger was a DB4 Series V, as they look virtually identical to the DB5, which at that time was not quite ready.

Chassis number '1001/L' is one of an estimated 19 Series V examples built with the Special Series (SS) engine, only six of which were of left-hand drive configuration like this car. Shipped to Aston Martin's French agent Garage Mirabeau on 4th October 1962, '1001/L' is a matching numbers example retaining its original engine, chassis, body, gearbox, exterior colour (Aegean Blue), and tan Connolly interior trim (VM 3280). The DB4 was delivered new on 27th October 1962 to its first owner, Mr Pierre Zannettacci, a French gentleman resident in the 16th District of Paris. Remarkably, the Aston has had only two owners since 1962, has belonged to the current vendor for more than 50 years, and has always remained Parisian since its arrival in France.

Some 10 years ago the engine was extensively refurbished; the gearbox synchros and clutch replaced; and the rear brake calipers rebuilt. The DB4 has been serviced regularly at Cecil Cars, and during a recent test drive, the engine started immediately and ran smoothly, revving without difficulties, performing well at low and high speeds, shifting gears smoothly.

Listed in James Taylor's book Factory-Original Aston Martin DB4/5/6, '1001/L' comes with sundry invoices; Garage Mirabeau's delivery note; the original purchase invoice; 2015 Expertise report; a valid French Carte Grise; and an up-to-date Contrôle Technique. A wonderful opportunity to acquire a highly original and well maintained Aston Martin DB4 Series V with Special Series engine - the first 'SS' Series V built - offered from long-term enthusiast ownership.

Unveiled in March 1961, the restyled Austin-Healey 3000 MkII boasted engine improvements in the form of triple SU carburettors and a revised camshaft, increasing maximum power to 132bhp. From November '61 a new gearbox was standardised, which at last moved the gear lever to the centre of the transmission tunnel. Contemporary road tests typically recorded performance figures of a 114mph top speed and a 0-60mph time of approximately 11 seconds.

This Austin-Healey 3000 MkII Convertible (BJ7) was despatched from the factory on 21st March 1963. Built for the North American export market, this left-hand drive car was originally finished in Ivory White with red interior trim and a black convertible hood. Factory-fitted equipment included wire wheels, heater, adjustable steering column, laminated windscreen, and overdrive. The car was destined for delivery to Royston, USA.

Our vendor purchased the Healey three years ago; it is currently finished in two-tone Ivory White over blue with dark blue leather interior. This Jowett Jupiter was registered new in the UK as 'JAK 592' on 1st December 1952, at which time it was painted British Racing Green. The Jupiter was first registered to the Jowett Car Co and then to one Leonard Chambers of Surrey in January 1953. From June 1961 it was owned by one J Batt of London, and from 24th October 1962 by Richard Hamlett of Reading, Berkshire. On 3rd October 1966 Mr Hamlett sold the Jowett to Mr Strinati, who imported it into Switzerland. Mr Strinati paid CHF 3,000 (purchase receipt on file). Mr Strinati had owned a new 1951 Jupiter with unique Ghia coachwork, given to him by his father. Information on how to maintain those cars was scarce, so he sold the Jupiter but later regretted it, hence his acquisition of this example (the unique Ghia was undoubtedly destroyed).

The Jowett sat unused until December 1993 when Mr Strinati had it restored by Geneva BMW specialists Pius Buch SA. The engine was rebuilt and the bodywork and hood were redone. The car has rarely been used since the restoration and still appears quite fresh. Nevertheless, recommissioning will be required following a period of inactivity. The car comes with various instruction manuals and plentiful correspondence with the Jowett Car Club. It should be noted that documentation on file records the original engine number as 'E2/SC/964R'.

historical_significance: Represents a rare and fascinating chapter in the sporting history of the Prancing Horse in the United States.
description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1990 DESCRIPTION:
• A genuine racing prototype built around the Ferrari V8 engine
• Highly original and extremely competitive
• Constructed by the late and renowned Joe Huffaker
• Originally commissioned by Paul Newman's racing associate, Bill Freeman
• Campaigned by its current owner in the Ultimate Cup Series in 2020 and 2021
• Approximately 390 bhp at 9,200 rpm for a weight of around 900 kg

Joe Huffaker (1927–2022) began building racing cars as early as the 1940s, before launching his professional career through a partnership with BMC following the competition success of his Austin-Healey 'Huffaker Special'. He subsequently produced a series of Genie sports cars powered by American V8 engines. In 1963, Huffaker entered the Indianapolis 500 under the MG banner.

The 1970s and 1980s proved particularly successful for Huffaker-prepared MG, Austin-Healey, Jaguar and Triumph models, with victories across the Can-Am, IMSA, SCCA and Trans-Am championships. Most notably, the Huffaker-prepared Pontiac Fieros achieved outstanding results in IMSA GTU, with Bob Earl securing ten victories and sixteen pole positions during the 1985 season alone.

Although the Ferrari 308 GTB was never conceived as a competition car, its inherent qualities were undeniable and quickly attracted the attention of independent constructors, most famously Michelotto. His Group 4 version enjoyed considerable success in rallying throughout Europe.

In the United States, Bill Freeman—close friend and racing associate of Paul Newman—identified the potential of the 308 and entered it into IMSA competition in the GTU category. Accordingly, in 1990, three cars were commissioned from Huffaker Motorsport by Newman Freeman Racing and CEO for the 1991 season. Built on tubular chassis derived from IndyCar technology, these 308s featured inboard pushrod suspension, Alcon brake calipers acting on 13-inch discs supplied by Coleman Racing Products, and 16-inch centre-lock BBS wheels. Pneumatic jacks enabled rapid lifting during pit stops.

Mechanically, the 3.0-litre quad-cam V8 was extensively reworked by Bill Pound Automotive, with the front of the block shortened to allow longitudinal rear mounting. The water pump was relocated, while the timing system was redesigned to accept Testarossa belts and adjustable pulleys. Custom-made camshafts were fitted, along with strengthened forged pistons and connecting rods. The 16 valves were optimised for both intake and exhaust, with titanium valve seats. Fuel injection was supplied by Hilborn components, managed by an EFI Technology control unit that also governed ignition for maximum efficiency. Lubrication was provided by a Weaver Bros dry-sump system. Producing approximately 390 bhp at 9,600 rpm, the engine was mated to a rear-mounted Hewland DGB five-speed gearbox.

The car was clothed in a composite body by Italian Design and Racing, echoing the styling cues of the Ferrari 288 GTO.

Unfortunately, changes to IMSA GTU regulations in 1991 prematurely ended the competitive career of the 308 GTB Huffaker. Built in just three examples, it saw only limited competition thereafter in SCCA GT2.

Chassis 003 arrived in France in 2008 after appearing at the Cavallino Classic in Monterey. Acquired by its current owner in 2017, it underwent a comprehensive overhaul in 2019 at Sébastien Darnand Moteur, including replacement of all four wheel bearings, fluid services and timing belts, as well as the installation of an automatic fire-extinguishing system. Since then, it has been driven by its owner at the 2019 Classic Days at Le Mans and in the Ultimate Cup Series at Dijon (2020) and Magny-Cours (2021).

Today, remarkably authentic and spared the excesses of prolonged competition, this Huffaker-Ferrari 308 GTB IMSA GTU represents a rare and fascinating chapter in the sporting history of the Prancing Horse in the United States. It would stand out in any marque-focused collection and is equally well suited to historic racing events or track days.

As a race car, it will be sold without a title but with accompanying invoices.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1938 DESCRIPTION:
• The ultimate expression of the eight-cylinder Delage
• Delivered new to and always resident in Switzerland
• Matching numbers and very well preserved
• Known ownership history
• Present ownership since circa 1960/1961
• Requires recommissioning

"Delage have to their credit many world's records, including a world's championship, and more awards at the principal Concours d'Élégance than any other car in the world... To these achievements Delage have added a third and greater. They have made the highest known degree of luxury and performance available at the price the average motorist can pay."

Delage's publicity had every right to sing the praises of what - arguably - was the finest French car of its day and the only one that could be mentioned in the same breath as the 32CV Hispano-Suiza in terms of elegance and engineering excellence. Founded in 1905 by Louis Delage, the company commenced production with a single-cylinder De Dion-engined runabout and within a few years was offering multi-cylinder designs. The publicity value of racing was recognised right from the start, a single-cylinder Delage winning the Coupe Des Voiturettes as early as 1908 and Louis himself taking the 1911 Coupe de l'Auto in a 3-litre four-cylinder. Victories at the Grand Prix du Mans and the Indianapolis 500-Mile Race were achieved prior to WWI, the company going on to become a major force in Grand Prix racing in the 1920s and setting a new World Land Speed Record mark in 1924 with a 10.7-litre overhead-valve V12.

Four- and six-cylinder D-series cars formed the mainstay of the company's touring car production in the 1920s, and then at the 1929 Paris Salon Delage launched the Maurice Gaultier-designed D8. A magnificent 4.0-litre overhead-valve straight-eight featuring an X-braced chassis and servo-assisted Perrot-type brakes, the D8 was destined to attract the creative attentions of Europe's finest coachbuilders. The impressive list of discerning D8 owners includes King Gustav V of Sweden, King Alexander of Yugoslavia, and Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia as well as leading businessmen, politicians, and film stars of the day. The Autocar magazine said this of the D8: "...all the speed that can possibly wanted, and extremely rapid acceleration are obtained with practically no noise at all, and driven normally the car is docile..."

Along with many other manufacturers of quality cars, Delage was badly affected by the economic downturn of the early 1930s. Despite the favourable reception for its new range, Automobiles Delage went into receivership in April 1935 and shortly thereafter was taken over by Delahaye. The Delahaye takeover spelled the end for the original D8. From then onwards, Delages were built to Delahaye designs but retained their own superior short-stroke engines and hydraulic brakes.

The post-war years were difficult times for makers of large and luxurious automobiles in France. Taxation rates were punitive for cars of over 2 litres, choking off demand, and in 1950 the combined total production of Delahaye and Delage was only 235 units. This unsustainable situation worsened over the next two years and in 1953 Delage production stopped. It was a sad end to a once great marque.

Representing the ultimate expression of the eight-cylinder Delage, this supremely elegant D8-120 was ordered in December 1938 by the Swiss Delage and Delahaye representative Albert Goy of Garage du Kursaal in Geneva for their customer, Mr Gossweiler of Bern. Delahaye commissioned the cabriolet body from the celebrated Parisian coachbuilder Henri Chapron, who completed the work the following summer.

The car comes with copies of the factory records stating that it was ordered in black with a red interior and a black alpaca hood, while a thin red coachline was applied to the body. The Delage was specifically ordered with Securit glass; two indicators at the front and at the rear; two extra fog lights; an extra powerful horn; and a steering column-mounted ignition key doubling as an anti-theft device. The client also specifically requested that the rear seats should be removable and that the rear floor was to be flat so he could store bulky luggage such as hunting gear (Chapron refused to comply with that last request blaming the shape of the chassis as an excuse).

There is a wealth of correspondence with all parties mentioned above, most interestingly a very detailed letter from Mr Gossweiler complaining about the poor build quality of the bodywork, most notably the fixing of the dashboard and the hood cover (which he had remade). Mr Gossweiler considered keeping the amount he was due to pay upon collecting the car as a guarantee for the work that was to be carried out on it!

This car has always stayed in Switzerland and was later owned - in 1949 - by the Industrialist Ludwig Zweifel of Glaris (CH) and then by dentist Walter Meier domiciled in Blonay (in the Vaud canton) from 1953. Pierre Strinati bought the Delage circa 1960/1961 from Carrosserie Graber, who fully repainted the car and retrimmed the hood in April 1961 (bill on file). The paintwork was changed to two-tone dark grey over black (probably during Mr Strinati's ownership), which suits the D8 very well. The leather interior remains original, as does the rest of the car.

More recently the Delage was pictured in Henry Rasmussen's book The Survivors. A copy of the latter is on file and the car also comes with old Swiss registration papers. Recommissioning will be required following a lengthy period of inactivity. Close inspection recommended.

The Willys-Overland company is forever associated with the original Jeep of WW2. Produced by the million, the Jeep saw service in every theatre of WW2 and continued in military service for several decades thereafter. Perhaps not surprisingly, Willys did not return to mainstream passenger car manufacturing at the war's end, preferring to market civilian versions of the Jeep, most of which were intended for commercial use. Its first post-war passenger car was the Station Wagon, introduced for 1946, which featured an all-steel body painted to resemble a timber-framed 'Woodie'. The front-end styling recalled that of the Jeep, and the Station Wagon was powered by a four-cylinder side-valve engine displacing 134.2ci (2.2 litres).

Arguably one of the very first examples of the 'Sport Utility Vehicle', this Station Wagon was purchased by Mr Strinati in August 1982 from Garage Kleefled in Bern, Switzerland. It was acquired as a memento of the similar example he bought from Garage P Jolliet of Geneva on 21st May 1954 and used on various expeditions all around the world.

The Jeep was most likely undergoing some restoration (probably a repaint in its most unusual Lilac colour) as the rear lights are missing. It is not known when the car was last used, and it will require recommissioning.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1961 DESCRIPTION:
• Delivered new to dealer Max Moritz in Reutlingen, Germany
• Part of a Spanish private collection since 2009
• Beautifully presented
• Porsche Certificate of Authenticity
• German registered

One of the all-time great sports cars, the 356 was the work of Ferry Porsche, who had been inspired by the FIAT-based Cisitalias of Piero Dusio. Ferry's 356 was based on the Volkswagen designed by his father, and like the immortal 'Beetle' employed a platform-type chassis with rear-mounted air-cooled engine and all-independent torsion-bar suspension. Introduced in 1948, the Porsche 356 set a new standard for small sports cars and proved adaptable to all forms of motor sport including circuit racing and rallying. In 1951 a works car finished first in the 1,100cc class at the Le Mans 24-Hour Race, thus beginning the marque's long and illustrious association with La Sarthe.

Cabriolets had been manufactured right from the start of 356 production, but the first open Porsche to make a significant impact was the Speedster, introduced in 1954 following the successful reception in the USA of a batch of 15 special roadsters. The Reutter-bodied Speedster was dropped in 1958 and replaced by the more civilised Convertible D, which differed principally by virtue of its larger windscreen and winding side windows. Porsche sub-contracted soft-top body construction to a number of different coachbuilders, predominantly Glaser and Reutter in the early years, while production of the Convertible D (now renamed 'Roadster') was undertaken by Drauz of Heilbronn and later d'Ieteren of Brussels. Reutter was predominantly responsible for the Coupé and Cabriolet.

By the time the 356B arrived in September 1959, the car had gained a one-piece rounded windscreen and 15"-diameter wheels, and the newcomer's introduction brought with it further styling revisions. The engine, now standardised at 1,600cc, was available in three different stages of tune, the most powerful - apart from the four-cam Carrera - being the 90bhp unit of the Super 90. The 356B represents significant advances in drive-ability and comfort over earlier 356 models and is a pleasingly quick way to enjoy the traditional Porsche values of quality, reliability and mechanical robustness.

According to the accompanying Porsche Certificate of Authenticity (issued by Porsche Spain), this beautifully presented 356B Cabriolet was delivered new in October 1961 to the historic Porsche dealer Max Moritz in Reutlingen (the first Porsche dealer in the world). The original colour combination was Champagne with a green leather interior. Other options listed are additional rear springs, a telescopic aerial, two loudspeakers and a self-dimming rear view mirror.

Since 2009 this car has formed part of a private collection in Spain and presents very well indeed. During restoration the car's colours were changed to the period-correct and equally beautiful silver metallic with a red leather interior and black hood. Accompanying paperwork includes copies of the Spanish registration papers; current German registration papers; the aforementioned Porsche CoA; and an expert's report confirming the car's generally very good condition.

• Dating from the first year of Sting Ray production

• Rare and desirable four-speed manual gearbox
• Imported into Sweden from the USA

Now recognised as representing a 'Golden Age' for Chevrolet's Corvette sports car, the Sting Ray version was manufactured from 1963 to 1967 and has since gone on to become a highly collectible modern classic. The first 'Split Window' model lasted for only one year, a single-piece rear screen becoming the norm thereafter, and is considered one of the most desirable of Corvette variants. A little over 21,000 Sting Rays were made in 1963, the production split being roughly 50/50 coupé/convertible. And, as is the case with most American cars of this period, the Corvette buyer could choose from a host of factory options with the result that seldom are two cars exactly alike.

The current owner imported this 'Split Window' model from the USA into Sweden in 2013, since when he has installed air conditioning and serviced the driveshaft, brakes and rear axle. Finished in light blue metallic with black interior, the Corvette is described by the private vendor as in generally good condition, though there is some slight damage visible in the right front wheelarch. There are some documents with the car, but nothing that states it has been restored; according to our vendor, the paint has not been measured but could possibly be original. The car is registered in Sweden and comes with Swedish registration documents.

This Mercedes-Benz 190 SL was purchased new by Madame Jeanne Strinati, Pierre Strinati's mother, on 28th June 1956 from Etoilauto SA, Mercedes-Benz's exclusive dealer in Geneva. She part-exchanged her 1955 Mercedes-Benz 180, which she had bought in November 1955 (both bills on file). The 190 SL was painted black with matching hardtop and a white natural interior (1097). It was also fitted with five whitewall tyres.

Interestingly, there is no structure for a convertible hood, and all in-period photographs of the car show it with the hardtop on. It would seem it was never taken off. We were told that Mr Strinati did not like to get cold and so preferred closed cars to convertibles. Perhaps was his mother the same?

One of the most original 190 SLs Bonhams has seen, it is still fitted with its rubber carpet at the front, retains its original Karl Baisch fitted luggage, and even has the bottle of touch-up paint in the boot! The current odometer reading is 4,612 kilometres, which we have reason to believe is the distance covered from new, such is the car's remarkable state of preservation. We also believe that the paintwork is original. Recommissioning will be required following a period of inactivity. The car comes with a period manual, period advertising brochures, various receipts, and tax and insurance invoices. Close inspection recommended.

YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 2018 DESCRIPTION:
• Delivered new in Germany

Introduced as long ago as 1979, the Mercedes-Benz G-Class 'Geländewagen' (cross-country vehicle) was the result of a joint venture with Steyr-Daimler-Puch of Austria, a firm with considerable experience in developing four-wheel-drive systems for off-road vehicles. Its purposeful appearance – fundamentally unchanged throughout its life – and engineering excellence has secured the G-Wagen cult status and earned it a reputation as one of the most coveted of classic 4x4s.

For 1991 an extensively revised (W463) chassis was introduced, incorporating the very latest in off-road traction technology in the form of three electronically engaged differentials in addition to anti-lock brakes. The W463 moved the G-Class from spartan and utilitarian to a luxury model able to compete with the rival Range Rover.

There have been countless updates to the W463 since then and a host of special variants. One of the final models released before production of the W463 ceased in 2018, the G63 was powered by AMG's 5.5-litre twin-turbocharged V8 engine developing 571PS, which was delivered to the ground via AMG's Speedshift Plus 7G-tronic automatic transmission. Boasting high ground clearance and long-travel suspension, the AMG G63 offered greater off-road capability than most customers would ever need in an immensely stylish conveyance with not inconsiderable on-the-road presence. Like the entire model series, the G63 AMG was produced in Graz, primarily in the factory's hand-finishing section.

Representing possibly a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to own one of these rare and super-exclusive luxury 4x4s, this stunning example of the fabulous Mercedes-AMG G63 was dispatched from the factory in Graz, Austria on 21st February 2018. Highlights of the options list include Designo Mystic White 2 Bright paintwork; Exclusive two-tone leather interior; brake calipers painted red; Harman Kardon sound system with Smartphone Integration and Carplay; electric sunroof; 21" AMG wheels; and the Design Exclusive package to name but a few.

The Mercedes was delivered new in Germany and first registered to a company but scarcely used, which explains the current odometer reading of just over 120 kilometres. As a result, this is as close to a new Mercedes-AMG G63 as one can buy; indeed, the interior still features the original protective plastic covering in some places. With only one registered owner from new, this highly desirable 'low mileage' G63 comes with Euro 6 emissions compliance; German registration documents, a copy of the Manufacturer's Certificate of Conformity; and its original books.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1966 DESCRIPTION:
• Delivered new to Rome, Italy
• One of 460 Series II cars
• Highly original and unrestored
• Matching numbers (chassis & engine)

Introduced in January 1964, the 330 GT 2+2 was the second of Ferrari's four-seater road cars, following the 250 GTE 2+2. Pininfarina was once again entrusted with the styling, adopting a four-headlamp frontal treatment that reflected the tastes of Ferrari's most important export market, the USA. The 330 GT's tubular chassis was 50mm longer in the wheelbase than before, which made conditions less cramped for the rear passengers, while improvements to the discs-all-round braking system saw separate hydraulic circuits adopted for front and rear.

Displacing 3,967cc, the single-overhead-camshaft, all-alloy V12 engine was good for 300-plus horsepower, an output sufficient to propel the 330 GT to a maximum velocity of 152mph (245km/h) making it, when introduced, the fastest road-going Ferrari. Equipped at first with a four-speeds-plus-overdrive gearbox, the 330 GT gained a five-speed transmission mid-1965 and later that year had its four-headlight front end replaced by a two-lamp arrangement, these later cars being known as the 'Series II'. By the time production ceased in 1967, Ferrari had built 1,088 330 GTs, of which 460 were to Series II specification.

This desirable two-headlamp Series II was delivered new in Rome, Italy on 12th February 1966 and registered to one Umberto Martinozzi, as recorded in the accompanying Carta di Circolazione and Foglio Complementare. On 12th May 1967 the Ferrari was sold to Giorgio Marcella in Rome, and at the end of 1968 was acquired by another Roman resident, Maurizio Rometti. The car's subsequent ownership history is not known prior to the current owner's acquisition two years ago. A highly original example, unusual in so far as it has never been restored, '8023' retains its matching engine, original metallic grey paintwork, and original light blue leather interior.

In addition to the aforementioned documents, the Ferrari also comes with its old Roman license plates. The car is not currently registered and is sold without a technical inspection. A wonderful opportunity to acquire a highly original example of this landmark Ferrari Gran Turismo, delivered new to Rome, which undoubtedly forms the basis of a beautiful restoration project.

Exceptional autograph album containing more than 70 signatures from Formula 1 drivers and leading figures of European and international endurance racing from the 1940s to the 1960s. Belgian drivers:

One of the most illustrious of Italian coachbuilders, Carrozzeria Vignale of Turin was founded in 1948 by Alfredo Vignale, whose career had begun pre-war with a successful design on the FIAT Topolino chassis. Enzo Ferrari's favoured coachbuilder during Maranello's formative years, Carrozzeria Vignale also designed and built cars for Lancia and Maserati among others, and in the 1960s branched out into automobile manufacture in its own right. By this time Vignale was turning out some 1,000 bodies a year, necessitating its relocation to larger premises at Grugliasco, not far from FIAT's factory at Mirafiori, Turin. Styling maestro Giovanni Michelotti was responsible for many of Vignale's designs of this period.

FIAT chassis formed the basis for many of Vignale's more popular models, including this 750 Spyder, which is based on the FIAT 600 D. The car was registered in the name of its first owner, a resident of Milan, on 8th May 1963. In 1968 it changed hands, this time passing to a lady owner, again a resident of Milan. She kept the car until 1987 when it was purchased by another lady, again in the same city.

It is most attractively finished in red with a black hood and black seats, while the door cards have been personalised at some point and are finished in white and black. This most elegant small convertible, styled by one of Italy's foremost coachbuilders, has obviously been well restored at some point in its life. It comes complete with its original Italian libretto; a FIAT Certificate of Origin (referring to the car as a FIAT 600 D, which it is based on); and an original Vignale sales brochure. The car was recently serviced and has passed the Italian "Revisione", the Italian road worthiness certificate.

Replacing the 1900 range, the 102 2000 series cars appeared in 1958. The Touring Superleggera technique was again used for the body, but this time the panels were pressed by machine rather than hammered by hand. Under the body, the 2000 remained fairly close to the latest 1900s, with independent front suspension, a rigid rear axle, a five-speed gearbox and drum brakes on all four wheels. The 2000's twin-cam engine combined elements of the 1900 (cast-iron block and separate cylinder heads) with elements of the new Giulietta (overhead cam tappet and cam-spring valve adjustment system). The Spider and Sprint versions were fitted with a 115 bhp engine, allowing them to reach a top speed of over 177 km/h.

Dismantled and repainted in 2005, this example has been in the hands of the late Jan Steutel (Dutch Alfa Romeo specialist) who rebuilt the engine and overhauled the mechanics nearly 15 years ago. The car then went to Carensance Classic Cars (Netherlands) where the interior was dismantled, the floors were treated against rust, a rebuilt dynamo was installed and an electronic 123 distribution was added. In 2016, Classic Alfa (the largest English specialist in Alfa Romeo parts) acquired this beautiful car from VSOC (Netherlands) and on its arrival in the UK, an electric power steering was installed, and the braking system was completely rebuilt (master cylinder, new wheel cylinders, restored drums, new linings installed).

This 2000 Spider was acquired by its current owner at our Goodwood Revival sale on 17 September 2022. At that time the car had only covered some 87,000 km and according to our seller it has only done a few hundred kilometres since and has always been well maintained and dry stored. The car comes with an Alfa Romeo Classiche certificate of origin and English registration documents (logged as exported).

In December 1919 the newly created Rolls-Royce of America Incorporated purchased the American Wire Wheel Company's plant in Springfield, Massachusetts, from which the first US-built Silver Ghost emerged in January 1921. Unlike its British-built counterpart, the American 'Ghost could be ordered with 'factory' bodywork, usually by Brewster, the latter company being taken over by Rolls-Royce in December 1925. Right-hand drive remained the norm for US-built cars until early in 1925, the penultimate year of Silver Ghost production, when the switch was made to left-hand drive. The model was replaced by the New Phantom (retrospectively Phantom I) in 1926.

Prior to its acquisition of Brewster, Rolls-Royce of America Inc had set up the Rolls-Royce Custom Coach Works (RRCCW) program to organise the supply of 'factory' bodywork, commencing with the Silver Ghost and continuing on its New Phantom successor. Various established coachbuilders supplied bodies badged as 'RRCCW', including Massachusetts-based Merrimac, whose sporting Piccadilly Roadster was deservedly popular, some 70 being completed.

Retaining its original Piccadilly coachwork, this Springfield Silver Ghost was delivered new on 18th September 1923 to Mr Charles E F Clarke of 40 Wall Street. New York City. The car is finished in Old English White with beige leather interior, and is an early Springfield Ghost with right-hand drive and the four-speed gearbox (the model was only delivered in this configuration for the first two years). The car is believed to have been owned at one time by the well-known Campbell family in the USA. The current owner purchased the Rolls-Royce from S. Prestley Blake in the spring of year 2000 and it has been in their family's possession ever since.

The 'Ghost is an older restoration believed carried out in the 1970s-1980s. Around 2005 the engine underwent a comprehensive overhaul by renowned Rolls-Royce expert in Sweden, Kjell Lind, who has been helping the current owners with starting and running the car in recent years. The Ghost is today described as in good original condition. It is currently registered in Sweden and comes with Swedish registration documents, a folder of invoices, copies of the first US title, and other historic documents. As one would expect, this car is mentioned in the book Rolls Royce in America by John Webb de Campi.
