Introduced at the Frankfurt Auto Show in April 1951, the Mercedes-Benz 220 was in effect a six-cylinder cousin to the four-cylinder 170S on the same 2,845mm-wheelbase chassis. Although closely based on the 170S, the 220 featured more modern styling with headlamps integrated into the wings. With 80bhp on tap courtesy of its 2.2-litre overhead-camshaft engine, delivered via a four-speed manual gearbox, the 220 saloon was good for a top speed of around 140km/h (87mph) - as was the Cabriolet B - with 145km/h (90mph) attainable by the Cabriolet A drophead coupé. In the best Mercedes-Benz tradition, both of these convertible models were exceptionally well equipped. Combined Cabriolet A/B production amounted to only 2,360 units in five years, 997 of which were the Cabriolet B version, as seen here. Today these exclusive models are both rare and highly sought after.

This particular Mercedes-Benz Cabriolet B was purchased by the current owner at a French auction in November 1994. The Mercedes has been serviced regularly by local specialists in France. Presented in nice condition both inside and out, the car comes with invoices for works and maintenance; the 1994 bill of sale; a French Carte Grise; an up-to-date Contrôle Technique; and an expertise report.

A proposed Group 5 'Silhouette Formula' for production-based cars triggered the M1 programme in the mid-1970s, a mid-engined concept car designed in-house at BMW by Paul Bracq providing the basis. Head of BMW's newly formed Motorsport Division, former racing driver Jochen Neerpasch was responsible for masterminding this ambitious project, whose aims included taking on rivals Porsche in the World Sportscar Championship and, ultimately, victory at Le Mans.

M1 development was contracted first to Lamborghini and then to Giorgetto Giugiaro's Ital Design, although almost all cars ended up being built by BMW in Germany. Giugiaro's compact coupé bodywork in glassfibre was wrapped around a multi-tubular spaceframe chassis, while a twin-overhead-cam, four-valves-per-cylinder version of BMW's 3.5-litre inline six, driving via a ZF five-speed transaxle, provided the motive power.

The M1's wedge-shaped coachwork proved highly efficient aerodynamically, needing very little in the way of additional spoilers and wings in race configuration. Lamborghini's Gianpaolo Dallara had been responsible for developing the suspension, which followed racing practice by using unequal-length wishbones at front and rear. Soberly trimmed in black and grey, the M1's interior was exceptionally well equipped for a sports car, featuring Recaro seats, air conditioning, electric windows, remotely operated door mirrors and a heated rear screen.

First shown at the Paris Motor Show in 1978, the road-going version came with 273bhp and a top speed of 165mph (265km/h). Only ever intended as a limited-edition model, the M1 ceased production after a little over 450 examples had been built, just exceeding the minimum of 400 required for Group 4 homologation, which would have preceded homologation for Group 5. In the event, the abandonment of the Group 5 Silhouette Formula robbed the car of its raison d'être, though the one-make Procar BMW M1 Championship series run at Formula 1 Grand Prix races in 1979 and '80 provided BMW Motorsport with a valuable showcase by way of consolation. The series ran for only those two years, Nicki Lauda winning the 1979 championship and Nelson Piquet the 1980 one. A new M1 road car was awarded to each winner.

Delivered new to its first owner in Berlin, Germany in the stunning colour combination of Inka Orange with black interior, this M1 is believed to have been enjoyed by the first owner's family from new until very recently, when it was purchased by our vendor. The car had been carefully enjoyed by its Berlin-based owner, who always had it meticulously serviced, mostly at the main BMW concessionaire in Berlin. By 1996 it had already covered some 105,000 kilometres, as evidenced by entries in the accompanying original service book, which has been stamped on no fewer than 19 occasions. At the time of cataloguing the odometer reading was 141,000 kilometres, a testament to BMW reliability and the fact that the M1 has always been, and still is, a very useable supercar.

A new clutch was installed in 2017, while more recent works include services in 2023 and October 2024, when new Pirelli tyres were fitted (P7 to the front, PZero Asimmetrico to the rear) and the oil and brake fluid changed. Since acquisition by our vendor, the central cooling water pipes (which are located in the central tunnel in the chassis and are a notorious M1 weakness) were replaced with original BMW items and the surrounding area thoroughly cleaned and sealed. Charmingly, the interior boasts a period Clarion sound system including radio, cassette player and amplifier as well as sportier Recaro bucket seats, trimmed in black leather.

An important landmark in BMW's history, and in particular of its involvement with motor sport in the post-war era, the M1 is already highly collectible and is surely destined to become increasingly sought after by discerning aficionados of the marque. Offered with German registration documents, its original service book and owner's manual, and various invoices, this BMW M1 ticks all the boxes: Giugiaro styling, superb and reliable BMW engine, beautiful colour combination and long-term enthusiastic ownership.

This was a total body-off restoration down to the last nut and bolt (all in the original Toyota finish) with the utmost attention paid to detail such as the spot-welding dots behind the wings.

This model, unlike the earlier BJ40s, has all the available options already installed by the factory: front disc brakes; power steering; original Toyota fifth gear; digital clock; six-digit odometer display; larger 3,400cc engine instead of 3,000cc etc, etc. This car is from one of the last batches produced and comes with the original matrix-printed tag behind the windscreen. Simply constructed, practical to own and offering 100mph-plus performance at a bargain price, the Triumph TR2 was an enormous success both at home and abroad, so it was only to be expected that its successor would represent evolution rather than revolution. Introduced in October 1955, the TR3 was little different from the TR2; changes to the 2.0-litre engine boosted power from 90 to 95bhp thanks to the use of large SU HS6 carburettors, but the most obvious difference was the 'egg box' radiator grille. By mid-1956 the engine developed 100bhp courtesy of a new cylinder head; then, in August, Girling front disc brakes and a stronger rear axle were standardised. Cosmetically revised but mechanically indistinguishable, the more refined TR3A version was phased in during 1957.

Finished in primrose yellow with black leather interior, the latter in good condition, this left-hand drive TR3A features its original four-speed/overdrive gearbox, original hardtop, headlight protection grilles, removable windows, luggage rack, and wire-spoked wheels. Owned by the same family for over 15 years, the TR3A has been restored and regularly serviced and has been driven regularly by the owner's daughter in recent times. In good cosmetic condition overall, the car comes with a file of invoices for recent maintenance work, an owner's workshop manual, technical documents, an expired French Contrôle Technique and a French Carte Grise.

The Lancia Aurelia was launched at the Turin Motor Show in 1950. It was the result of a close collaboration between designer Felice Mario Boano of Ghia, Carrozzeria Pininfarina and an engineering team led by Vittorio Jano, a former Alfa Romeo engineer and a leading figure in automotive engineering at the time. With its pioneering monocoque design, it was the first production car to be equipped with a V6 engine. The B20 of the third series and subsequent series, launched in 1953, were equipped with a 2,451 cc pushrod V6 engine developing 118 hp.

The chassis B20-3271 was completed on 23 September 1954 before being first registered on 23 November 1954 in the name of Lancia GB, in Alperton, England and delivered new on 1 December 1954 to A B Blanch & Co, in England. It is believed to be one of only six Aurelia B20 Series IVs delivered to the UK. It then belonged to Blanch Lely, in Wiltshire (from 11 January 1964), and then successively to A. McArthur, Beacon Motors, David Hayne, John Glen and Austin Watts, all in the Bristol area. In 1986, the Lancia was purchased by David Sankey, who undertook a complete and documented restoration, with Tim Burrett (an Aurelia specialist) rebuilding the engine with high-lift Nardi camshafts. On 1 December 2003, the Aurelia was purchased by Catherine Janssens, at a Bonhams sale. Maintenance and servicing continued to be carried out by Tim Burrett. In October 2010, the car was sold at auction in London, UK, to Brian Classick & Co, before being sold again in 2011. In 2013, the Lancia was repainted in the original Lancia colour, amaranto, by the Haslams restorers in Bolton, UK. The car was serviced by brand specialists, R&D Automotive Limited of Manchester, with parts supplied by Omicron Engineering Limited (including an MSD ignition conversion to aid starting and the fitting of a battery isolator).

Purchased by its current owner at our Goodwood Revival sale on 17 September 2022, it has since only covered a few hundred miles, always maintained with care and stored dry as advised by its owner. The car comes with an FCA Heritage Classiche certification (issued in July 2018), a FIVA passport, a FIA Historic Regularity documentation and English registration documents (logged as exported). The following items also come with the car: folder and plaque, documented historical folder, original 'bench-seating' frame, jack bag and embroidered Lancia interior car cover.

"The most luxurious BMW from the pre-war period was the BMW 335, which was the last BMW to go into series production before the war broke out in 1939. The body was essentially a 326 body extended by 23 cm. The increased weight required more powerful brakes and wider tyres. The 3.5 litre inline six-cylinder engine was completely new with a maximum output of 90 hp. The luxurious interior and the top speed of 145 km/h made the BMW 335 a comfortable yet fast touring car and enabled BMW to enter the segment for luxury cars." - BMW.

The success of the Type 326 and its derivatives prompted BMW to build a larger car to take on the likes of Mercedes-Benz and Horch. That first upmarket model was the 335. Three versions were offered: a four-door saloon and two- and four-door cabriolets. Only some 410-420 had been made up to 1941 when production ceased.

One of the very last manufactured, this ultra-rare BMW 335 two-door cabriolet is finished in two-tone grey/green with grey interior. Mr Strinati purchased the car on 30th August 1963 (Swiss taxes had been paid in January 1947). Unfortunately, very little is known about its earlier history, but as with most of the cars in the Collection, we believe it was never restored. Recommissioning will be required before the car returns to the road.

This example of Ferrari's sought-after modern classic 512 TR supercar is finished in the timeless colour combination of Rosso Corsa with black leather interior. auction_title: Scuderia Ferrari F1 – 1950 to 2019 - Over one hundred driver autographs – Collection of 136 models at 1/43 scale
historical_significance: Collection traces the evolution of Scuderia Ferrari Formula 1 cars from 1950 to 2019.
description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1950 DESCRIPTION:
An exceptional collection of 136 Ferrari Formula 1 models at 1/43 scale, each accompanied by a standing driver figure wearing full racing suit and helmet.
Each model originally derives from a high-quality kit, predominantly in white metal (such as BBR, Tameo, and others), and has been assembled by professional model makers.
Almost all models are accompanied by the autograph of the driver represented.
This collection traces the evolution of Scuderia Ferrari Formula 1 cars from 1950 to 2019.
Each car is presented with a plaque indicating the Grand Prix, model type, race number, and the signature of the model maker.
Beside each car stands its driver in full racing attire, with a separate plaque at his feet bearing his autograph.
The collection includes signatures from many legendary drivers, among them:
Fangio, Hawthorn, Hill, Ickx, Amon, Andretti, Lauda, Villeneuve, Prost, Barrichello, Massa, Alonso, Räikkönen, Schumacher, Irvine, Brooks, Mairesse, Vettel, Berger, Pironi, Regazzoni, and many others.
Also featured are autographs of drivers tragically killed during races:
Ascari (1955), Castellotti (1957), Collins (1958), Hawthorn (1959), von Trips (1961).
The ensemble represents an average of two models per year.
This lifetime collection was made possible only through privileged personal contact with the drivers and their representatives.

historical_significance: Represents the Porsche 911 in its earliest and purest form
description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1966 DESCRIPTION:
• Delivered new in Germany
• Matching chassis and engine numbers
• Known single family ownership history
• Restored by Porsche in 1998 (invoice available)
• Original colour scheme

Few sports cars have proved as versatile as Porsche's perennial 911, a model that, for the last 60-plus years, has proved equally capable as a Grand Tourer, circuit racer, or rally car. A 'modern classic' if ever there was one, the 911 first appeared at the 1963 Frankfurt Show as the '901', but shortly after production proper commenced in 1964 had become the '911' following Peugeot's complaints about the use of '0' model numbers. The preceding Type 356's rear-engined layout was retained, but the 911 switched to unitary construction for the chassis/body and dropped the 356's VW-based suspension in favour of a more modern McPherson strut and trailing arm arrangement. In its first incarnation, Porsche's single-overhead-camshaft, air-cooled flat six engine displaced 1,991cc and produced 130bhp; progressively enlarged and developed, it would eventually grow to more than 3.0 litres and, in turbo-charged form, put out well over 300 horsepower.

This Porsche 911 offered here, chassis number '304 449', is one of the early, short-wheelbase cars of the type much favoured by the historic rallying fraternity, a situation that has led to original examples such as this one becoming a great rarity and consequently much in demand. It is a 1966 model year car, and belongs to the '0-Programme' series built from the start of production in August 1964 up to the introduction of the 'A-Programme' model in August 1967, and thus represents the Porsche 911 in its earliest and purest form.

This car was delivered new on 13th May 1966 to company owner Fritz Fuss through the Max Moritz Porsche dealership in Reutlingen, Germany. In 1998, following restoration at Porsche costing over 50,000 DM (invoice on file), its registration status was changed from commercial to private use. At the end of 2004 the 911's ownership was transferred to the owner's son-in-law. It currently has a German registration.

The car comes with its original folder containing all documents (owner's manual, service books, sunroof manual, etc); a Porsche Certificate of Authenticity; and its first, second and third German titles, which had to be updated over the decades due to new regulations imposed by the German government. Indeed, this is a good documented early 911, that is a rare 'full-matching-numbers' example with a 87,990 kilometres recorded. Understood to have never been raced or rallied, it appears to be in very good condition throughout, retaining its original interior and fitted with a radio in the glove compartment (easily removed).

This exceptional short-wheelbase Porsche 911 is the perfect car for historic rallies, being both fast and competitive.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1967 DESCRIPTION:
• Fitted with the sought-after ZF 5-speed gearbox
• Recently recommissioned by Provost Automobiles Le Mans
• More than €30.000 spent in service in the last two years
• Elegant colour combination

Motor magazine was particularly impressed by the power and balance of the Vantage it tested: "The DB6 has a habit of making the 70 mph speed limit seem ridiculous, reaching it with an ease few other cars can rival. At its maximum speed—more than twice as high—it displays reassuring stability, probably more so than many cars struggling to maintain 70 mph. Should one need to stop from high speed, the brakes are exceptionally powerful, to the point that one must constantly check the rear-view mirror for less well-equipped followers. And its road-holding, both in the dry and in the wet, is superior to almost every production two-seat sports car we have tested, with only two exceptions".

Curiously, having brought the DB4 concept to near perfection with the DB6, Aston Martin chose to change direction with the larger DBS and its successors, adopting a V8 engine. Today, the highly accomplished DB6—arguably the most refined and user-friendly of all the DB models—is paradoxically also the most accessible. Production of the DB6 Coupé totalled 1,327 units, including seven shooting brake conversions by Harold Radford.

This Aston Martin DB6 Vantage was delivered on 13 April 1967 to Wilmslow Garage. It was specified with the Vantage engine, chromed wheels with three-eared centre-lock spinners and was originally finished in Pacific Blue with Natural Connolly leather upholstery. The factory build sheet confirms that it left the works fitted with engine number 400/2895/V, identifying it as a genuine Vantage model. Records also show that it was maintained within the Aston Martin dealer network until 1974. It is likely during this period that the engine was replaced with unit number 400/4413/SVC, dated 1970 and identical in specification to the original. The car's identification plate correctly corresponds with the current engine and chassis numbers.

Later registered in France and converted to left-hand drive, the car reappears in documentation in 1995 when it passed its roadworthiness inspection, which was renewed regularly until 2006, coinciding with its registration in the Calvados region. In 2008, it was sold through Royale Automobile in La Baule to one of the most prominent Aston Martin collectors. At that time, the DB6 was exported to the Arabian Peninsula and displayed in the new owner's private museum, where it remained on static exhibition for fifteen years.

The car subsequently returned to France, appearing at the Bonhams|Cars sale at the Grand Palais Éphémère, where it was acquired by its current owner, an enthusiast of great automotive classics. It then underwent a significant mechanical refurbishment by Provost Automobiles in Le Mans. The suspension was overhauled, the steering system refurbished, mechanical seals renewed, and the engine—along with its fuel and cooling systems—received extensive attention. Documented by invoices available in the file, this work represents over €30,000 of expenditure, the quality of which was confirmed during a road test.

Today, this Aston Martin DB6 Vantage is finished in an elegant Oyster Shell exterior colour, complemented by a beautifully patinated period red leather interior.

Accompanied by a comprehensive history file and its valid French registration documents, this fine British motor car would be an ideal companion for historic rallies or simply for effortless two- or four-person touring across Europe.

"Introduced in 1937, the Mercedes-Benz 320 was a comfortable car available in a huge range of bodywork configurations, from a four-door saloon costing 8,950 marks, via a six-seater touring car, a number of cabriolets and a roadster, up to a streamlined saloon available for 14,550 marks." - Schlegelmilch & Lehbrink, Mercedes.

Mercedes-Benz's luxurious 320 series was introduced in 1937 as a replacement for the 290 series. Built initially in two wheelbase lengths - regular and short (N) - the 320 was down to just one from 1938 onwards, though a wide variety of open and closed body styles remained available, including a state-of-the-art streamlined saloon. The 320's six-cylinder side valve engine started out at 3,208cc before being bored out to 3,405cc towards the end of production to compensate for inferior quality fuel. Maximum power increased to 78bhp and overall performance greatly improved, while coil-sprung independent suspension all round ensured that the ride afforded the ultimate in comfort at all times. Mercedes-Benz made only a little over 4,300 320s in all body styles, so this 320N Cabriolet is both rare and collectible.

Benefiting from the larger, 3.4-litre engine, chassis number '408250' is probably one of only six 320N cabriolets completed. Unfortunately, all purchase order books were destroyed during WW2, which means that there is no official data available concerning chassis and engine numbers. Research, and the files with the car, suggest that this could be one of the original six built at the Mannheim factory.

Restored in 2002 by the renowned restorer Szielasko from Switzerland, this 320N comes complete with tool kit, a set of suitcases, and a history file containing numerous photographs of the rebuild. The car is ready to be enjoyed!

description_block:

André Citroën's brainchild, the 'Traction Avant' broke new ground in almost every aspect of automobile engineering on its launch in 1934. Unitary construction of the body/chassis; front-wheel drive; all-independent suspension sprung by torsion bars; hydraulic brakes; synchromesh gears; and a four-cylinder, overhead-valve, wet-liner engine were all incorporated in the newcomer at a time when most of its rivals employed a separate chassis, cart springs, sidevalve engines, and mechanical brakes.

Fervent admirer of the model, having owned several, Pierre Strinati purchased this Traction Avant on 17th October 1961 for CHF900 (receipt on file). On 6th March 1972 a major service was undertaken costing CHF1,260.95, during which the electrical system was checked and the valve timing adjusted. Later that same month, repairs were made to the right rear door and wing; the repaired areas were repainted, as were the sills and wheels, while the bumpers were sent away to be re-chromed.

We believe that the 89,692 kilometres odometer reading could very well be correct as the car is in a remarkable state of preservation and retains its original interior. It comes with its original radiator shield and grilles for winter driving, together with some original instruction manuals, service books, old insurance cards, tax receipts, sundry bills, old Swiss registration papers, and a copy of Citroën Traction Avant Gold Portfolio. Recommissioning will be required following a lengthy period of inactivity.

Gabriel Voisin was perhaps France's greatest aviation pioneer. In 1907 he built the first practical aeroplane capable of leaving the ground under its own power, and his Avions Voisin company was the first mass producer of aircraft in the world. The end of WWI in 1918 brought a halt to Voisin's aviation ventures and forced him to look elsewhere to provide employment for his workforce. The result was some of the most original and innovative automobile engineering of the inter-war era, especially in the field of passenger-car aerodynamics, as exemplified by this C30.

In 1937, following the restructuring of Voisin, the company's new owner commissioned the production of a new model: the C30. Continental Motors' 3.6-litre six-cylinder Graham engine was chosen for the C30 and could be ordered with a supercharger, which boosted maximum power from 90 to 116bhp. The outbreak of WW2 put a stop to the C30's brief production run (around 20 or 30 were made, only five of which are known to survive) and they are historically significant as the last Voisin automobiles.

This C30 was first registered on 27th June 1939 as '7405 RM 6', then a Parisian number. It was subsequently registered as '8673 DR 75' to one Emile Janet, residing at 4, rue Clement Marot in Paris, on 24th March 1955. There is a plaque on the dashboard saying 'René Janet, 16, rue Franklin, Paris', which was mistakenly thought to refer to the coachbuilder (it may refer to an owner of the car, maybe linked to Emile Janet?); however, the car's actual coachbuilder is still unknown. Mr Strinati imported the Voisin from France into Switzerland in October 1963.

In December 1984, the car was treated to some restoration work: the body was repainted in BMW Savanna Beige, the headlining redone, the radiator shell repaired, the chrome re-plated, and the Plexiglas windows in the roof replaced. Some black and white photographs of the C30 (still wearing its French Parisian registration plates) taken by Mr Strinati show it in a darker colour. We believe that the car was originally painted dark green, as upon close inspection traces of dark green paint were found in various places. Apart from the aforementioned changes the car remains highly original.

More recently, the Voisin, together with other cars belonging to Mr Strinati's collection, was exhibited in the 'Musée Jean Tua de l'Automobile' in Geneva. This car was also reproduced as a model, which unfortunately does not come with it. Like the others of the collection, this car has been stored for several years and will require recommissioning. Offered with a file of registration documents and other paperwork.

• Limited-slip differential, electrically heated sports seats, air conditioning, sunroof

Group 4 homologation rules, which required 400 road cars to be built, spurred the development of 'Project 930' - the legendary 911 Turbo. In production from April 1975, the 930 Turbo married a KKK turbocharger to the 3.0-litre RSR engine, in road trim a combination that delivered 260bhp for a top speed of 153mph (246km/h). For 1978 the Turbo's engine was enlarged to 3.3 litres, gaining an inter-cooler in the process; power increased to 300bhp and the top speed of what was the fastest-accelerating road car of its day went up to 160mph (257km/h).

The 911 Turbo's raison d'être - the racing 935 - had pioneered what would become known as the 'flat nose' (flachbau) or 'slant nose' (a more aerodynamically efficient front end) and this new look was soon in demand from 911 customers. Kremer Racing offered a conversion and this service as later taken up by the factory's own Customer Department to special order (Sunderwunschen) from 1981, only becoming an official option in 1986. The front wings were steel, incorporating cooling vents and pop-up headlamps (early examples had them in the air dam) while the rears had extra cooling intakes. There were different sills and, along with the body modifications, came an even more luxurious interior.

More refined than hitherto yet retaining its high-performance edge, the Porsche 911 Turbo sold in the thousands, becoming the definitive sports car of its age. When Porsche revealed that the original 911 would be replaced by the new Type 964, dealer stocks of the existing Turbo model sold out overnight. Production of the Type 930 ceased in September 1989, and there would not be another 911 Turbo until the Type 964 version was launched in September 1990.

Finished in its factory-correct colour combination of Grand Prix White with special-order Can Can Red extended leather interior, the 1986 model-year 911 Turbo 'Flat Nose' we offer is one of an estimated 948 built new with that distinctive feature. Other notable options include a sunroof, air conditioning, electrically heated sports seats, a limited-slip differential, and white centres to the deep-dish Fuchs wheels. This 911 was delivered new to Sweden and is believed to have remained in Scandinavia for its entire life. The current odometer reading is 169,902 kilometres, and the car presents well following sympathetic refurbishment. This most desirable Porsche rarity comes complete with a comprehensively stamped service booklet; a leather tool roll; and a Porsche folio containing instruction manuals.

To fully exploit the Giulietta's competition potential, Alfa Romeo knew that lighter and more aerodynamic bodywork would be necessary, a requirement which resulted in the ultimate Giuliettas: Bertone's Sprint Special and the Sprint Zagato, both built on the short-wheelbase Spider platform and powered by the 100bhp version of Alfa's classic, 1,290cc, twin-cam four. Conceived as an out-and-out competition car, the Sprint Zagato coupé employed lightweight aluminium-alloy coachwork and demonstrated its designer's commitment to weight saving in every detail, tipping the scales at an astonishing 770kg. With a top speed of around 200km/h the SZ was easily the fastest of the Giuliettas, and even today there are few 1.3-litre cars capable of matching this level of performance. The SZ's inherent stability and instantaneous response to steering input made it a driver's car par excellence. On the racetrack it proved virtually unbeatable, and the Sprint Zagato remains a major force to be reckoned with in Historic motor sport, being eligible for a wide variety of prestigious events.

Two series of Sprint Zagato were produced between 1959 and 1962, the second series (SZ2) cars being distinguishable by a redesigned, larger and more aerodynamically efficient body incorporating a 'sawn off' Kamm-type tail, a feature which gave rise to the model's Coda Tronca sobriquet (the first series became known as the Coda Tonda – Round Tail). Under the skin the new SZ remained much as before apart from the welcome incorporation of Girling front disc brakes. SZ chassis numbers ran from '001' to '217', a total of 217 cars, an estimated 44 of which were the later SZ2 Coda Tronca version.

The Alfa Romeo factory records indicate that the car was produced on 29 March 1961 in the colour "Bianco Gardenia" (the same as today), and according to The Italian Car Registry by John de Boer, this delightful SZ Coda Tonda was delivered new on 10 April 1961 to Alfa Romeo in Lugano, Switzerland. In 2009 it was purchased by a very well-known collector in Italy and remained in his private collection until 2021 when it was purchased for his private collection by our vendor, another noted collector based near Milan. Only recently the car benefited from restoration of the bodywork and paint, while the interior showcases the roll bar and lovely Zagato seats in black vinyl. The car will be offered for sale with Italian registration documents and a valid Italian Revisione (roadworthiness certificate).

A very rare Alfa Romeo with the lively Giulietta twin-cam engine and lightweight coachwork by Zagato, this little sports car ticks all the right boxes and is eligible for numerous events worldwide.

auction_title: Michelin House Stained Glass Windows – London – Bibendum
description_block:
Set of two large-scale reproductions of the stained glass windows that once adorned the Michelin House in London, created after the famous posters "Le Coup de semelle" and "Pneu Vélo Michelin." These compositions feature the character Bibendum, created in 1898 by O'Galop (Marius Rossillon, 1867–1946).

One panel depicts the Michelin Bibendum, cigar in mouth, presenting his studded sole; the other shows him riding a bicycle while smoking a cigar. Produced by an Italian workshop, these works stand out for their vivid colours and exceptional quality of execution. Each stained glass panel is protected by a front glass pane and housed within a reinforced metal frame.

The Michelin House, inaugurated on 20 January 1911, served as the first British headquarters and tyre depot of Michelin Tyre Company Ltd. During the Second World War, due to the bombing of London, the original stained glass windows were dismantled in the 1940s and were never recovered after the war.

Michelin vacated the building in 1985, when it was acquired and converted into the Bibendum Restaurant & Oyster Bar.

On the occasion of the building's centenary in 2011, the event was celebrated by the occupants at the time—the Bibendum Restaurant and The Conran Shop—as well as by Michelin, the former owner. In this context, Michelin renewed efforts to locate the original stained glass windows, establishing a dedicated website and telephone line, highlighting the importance of these works to the company's heritage.

Like the rival BMW 328, the Wanderer W25K sports car was powered by a 2.0-litre, six-cylinder engine, in the Wanderer's case equipped with a Roots supercharger and producing 85php, hence the 'K' (Kompressor) designation. The engine was designed by Ferdinand Porsche and the car's beautiful lines styled by Helmut Schwandler, the bodywork being built by Wendler Karrosserie in Reutlingen. While the slightly heavier Wanderer couldn't quite match the performance of its Bavarian counterpart, it was still a marvellous sports car,

Chassis number '180244' is one of a handful of known survivors from the limited run of 258 Wanderer W25K roadsters produced between 1936 and 1938. This example has belonged to a German collector since 1994 and is probably the most original Wanderer W25K available worldwide.

The seller notes that the car - believed to be an older restoration - is in good condition for its age and outstandingly original; the black paint and exterior brightwork is well-preserved, and the red leather interior is in good condition also. However, the engine does not run, having been removed and disassembled many years ago for repairs, and now needs to be overhauled. The fortunate next owner will have an exciting opportunity to restore this rare German sports car to its former glory.

Powered by ether a 4.2-litre or 4.9-litre V8 engine, the Maserati Kyalami was manufactured between 1976 and 1983, by which time some 198 examples of this most exclusive luxury Gran Turismo had been built, the 4.2/4.9 split being 124/74 (source: Maserati Club UK's official factory figures).

Chassis number '38', body number '16', is the 19th left-hand drive Kyalami made. A 4.2-litre model, the Maserati was delivered new to its (unknown) first owner in Italy. The second custodian was a Mr Heimo Strauhal of Innsbruck, Austria, who was followed by Mr Fritz Kostenzer of Eben am Achensee, Austria. While in Mr Kostenzer's care the Kyalami was restored over a three-year period (2012-2015) by Mr Christoph Dapont of Strass, Austria. A Bonhams representative visited this car in 2013 during its restoration in Austria when it was in bare metal and completely dismantled. It is possible that the car's original exterior colour was Luci del Bosco, but the original interior colour is not known. The car is currently finished in black metallic with Crema (cream) upholstery. Extensive restoration records are available, but no photographs.

A resident of Rosenheim, Germany, the current vendor has owned the car since 2015. Additional accompanying paperwork consists of Austrian historic registration (Einzelgenehmigung) and German historic registration (Oldtimer Gutachten).

Eustace Watkins enjoyed close links with London-based coachbuilders Whittingham & Mitchel (they ended up buying W&M in the early 1930s) and this car's original body may well have been one of theirs. "The HK500 was the most interesting car we ever made but the Facel II was the best. It was totally elegant." – Jean Daninos.

During its short existence, Facel built nearly 2,900 cars, all assembled by hand and all intended for a select clientele, including Tony Curtis, Ringo Starr, Ava Gardner, Stirling Moss and Maurice Trintignant.

Facel, founded in December 1939 as a subsidiary of Bronzavia (a supplier grisof military aeronautical equipment), merged with Métallon after the Second World War and began producing bodywork for Panhard, Simca and Ford before becoming an independent car manufacturer. After the war, despite regulations that had caused the last French luxury car manufacturers to disappear, Jean Daninos decided to pursue his project to build a luxury saloon car in France: the Vega. Unable to find a suitable engine in France, Daninos turned to the United States and retained this option for all his models. The first improvements to the FV were not long in coming, and the FV1 launched in March 1955 featured a longer wheelbase and a 4.8-litre Chrysler V8 engine. In 1957, an improved model appeared, the HK 500, equipped with the latest version of the 5.9-litre Chrysler V8, capable of reaching 225 km/h, reaching 100 km/h in less than 9 seconds and delivering 360 horsepower.

Launched in 1961, the Facel II was to be the last model with a V8 engine. During a test drive in 1962, Autocar wrote: 'The large Facel, a striking combination of French, American and British components, covers the miles at high speed without any mechanical problems.' But following an unsuccessful attempt to produce the Facellia's engines in-house, which bankrupted the company, production ceased in 1964 after around 180 Facel IIs had been produced. The Facel II, the direct successor to the HK500, although more refined, lighter and more sophisticated, also embodies French luxury and elegance: Connolly leather, precious woods, instrumentation by Parisian watchmaker Jaeger, etc. Today, these rare Franco-American GTs are among the most sought-after post-war classics.

This magnificent Facel II was purchased new in November 1962 from Pierre Savoye Automobile in Paris by its first owner, Mr Bernard Delbreil-Berges (original invoice, financing contract, Facel order form, Pierre Savoye Automobile order form and correspondence between Mr Delbreil-Berges and Pierre Savoye Automobile included in the file). The car was ordered from Facel with the following options: manual gearbox, black leather dashboard, tinted windows, power steering, air conditioning, seat belts and headrests for the front right seat.

Thanks to the archives accompanying the car, we learn that in early 1963, Mr Delbreil-Berges had a collision on the road between Cahors and Toulouse, the car was sent to Facel in Paris to have the right side of the bodywork restored and to be completely repainted in its original colour, Gregio Glacé (the file contains the bailiff's report, the expert's report, Facel's restoration invoices and all the original correspondence between the various parties involved). The correspondence between Mr Delbreil-Berges and Facel, included in the car's file, tells us that the engine was changed in the summer of 1963 by Facel, as the car's first owner was dissatisfied with its performance. The car was thus fitted with a 6.2-litre Chrysler V8 with twin carburettors. In another letter from 1964, sent by the first owner to Facel regarding an upcoming tyre change, we discover that with this new engine, Mr Delbreil-Berges enjoyed driving at very high speeds, admitting to regularly driving between 150km/h and 200km/h!

Before selling the car to its current owner (the second) in May 2005, its first owner had various repairs carried out at ALS in Beauzelle for a total of over €15,000 (corresponding invoices in the file). Since then, the car has been serviced by the current owner's mechanic.

The car comes with an extensive history file, contained in a 100-page binder containing the original documents (invoices, correspondence, expert reports, etc.) compiled by the two owners. The file contains extensive correspondence between the first owner, Facel Vega and Pierre Savoye Automobile, the original purchase invoice, the corresponding financing contract, various maintenance and repair invoices (from both owners), the current owner's purchase invoice, a 2013 expert report, various maintenance invoices, the owner's workshop manual, technical documents, a valid French MOT certificate and a French registration document.

This is undoubtedly a unique opportunity to acquire what was considered at the time to be the fastest four-seater of its era, having had only two owners and coming with a very important historical file.

Although best remembered as a 1960s style icon favoured by the fashion-conscious 'Mods', the Lambretta motor scooter - together with Piaggio's rival Vespa - had been intended as basic transport for the non-enthusiast masses. Manufactured by the Italian industrial giant Innocenti, the Lambretta gained instant acceptance in the immediate post-war years, its cleanliness and convenience in particular appealing to those who regarded the true motorcycle with suspicion. Introduced in 1947, the first Lambretta 'A' employed an open frame with pressed-steel front section and tubular rear, in which sat a 125cc two-stroke engine, setting the pattern for all Lambrettas to follow. By the end of 1950 Innocenti was producing up to 100 per day. Predecessor of the Li and TV series, the LD arrived in 125cc form in 1951 and became available with a 150cc engine three years later. The LD 125's engine produced 4.8bhp, giving the model a top speed of around 45mph (72/km/h). LD production continued until the end of the 1950s.

This charming Lambretta and sidecar combination was purchased by the vendor from a large private collection in Germany, whose owner sold it due to its advancing years. The combination presents well and comes with Italian registration documents. If you are planning a Roman holiday, here is your ideal transport!

This gorgeous automobile offered here is one of the rarest and most exclusive of modern-day Bentleys: the Continental R Millennium Edition, only ten of which were made to commemorate the start of the 21st Century. The Millennium was based on the Continental R Mulliner; all were left-hand drive and all went to the North American Market.

Introduced at Geneva in the spring of 1999, the Continental R Mulliner was as powerful as the short-wheelbase Continental T, boasting a maximum output of 420bhp and a staggering 650ft/lb of torque, the latter delivered at all of 2,200rpm. The 0-60mph time dropped to a fraction under 6 seconds, while top speed increased to 167mph (268km/h). Improved suspension, quicker steering, switchable traction control and massive 18" diameter wheels helped keep the 2,450kg plot under control.

Manufactured in October 1999, this Continental R Millennium has the special Mulliner wide body with 4" wheelarch flares; the 420bhp 6.75-litre turbocharged engine; a stainless steel laser-cut matrix grille; and 18" chrome wheels. Unique interior features include a push-button starter and numbered tread plates with 'Millennium Edition' engraving; this car is engraved 'No.1'.

When introduced, the Millennium was the most expensive Bentley of the 20th Century and most expensive production car of the year 2000, with a base price of around US$400.000. Of the ten, only two Millennium models were completed with the desirable triple-black livery (1, 2) and only three Millenniums are located in Europe (1, 4, 7). Our vendor purchased the Bentley in 2009 from the Daniel Schmitt dealership in St Louis, Missouri; it has covered circa 42,000km (26,100mls) from new and is believed to have had only two or three previous owners. Since acquisition the Millennium has been serviced by Harold Jacobs, Silver Hill, Netherlands. It comes with German registration documents. Details of this car may be found on Marinus Rijkers' web site, rrsilverspirit.com.

Right from the marque's creation in 1926 by the merger of Daimler-Benz and Mercedes, Mercedes-Benz's top-of-the-range models have ranked in the forefront of the world's greatest automobiles. Throughout the 1950s the company's flagship model was the 300S, a luxurious Grand Tourer in the tradition of the pre-war 540 K, which was both lighter and faster than its illustrious predecessor. Mercedes-Benz's first prestige car of the post-WW2 period, the 300 debuted at the Paris Salon in 1951. The range comprised the six-light, four-door saloon and similar-sized cabriolet, plus a trio of two-door variants built on a shorter wheelbase.

Like the majority of 1950s luxury cars, the 300 retained a separate chassis, though unlike most of its rivals could boast all-independent suspension. Later to form the basis of the immortal 300 SL sports car's, the 3.0-litre, overhead-camshaft, six-cylinder engine produced 115bhp, an output good enough to endow the saloon with a genuine 100mph maximum speed despite an all-up weight of 1,780kg (almost 4,000lbs). And while not unique in that respect, the 300 could cruise at close to its maximum speed while transporting six passengers in comfort in a manner that few of its contemporaries could match.

Even more performance was available to those in a position to afford a 300S. At US$12,500 the latter was more than double the price of the most expensive Cadillac and costlier than a 300 SL, so remained the province of a highly select clientele. Built in coupé, cabriolet and roadster versions, the 300S enjoyed an extra 35bhp courtesy of an increased compression ratio and three - as opposed to two - Solex downdraft carburettors. Its top speed was 176km/h (109mph), a figure improved upon by the subsequent 300Sc.

This 300S coupé was restored in 2002 and comes with numerous photographs relating to the rebuild. Finished in dark red with beige leather interior, the Mercedes is in very nice condition throughout and it has a very elegant appearance. It has a Dutch registration. Accompanying documentation consists of history files (dating back 30 years), an old-style logbook and a 'datenkarte'. Also, with the car comes a tool kit and a set of suitcases. This car is ready to be enjoyed on a summer trip through the country side.

In 1952 Porsche constructed a trial batch of 15 roadsters at the behest of US importer Max Hoffman, who had persuaded the German manufacturer of the potential for a 'cut-price' entry-level model that would appeal to the North American market. The roadsters' successful reception in the USA led to the introduction of the Speedster model in 1954; in effect, an 'economy' model intended to compete with the cheaper British sports cars.

Stripped of all unnecessary amenities - even the heater was optional - the Speedster established a formidable presence on both the road and in the burgeoning American sports car racing scene. Its combination of style, performance and value for money made the Speedster deservedly popular, and today this most handsome of the 356 variants enjoys iconic status.

Chassis number '84070' was delivered new to the USA and first registered on 1st July 1958. The car was comprehensively restored during 2015-2017 and comes with invoices totalling approximately €120,000, testifying to the rebuild's extensive scope.

When purchased by the current owner in 1999, the car had an older restoration and was used frequently for rallies across Europe. In 2015 to facilitate its restoration the body was mounted on a straightening jig to make subsequent work easier and ensure exact gap dimensions. The body was then immersed in a KTL sealing bath.

A recent third party test protocol states that the engine has been comprehensively overhauled and that it starts easily and runs well, while the gearbox has been exchanged for a reconditioned unit and reportedly shifts smoothly.

Additionally, the car is equipped with a roll-bar and a twin-pipe exhaust system. An OMP fire extinguisher is installed in the space provided for the rear seat, and OMP seatbelts are installed.

Further to emphasise the Speedster's sporty character, the bumpers were removed, the headlights fitted with protective grilles, and fog lights installed. The speedometer and rev counter are highlighted in green. In addition, an oil temperature gauge is installed beneath the dashboard, and a daily odometer on the right-hand side. The steering wheel is a three-spoke wooden item.

The current owner has attended various historic rallies with the Speedster, which has been used sparingly since 2017. The car comes with German registration documents; a third party condition report by Franc Gourge at KFZ-Sachverständige; a rare factory hardtop; and the aforementioned restoration invoices.

That a major US manufacturer could come up with such an exciting concept car was startling enough, but Chrysler's decision to put the Viper into production was nothing short of astonishing. Inspired, as its name suggests, by the legendary Cobra, Tom Gale's design study made its auto-show debut in 1989, its appearance triggering an avalanche of deposit cheques. Without doubt, a large part of the Viper's 'back to basics' appeal stemmed from its unique selling point: a massively powerful 8.0-litre V10 engine. Despite being relatively 'low-tech', the Lamborghini-developed pushrod V10 churned out 400bhp and a brutal 450lb/ft of torque, good enough for a 0-100 km/h time of 4.7 seconds and a top speed of 265 km/h. Early Vipers lack modern driver aids such as traction control and anti-lock brakes. Early cars also have the rear antenna mounted visible.

Combining Citröen's advanced chassis technology and Maserati's engine know-how, the SM (Série Maserati) featured DS-style hydro-pneumatic self-levelling suspension; power-assisted all-round disc brakes; self-centring steering; and steered headlamps. Eventually, a capacity of 2,670cc would be settled on for a power output of 170bhp from the 90-degree V6 engine. Citröen was the world leader in passenger car aerodynamics at the time, the SM's class-leading drag coefficient enabling it to reach 140mph, making it the fastest front-wheel-drive car ever when introduced. Fuel injection arrived in 1972; an automatic transmission option the following year; and the engine was enlarged to 2,974cc before the model was prematurely axed in 1975 following Citröen's acquisition by Peugeot. Fondly remembered, these technically advanced and functionally beautiful cars remain highly sought after today.

The vendor's family purchased this SM over 30 years ago from the renowned Citröen specialist Georges Regembeau, who was responsible for tuning the engine. A feature particularly worthy of note is the very rare optional resin wheels manufactured by Michelin. Finished in Beige Tholonnet Métalisé with black leather interior, the car comes with an SM owner's handbook; an expired French contrôle technique; a French carte grise; and a file of invoices for maintenance work.

More expensive than the 300 SL sports car and almost double the price of the contemporary top-of-the-range Cadillac, the Mercedes-Benz 300S was one of the world's most exclusive automobiles. Elegantly styled in the pre-war manner yet technologically bang up to date, the 300S was built to the Stuttgart firm's uncompromising quality standards. Inevitably, production was limited, only 760 examples of the 300S/Sc (560/200) leaving the factory between 1951 and 1958.

The 300S (Super) was a short-wheelbase derivative of the 300 saloon, one of Mercedes-Benz's first all-new designs of the post-war era, which had debuted at the Frankfurt Auto Show in 1951. The 300's arrival re-established Mercedes-Benz in the front rank of prestige car manufacturers, marking as it did a return to the marque's tradition of building high-performance luxury automobiles of the finest quality.

The 300's cross-braced, oval-tube chassis followed the lines of the 170S and 220, boasting independent suspension all round, but incorporated the added refinements of hypoid bevel final drive, dynamically balanced wheels, and remote control of the rear suspension ride height. Initially developing 115bhp, the 3.0-litre, overhead-camshaft, six-cylinder engine was also used in fuel-injected form in the 300 SL sports car. Custom built by Mercedes-Benz's most experienced craftsmen, the Mercedes-Benz 300 was luxuriously appointed and trimmed with materials of the highest quality.

Introduced at the Paris Salon in October 1951 and built in coupé and cabriolet forms on a shortened 300 saloon chassis, the 300S succeeded in recapturing all the elegance of the pre-war 540K. Today the 300S is among the most sought after of post-war Mercedes-Benz automobiles.

This 300S Cabriolet was restored in 2020 and comes with numerous photographs relating to the rebuild. Finished in blue with a beige leather interior, this Mercedes breaths elegance and style. The engine runs very smooth and the bodywork and interior are in a nice and good condition. Accompanying documentation consists of history files (dating back 30 years), an old-style logbook and a 'daten karte'. The car also comes with a tool kit and a Dutch registration.

One consequence of the E-Type Jaguar's long process of development had been a gradual increase in weight, but a good measure of the concomitant loss of performance was restored in 1971 with the arrival of what would be the final version: the 'Series 3' V12. Weighing only 80lb (36.4kg) more than the cast-iron-block 4.2-litre XK six, the new all-alloy, 5.3-litre, overhead-camshaft V12 produced 314 bhp (272 ch DIN), an output good enough for a top speed comfortably in excess of 140mph. Further good news was that the 0-100mph (0-160km/h) time of around 16 seconds made the V12 the fastest-accelerating production E-Type ever made. Built in two-seat roadster and 2+2 coupé versions, both of which used the long-wheelbase floor pan introduced on the Series 2 2+2, the Series 3 E-Type continued the Jaguar tradition of offering a level of performance and luxury unrivalled at the price.

Manufactured on 30th May 1974, this beautiful Series 3 E-Type roadster is a matching numbers example retaining its original chassis, engine and Regency Red exterior colour. Equipped with the manual transmission preferred by enthusiasts, the car was delivered new in the USA via British Leyland, New York City on 10th July 1974.

Since the current owner acquired the car in 2022, the E-Type has been serviced regularly by a local British-cars specialist in South of France, and comes with all the invoices relating to services undertaken over the last seven years. The car also comes with a Jaguar Daimler Heritage Trust Certificate; French Carte Grise; an up-to-date Contrôle Technique; and an Expertise report. This is probably the ideal car for country drives with the wind in your hair!

"Apart from being very fast and exciting, the Porsche is a practical car. Unlike most rivals which can be regarded as Sunday morning adrenalin pumps because of their intractability, or cramped accommodation, the Turbo can be used as comfortable daily transport. Yet its handling and roadholding are probably as good as any other car in the world. Few, if any, cars have impressed us so much." - Motor magazine, 8th November 1975.

Anyone who has driven a Porsche 911 Turbo will agree with the above, whether they are a professional road-tester or merely one of thousands of enthusiastic owners; indeed, one of the most celebrated of the former, Paul Frère, declared that the Porsche 911 Turbo offered "the finest blend of ultimate performance and refinement I have ever come across..."

Much of the Porsche 911's development had resulted from the factory's racing programme, and it was the then Group 4 homologation rules, which required 400 road cars to be built, which spurred the development of 'Project 930' - the legendary 911 Turbo. In production from April 1975, the Turbo married a KKK turbocharger to the 3.0-litre Carrera RSR engine: in road trim a combination that delivered 260bhp for a top speed of 250km/h (155mph). However, the Turbo wasn't just about top speed, it was also the best-equipped 911 and amazingly flexible - hence only four speeds in the gearbox - being capable of racing from a standstill to 100mph (161km/h) in 14 seconds. But what set the 911 Turbo apart from its peers was the relaxed way this stupefying performance was delivered.

The Turbo's characteristic flared wheelarches and 'tea tray' rear spoiler had already been seen on the Carrera model, while the interior was the most luxurious yet seen in a 911, featuring leather upholstery, air conditioning and electric windows. For 1978 the Turbo's engine was enlarged to 3.3 litres, gaining an inter-cooler in the process; power increased to 300bhp and the top speed of what was the fastest-accelerating road car of its day went up to 170mph (257km/h). More refined than hitherto yet retaining its high-performance edge, the Porsche 911 Turbo sold in the thousands, becoming the definitive sports car of its age.
Representing a major step forward for the 911, the new Carrera 4 and Carrera 2 - coded '964' - were launched in 1989, the former marking the first time that four-wheel drive had been seen on a series-production 911. Face-lifted but retaining that familiar shape, the new models had been given a more extensive work-over mechanically, 87% of parts being claimed as entirely new. Although the naturally aspirated duo shared the same 3.6-litre, 247bhp, air-cooled flat-six engine, the Turbo initially kept its existing 3.3-litre unit, which now developed 320bhp. Power-assisted steering (another 911 'first'), anti-lock brakes and a five-speed manual transmission were standard, with the Tiptronic auto 'box a Carrera 2-only option.

For 1993 the Turbo was upgraded, receiving the 3.6-litre engine, based on that of the Carrera 4, which in blown form delivered 360bhp. In addition, the Turbo 3.6 boasted larger 18" wheels, lowered suspension, a front anti-roll bar, and more aggressive styling. With the introduction of the successor Type 993 models scheduled for 1995, the 3.6-litre Turbo was destined to be available for one year only (1993-1994), during which period fewer than 1,500 were built.

One of the rarer Porsche 911 variants, the example we offer was delivered new in Belgium to its first owner, a local doctor. First registered on 16th March 1993, the car was ordered in the highly desirable Oak Green Metallic with Sherwood Green leather interior, and is one of a believed three completed with this specification. This car was ordered with a generous complement of optional equipment, highlights of which include a limited-slip differential, headlamp washer, electrically adjustable sports seats, rear window wiper, five-speed manual gearbox, sun-moon-roof, and power steering (see Porsche Certificate of Authenticity on file).

The car remained with its first owner for 27 years, and was only sold in 2020 to one of his best friends, the current owner. With only two owners from new and circa 163,200 kilometres recorded, this Turbo 3.6 is as original as can be; indeed, the original 18" wheels still display the factory-applied 'SPEEDLINE for PORSCHE' decals. The radio has been upgraded with an original Porsche Classic Navigation unit, while the original Blaupunkt Symphony radio/cassette is included in the sale.

The car comes with a comprehensively documented service history; there are no fewer than 21 official dealer stamps in the service book, and a historical overview of all invoices since delivery in a 30+page file. The original Porsche books and manuals are included, and the car is offered with current Belgian registration; technical control valid until 9th September 2027; a detailed technical report dated 21/4/2024; and the aforementioned Porsche CoA confirming matching numbers.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1953 DESCRIPTION:

Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, Carrozzeria Ghia enjoyed a fruitful relationship with the Chrysler Corporation. The result was some of the most spectacular styling exercises and concept cars ever seen, which were the sensations of the era's motor shows.

Chrysler's products of the late 1940s were typically well engineered but somewhat dated in appearance, although that would change in 1949 with the arrival from Studebaker of master stylist Virgil Exner. Exner rejuvenated Chrysler's line up and collaborated with Ghia to create to create some of the era's most memorable styling exercises, commencing with the XX-500 of 1951. This large coupé was styled by Exner and manufactured by Ghia, though later concept cars would be designed and built entirely in Italy.

Taking its name from C B Thomas – head of Chrysler's export division – the 'Thomas Special' was based on the Exner-designed, Ghia-built Styling Special but on the longer standard wheelbase, making it a full five-seater. Thomas used it as his personal car. Virtually identical apart from a different front grille, the GS1 variant was shown at the Paris Motor Show in 1953, and Ghia would go on to build a limited run (18-19) of similar cars.

Little else is known of this Thomas Special until 1982 when it featured in an article by Denis Adler published in Car Collector magazine's December edition: "the sports coupe is possible (sic) the original Thomas Special although there is no documentation." According to historian Raphael Burnett, the car was in Switzerland, as evidenced by photographs showing a Swiss sticker on the front bumper.

Eventually the Thomas Special was sold to restorer Fran Roxas, and in the 1980s was restored by him for the second time, such was his commitment to perfection; indeed, the Thomas Special was considered one of the finest restorations in his collection. In 1992 the Thomas Special was sold to the Bortz Auto Collection, home to some of the most spectacular concept/dream cars of the 1950s and 1960s. The interior was restored by Chris Nersthiemer and the car exhibited at the Pebble Beach Concours d'Elegance that same year. In 1997 the Thomas Special was one of 27 cars from the Bortz Auto Collection featured in the Chicago Tribune.

The Thomas Special was meticulously cared for and used sparingly, and by the time it was sold at a US auction circa 2007 had covered a mere 1,000-or-so miles while in Mr Bortz's custodianship. In 2010 the car was exhibited at Meadow Brook and on 1st April 2016 was registered in the UK. It has been registered in Romania since 2020/2021.

Combining the best of American styling and Italian coachwork, the Thomas Special is worthy of a place in any important private collection.

"Top up or top down, it makes no difference. Anywhere the Porsche 911 Speedster goes, it draws an embarrassing amount of attention. It just looks so darn-well, speedy...
The Speedster is an instant classic – likely to hold or even gain in value. It strikes a chord with some buyers that's simply irresistible." - Motor Trend.

Based on the 911 Turbo Cabriolet, though normally aspirated, the 3.2-litre Speedster was launched immediately prior to the introduction of the new Type 964 bodyshell, and thus was the last 911 model to feature the old-style body based on the brilliant original design of 1963. The latter had been reworked by chief stylist Tony Lapine, incorporating numerous references to the original 356 Speedster as well as a pair of controversial 'camel hump' cowlings behind the seats concealing the stowed-away manual hood, a simplified affair described by the factory as for 'temporary' use.

From 1984 Porsche had offered the 'Turbo-Look' body style - flared wheelarches, large rear wing and deeper front spoiler - on its naturally aspirated models including the Speedster, the vast majority of which were ordered with this option. The flat-six engine produced 231bhp in the Speedster, which was good enough for a top speed of just over 150mph (245km/h).

The Speedster's list price was US$65,000, but such was the demand that many were sold at a substantial premium above that. One of the rarest of the 911 family, the Speedster was built during 1989 only, a mere 2,104 cars being completed, of which only 161 units had the narrow, non-Turbo-Look body.

One of the ultra-rare 'narrow body' models on the soon-to-be-superseded Type 930 chassis, this matching numbers Porsche 911 Speedster was built for the Swedish market (C09) and delivered new in Sweden by the Porsche dealer in Stockholm. It left the factory finished in Guards Red with black leather interior, and was equipped with a black soft-top, 16" Fuchs wheels, short shifter, anti-theft device, and electrically adjustable sport seats.

Always serviced by Porsche specialists, the Speedster has covered around 36,000 kilometres from new and is in highly original condition. The Speedster has been cherished by its sole private owner since he purchased it in 1990 from an official Porsche dealership in Sweden as an almost-new car. It comes complete with tool roll, owner's manual, stamped service book, German registration documents, service receipts, and an independent condition appraisal from Germany.

The Spijker company started out as coachbuilders in Amsterdam before constructing its first automobile in 1898. Spijker was technologically adventurous, introducing the first six-cylinder car with four-wheel drive and all-round brakes in 1903, by which time the name had changed to the more internationally acceptable 'Spyker'.
Despite a reputation for quality and the achievement of some notable competition successes, the original Spyker company disappeared in 1925. Its name and reputation for producing well-engineered, high-performance motor cars had not been forgotten though, and an entirely new Spyker possessing the same goals emerged with the Spyker C8, which debuted at the Birmingham International Motor Show in October 2000.

An advanced, mid-engined, two-seat barchetta, the C8 Spyder was powered by a 4.2-litre Audi V8 engine producing approximately 400bhp, and had a top speed of around 300km/h (186mph). Despite its 'new kid on the block' status, Spyker succeeded in establishing a strong presence in the supercar market. Indeed, the C8 won instant acclaim, receiving the Institute of Vehicle Engineers Design Award soon after its introduction. In 2002 the first competition version, the C8 Double12R endurance racer, was entered by the Spyker Squadron factory racing team at Le Mans. On 14th July 2005, it was announced that the C8 was approved for sale on the United States market.

Finished in striking one-off Lamborghini Balloon White with Ruby Red leather interior, this Spyker C8 Spyder was registered new in the Netherlands by Spyker Factory and retained by them until it was acquired in 2023 by Jasper den Dopper, a well-known Spyker specialist and marque authority. The car has since formed part of his private collection, where it has been preserved with exceptional care and attention to originality.

The very first built customer right-hand drive C8 Spyder, this car is understood to be the lowest-mileage RHD example in existence, having covered a trifling 73 miles from new. Boasting the more powerful Audi S8 V8 engine rather than the A8 power unit, it also features a number of desirable factory upgrades, including 19" wheels, quilted leather upholstery, and the distinctive 'propeller' steering wheel.

Importantly, the car has recently been inspected and prepared by Jasper den Dopper himself, ensuring that it meets the exacting standards expected of such a rare and significant Spyker. As one would expect of a little-used and carefully maintained example, the Spyder can be described as pristine and almost perfect, with engine and transmission described as 'like new'. It also benefits from a recent fuel tank service and timing belt service, with related bills available.

Offered with a Certificate of Conformity and German title, this remarkable Spyker C8 Spyder represents a unique opportunity to acquire an ultra-low mileage, early right-hand drive example with outstanding provenance, specialist care, and unquestionable collector appeal—ready to be enjoyed on the road or admired as part of a world-class private collection.

"This is what true innovation looks like. From its 3.5L EcoBoost® technology to its ultra-efficient aerodynamics, the Ford GT is the culmination of everything great we do at Ford. ...everything about the Ford GT is designed to deliver pure performance." - Ford Motor Company.

Based on Eric Broadley's Lola GT, the original Ford GT40 was spawned by the Dearborn giant's ambition to beat Ferrari at Le Mans, a feat it duly achieved for the first time in 1966. The GT40 project had commenced three years previously, following Ford's failed attempt to buy into Ferrari, and was based at the Ford Advanced Vehicles plant at Slough, England. The GT40 first ran competitively in 1964 but failed at Le Mans that year and again in 1965. That first sweet Le Mans victory would fall to the 7.0-litre Mark II, with victory the following year going to a US-built Mark IV 'J' car. (The GT40 Mark III was the British-built road-going version). Of the three GT40s that lined up together for that famous 1-2-3 clean-sweep finish at Le Mans in 1966, the first two were entered by Shelby American while the third, driven by Ronnie Bucknam and Dick Hutcherson, was entered by Holman & Moody.

A decade later and the GT40's status as an all-time great classic sports car had been firmly established, leading to an increased demand for unmolested originals and the start of a replica-building industry. Perhaps the only surprise concerning the emergence of a reconstituted 'official' version is that it took Ford the best part of 40 years to get around to it.

The 'new generation' GT was developed by Ford's Special Vehicle Team Engineering department under the direction of John Coletti and Fred Goodnow. The composite body panels were unstressed, as on the original, but instead of the monocoque chassis construction used in the 1960s, SVT Engineering developed an all-new aluminium spaceframe combining extruded sections and panels. Doubling as fuel reservoirs, a pair of massive sills contributed much to the original's chassis stiffness, whereas the new GT relied on a centre-tunnel 'backbone' that greatly improved ease of entry and exit. The suspension design was an advance on the original's, consisting of unequal-length control arms and a pushrod/bell-crank system acting on horizontally mounted coil spring/damper units. Braking was handled by six-piston, Alcon callipers with cross-drilled and ventilated discs all round.

In defeating Ferrari's more highly stressed V12s, Ford proved that the traditional American V8 possessed all that was necessary to compete at the cutting edge of international endurance racing. A far cry from the simple pushrod units of the 1960s, the supercharged MOD 5.4-litre V8 produced 550bhp at 5,250rpm and 500lb/ft of torque at 3,250 revs; figures on a par with those of the 7.0-litre engine that won at Le Mans in 1966 and 1967. The all-synchromesh six-speed transaxle used ZF internals and was sourced from RBT Transmissions, whose founder Roy Butfoy had been a member of Ford's racing team at Le Mans. The interior featured leather-upholstered, Recaro bucket seats with aluminium ventilation grommets embedded into the panels. The instrument layout followed the original's, comprising analogue gauges and a large tachometer complemented by modern versions of the traditional toggle switches.

Back in 1966, the Ford GT40 endurance racer became the first car to exceed 200mph along the Mulsanne straight at Le Mans. Matching that would be some achievement for the production road car, even allowing for nearly 40 years of technological progress. Tested for Motor Trend magazine by Indycar racing legend Bryan Herta, the new Ford GT duly topped 200mph at Ford's Kingman test facility in Arizona, emphatically demonstrating that it was indeed worthy of that famous name. A total of 4,038 cars had been completed when production ceased at the end of 2006, over three quarters of which were delivered in the USA.

In 2015 a third-generation Ford GT was unveiled at the North American International Auto Show. Technologically a far cry from its predecessors, the new Ford GT featured a 3.5-litre twin-turbocharged V6 engine; a carbon-fibre monocoque chassis; carbon-fibre body panels; pushrod suspension; and active aerodynamics. Producing 647bhp, the EcoBoost turbo V6 drove the rear wheels via a Getrag seven-speed DCT gearbox. The factory claims a sub-3.0 second 0-60mph time and a top speed of 216mph (347km/h), which makes the Brembo carbon-ceramic brakes a necessity rather than a luxury.

In fact, Ford's new supercar had been created with GT racing in mind, hence the presence of an integral roll cage and a host of other competition-car technologies. Yet despite its start-of-the-art track-focused suspension, the GT has a ride quality rivalling that of a luxury saloon. Autocar's Matt Prior was obviously impressed: "the GT... has a level of composure - that balance between ride and handling – that I'm not sure I've better experienced in 20 years of road testing. It's so compliant, yet there's so little roll, and body movements are so well controlled, that is genuinely astonishing". All of the planned 1,000 road models had been sold before deliveries commenced in 2017, and these exclusive supercars remain highly sought after today.
And as for its maker's racing aspirations, the new GT did not disappoint. At Le Mans on 19th June 2016, the number '68' Ford GT of Ford Chip Ganassi Racing driven by Hand/Müller/Bourdais finished 1st in the LM GTE-Pro class, their victory marking 50 years after Ford's first Le Mans win in 1966 with the original GT40.

In 2018 Ford announced a new limited edition model: the Carbon Series, which was positioned in the range midway between the regular GT and the Competition Series. As its name suggests, the Carbon Series made much more extensive use of this lightweight material than the GT, while the adoption of a titanium exhaust and carbon-fibre wheels helped reduce the weight by 18kg. Air conditioning and an infotainment system were retained (unlike in the US-only Competition Series) while other notable special features included anodised paddle shifters and silver stitching on the seats and steering wheel. The GT's engine was retained unchanged.

Ford updated the GT for the 2020 model year, introducing several mechanical upgrades and new special editions. The 3.5-litre blown V6 now incorporated gallery-cooled pistons, higher-energy ignition coils and larger intercoolers, and produced 651bhp while at the same time delivering a 'broader torque band' according to Ford, although peak torque remained unaltered. Previously optional, the standard exhaust was now the lighter titanium system by Akrapovič, which still delivered the GT's evocative engine note. The suspension was now stiffer in Track mode, and the rear buttresses had been redesigned to increase airflow over the car. Production of the second-generation GT ceased in 2022.

This Ford GT Carbon Series, "GT N166", left the factory on 13 September 2022 and was delivered in France to its first and current owner. Finished in silver grey, complemented by exposed carbon fibre stripes, it features red Brembo brake calipers and exposed carbon fibre door mirrors. In keeping with the Carbon Series specification, it is equipped with a titanium exhaust system, as well as gloss carbon fibre wheels secured by titanium wheel nuts. The interior also makes extensive use of carbon fibre, while the steering wheel is trimmed in Alcantara with stitching matching the GT's exterior colour.

Preserved in its owner's private collection since delivery, this extremely rare GT Carbon Series has covered only 23 kilometres at the time of cataloguing.

Offered with its service booklets still factory sealed, its tool kit, battery maintainer and original car cover, it has furthermore been registered in France since 2025, with all taxes paid, and therefore comes with a French registration document. It is also supplied with its spare set of keys, along with its production file, including factory build sheets and manufacturing photographs.

Representing what is likely one of the last examples of its kind, the Ford GT is a pure, non-hybrid hypercar. This example, virtually new yet already registered, is therefore ready to be enjoyed both on the road and on the track.

Aston Martin's periodic revival of the Lagonda name saw it applied to a stretched, four-door AM V8 in the mid 1970s: the Series 1, a mere handful of which was constructed. When the concept re-emerged it was the sensation of the 1976 London Motor Show. Clothed in striking 'razor edge' bodywork by William Towns, the new Lagonda Series 2 saloon used the same long-wheelbase V8 chassis as its immediate predecessor while breaking new ground in terms of electronic instrumentation and switchgear. Problems with the latter would delay production until April 1978, by which time a less radical design had been adopted. The interior though, was every bit as luxurious as the exterior was futuristic, featuring selected Connolly hides, Wilton carpeting and walnut veneer, all hand-finished by skilled craftsmen in the Aston Martin tradition. Manufacture ceased in 1989 after 645 production cars had been built.

This left-hand drive Lagonda has been owned by the same family for over 25 years. Regularly serviced and presented in good overall cosmetic condition (the digital instrumentation is working), the engine starts and the gears are shifting smoothly. Finished in dark red with cream leather interior (in good condition), it comes with a Lagonda owner's handbook, expired French contrôle technique, French carte grise and a file of invoices for maintenance work.

According to 1989 correspondence on file from Carlo Felice Bianchi Anderloni, former CEO of Touring Superleggera, this 'Experimental Sport Series Type IV, triple-carburettor touring (long) chassis 918100' was completed on 15th April 1952 finished in grey with a blue leather interior and matching convertible top. This car is one of only five long-wheelbase 6C 2500 models produced, of which only two or three survive. Alfa Romeo Classiche's Certificato di Origine is on file.

Shortly after completion, the car was purchased new by James Omar Radford of Abilene, Texas. A millionaire heir to a thriving wholesale grocery and real estate business, Radford spent most of his time in Hollywood working as a film producer. A few years later, this remarkable Alfa Romeo Cabriolet passed to the famous American architect, William Kesling.

The next recorded owner (from 1972) was L H 'Bud' Von Nordheim of National City, California. Records indicate that Von Nordheim carefully maintained the Alfa until August 1979. The car was then left on his property in a state of partial restoration until it was rescued in 1987 by Alfa Romeo enthusiast David Skora of Escondido, California. Photographs on file show that the car had been repainted several times since 1952 while retaining much of its original interior under a light-coloured top. A set of Borrani wire wheels had been fitted (preserved by subsequent owners to the present day).

Bruce Robertson of Lake Forest, Illinois found this 6C 2500 Cabriolet in 1997 in the middle of a restoration commissioned by Skora. Robertson ensured that it was returned to the factory-correct colour combination and completed to the highest standards by Eric Roseneau. The car left Roseneau in 2003 and immediately claimed awards for 'Best Alfa Romeo' and 'Best of Show' at the Detroit Concorso d'Italia. Robertson later exhibited this beautiful car at the Amelia Island Concours d'Elegance and various local events near Chicago, before selling it to Oscar Davis in 2008.

With superbly elegant lines, this is undoubtedly one of the most desirable variants of the Alfa Romeo 6C 2500 with exclusive coachwork by Touring. It even comes with correspondence with the great Sig. Anderloni himself and will surely to be welcomed at the world's most prestigious concours events. The car is offered with a history file and comes with a US-title. All EU-taxes have been paid.
