Sensation of the 1934 Berlin Auto Show, Mercedes-Benz's legendary pre-war 500K supercar cost a small fortune when new and today commands a king's ransom, such is its rarity. The 1930s decade was a period of unprecedented fertility in motor car styling, of which the sublime 500K represented the very pinnacle of excellence. Its timeless appeal endures to this day (the original name of the model, 'Typ 500 mit Kompressor', was later shortened to '500K').

Beneath its seemingly endless bonnet, the 500K's eight-cylinder engine developed 100bhp un-supercharged or 160bhp with the compressor engaged. The car had a top speed approaching 110mph (177km/h). After testing a 500K cabriolet in 1936, The Autocar declared: "This is a master car, for the very few. The sheer insolence of its great power affords an experience on its own."

The Mercedes-Benz 500K and its successor, the 540K, are among the most iconic models of the classic era. A total of 761 chassis of the two W29 models—the 500K and 540K—were produced at the Stuttgart-Untertürkheim plant between February 1934 and November 1939: 342 with a 5-litre engine and 419 with a 5.4-litre engine. Of these, 691 units were fitted with bodies by the "Sonderwagenbau" department at the Sindelfingen plant, while only 70 chassis were delivered to external coachbuilders for bodywork. The most popular model was the Cabriolet B, with 296 units produced, while the exclusive and dignified Special Roadster achieved a total production run of around 50 units. The various coupé variants amounted to only 12 cars, and just 6 examples of the Autobahn Kurier were built.

The chassis of the 500K and 540K had a wheelbase of 3,290 mm and was available in two versions. In addition to the standard configuration, there was a variant in which the radiator, engine-gearbox unit, steering gear and seats were moved rearwards by just over 10 cm. Roadsters, Special Roadsters, Cabriolet A and Autobahn Kurier models were built on this rearward-engine chassis, while all other body variants were constructed on the standard chassis.

According to Mercedes-Benz Classic in Stuttgart, the delivery of chassis no. U105.394 to the Paris branch was recorded in the commission book on 29 November 1934, shortly after the model's first presentation at the Paris Salon in October. Unfortunately, there is no mention of either the customer or the coachbuilder. (According to a letter from DaimlerChrysler Schweiz AG dated 27 November 2006, this car—chassis number "U105394"—was delivered new to Germany; this information has since been proven to be incorrect.)

The number 102401.59 stamped on the engine block provides the following information:
10 for the Untertürkheim plant
24 for the new M24 engine type
01 for the series
59 for the 59th engine of the first series

This corresponds with the total production of 105 units in 1934 and, together with the original engine plate no. U105.394, confirms that this car is matching numbers.

Although sales opportunities for Mercedes-Benz on the French market were limited by exorbitant import duties of 45%, the company maintained a showroom on the Champs-Élysées and regularly exhibited its latest models at the Paris Salon in October. Internal documents from the Mercedes-Benz board of directors show that attendance at the Salon was considered a "must" in order to present the brand to international customers. One way to partially circumvent import duties was to deliver bare chassis—a strategy that proved successful, as the 500K/540K chassis attracted the interest of the most prestigious coachbuilders of the time.

This particular example features a fixed-head coupé body by Vanvooren, one of the most renowned and successful French luxury-car coachbuilders of the 1930s. Carrosserie Vanvooren, based in Courbevoie in north-west Paris, bodied the majority of Hispano-Suiza chassis during this period and also designed and built numerous bodies for Bugatti, Delage, Rolls-Royce, Bentley, Packard and Cadillac. These automotive gems are among the most exclusive one-off creations and can be found today in the world's most prestigious collections.
As confirmed during a thorough inspection by Vanvooren specialist Martin Waltz in December 2025, the Vanvooren body number 2933 appears in several locations on the vehicle and dates from August 1938. What happened to the chassis during the three years following its delivery from Stuttgart to Paris remains unknown. It is possible that it remained unsold during this period, but it may also have received an initial body that was later replaced in 1938. Among the Parisian elite of the 1930s, it was common practice either to purchase new cars at short intervals or to have existing ones modernised. There are countless examples of this trend, often driven by the regularly held Concours d'Élégance, which demanded the very best. Alternatively, it may simply have been a matter of a new owner with new tastes.

As was customary, Vanvooren prepared a design proposal for the customer, illustrated in Jan Melin and Sven Hernström's book Mercedes-Benz 8: The Supercharged 8-Cylinder Cars of the 1930s, Volume 2 (copies of the relevant pages on file). In addition to the spectacular front wings and the rearward-mounted engine/radiator unit, the use of a design feature introduced two years earlier by the coachbuilder Letourneur & Marchand is particularly striking: the pillarless, overlapping front and rear side windows with a rearward-sloping line. Vanvooren employed this feature on several other bodies as well. It is not known with certainty whether the car's first paintwork was dark green, as it is today; however, there is much to suggest this was the case, as the largely original all-green interior—with leather-covered dashboard and window surrounds—corresponds perfectly with Vanvooren's preference for single-colour paintwork and interiors.

It can be assumed that the Mercedes remained in France until 1947, when it first appeared in Geneva, Switzerland. That year, the Vanvooren-bodied Mercedes caught the attention of 18-year-old schoolboy Pierre Strinati. Carrying Swiss dealer plates "GE 2325," it was parked on the curb in front of Garage Verolet at 107 Boulevard de la Cluse (see pictures). Immediately fascinated, Strinati found the courage to enquire about the extraordinary vehicle, despite not yet having a driving licence. The green car was offered for sale at CHF 3,500. He photographed it and cherished the images from that moment on, never expecting to see the Mercedes again (handwritten notes and photographs by Mr Strinati are on file).

The 500K was photographed once more, this time in front of the Eaux-Vives Garage owned by Blanc & Paiches, now without a number plate (the photographer is unknown). Together with Strinati's images, these are the earliest known photographs of the car. Official importation from France to Switzerland followed the next year, as evidenced by the customs clearance certificate dated 31 July 1948 (document on file).
Eleven years later, during a visit to Montreux on the opposite side of Lake Geneva, Pierre Strinati was unexpectedly reacquainted with his dream car. Now painted black, it was driving slowly through town. He ran after it and, when it stopped in front of the "Le Pavillon" tea house, approached the driver, Kaspar Schmid—who was also the proprietor of the establishment. When Strinati asked whether he might consider selling the car, Schmid replied in the affirmative, much to his surprise. Thus, on 29 January 1959—67 years ago to the day—the Mercedes changed hands for the final time, for CHF 10,000.

This Mercedes became the first car in what would grow into one of the most remarkable private collections in the world. Strinati, the only son of a wealthy textile manufacturer, had been cultivating his passion for automotive design since the mid-1950s and, by the mid-1960s, had assembled in his private garage nearly every marque now considered a blue-chip classic. The collection included outstanding examples from Bugatti, Delage, Delahaye, Talbot, Voisin, Ferrari, Lancia, Alfa Romeo, Horch, Maybach, Mercedes-Benz, BMW, Lagonda, Jaguar, Aston Martin and Pegaso. Although he sold several cars during the 1980s and 1990s, he never parted with the Mercedes-Benz 500K Vanvooren, his personal favourite.

Following its purchase, Mr Strinati commissioned Carrosserie Roland Bodi to adjust the bonnet, repair the radiator, re-chrome the bumpers, repair the seats (likely referring to elements of the door panels, as the seats themselves appear completely original), and repaint the car in green—the colour it had when he first encountered it. The related quotation dated 25 February 1960 and the invoice for CHF 2,415 dated 26 April 1960 are on file. Strinati registered the Mercedes on 31 May 1960 under the number "GE 33961" and used it almost daily, often accompanied by his mother, who shared his deep affection for the car. In the 1970s, the 500K was taken out of service and placed into storage. In 1993, it was briefly exhibited at the Musée de l'Automobile Jean Tua in Geneva before being stored on axle stands in a purpose-built garage for the next 30 years.

In 2015, Martin Waltz—then researching a book on Vanvooren—wrote to Mr Strinati and inspected the 500K (documentation on file). More recently, he authored an article on the car in German, also on file.
A high-quality 1:43-scale collector's model of the car presented here is included in the sale. Released in 2014 by EMC/B&G in a limited edition of 150 examples, it is of outstanding quality—thanks in part to the support of Mr Strinati (correspondence on file).

This exceptional automobile, a unique fusion of German engineering and French design, is accompanied by an extensive archive of correspondence, period photographs, brochures, invoices and letters. Despite having been resprayed, in the 1960s, it remains in an outstanding state of originality and preservation, with the sumptuous green leather interior believed to be largely original. In recent years, the rarity, elegance and performance of these large, supercharged Mercedes models have made them among the most sought-after classic cars whenever they appear on the open market. This exceptionally well-documented example, hidden from public view for decades, is worthy of the closest inspection.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1966 DESCRIPTION:
• One of only ca. 27 DS 21 'Majesty' models built by Henri Chapron
• Rare internal division
• Directly commissioned from Henri Chapron by Simone Fournier
• Long-standing ownership within the Chapron family
• No-expense-spared restoration
• Certificate of authenticity from Noëlle Chapron

"Perhaps France's most prolific coachbuilders, Henri Chapron's label epitomized the classic style of body design through several generations, evolving at the same pace as popular taste – often in the vanguard, but careful never to be ahead of his time." - The Beaulieu Encyclopedia of the Automobile – Coachbuilding.

Today, the name of Henri Chapron is forever associated with his sublime soft-tops on the Citroën DS platform. Chapron's interpretations of the Citroën DS and ID were quite different from the regular production versions. Chapron added fins to the rear wing tops of Citroëns as early as 1965 and launched his own version of an upmarket DS at the Porte de Versailles Salon de l'Auto in October 1964 using the name 'Majesty'. Its purpose was to satisfy the few customers who considered the upmarket DS Prestige insufficiently exclusive, although that too was built by Chapron for Citroën. The Majesty featured a higher and more angular roofline compared to the factory DS, similar to the 'Concorde' coach, affording increased headroom for the rear passengers and greater interior space. This limited edition model was produced up to 1969, with only 27 examples being built in total.

A masterpiece of French automotive craftsmanship, this 1966 Citroën DS 21 Majesty saloon is one of the ca. 27 meticulously handcrafted by the legendary Parisian coachbuilder, Henri Chapron. Commissioned in July 1966 by Madame Simone Fournier directly from her son-in-law, Henri Chapron, the car was delivered on 10th November 1966 and first registered in Paris on 15th November 1966, with the license plate '6535 TM 75'. The Chapron family owned this car for many years, underscoring its exceptional provenance.

This Majesty boasts an elegant blue paint finish and a stylish interior trimmed in beige leather and fabric, while the partition separating the chauffeur's compartment is both rare and particularly desirable. The car has undergone a compprehensive restoration, carried out at huge expense and with uncompromising attention to detail. It is reported that all major mechanical components have been overhauled for maximum reliability.

With only four owners since delivery and a Certificate of Authenticity issued by Madame Noëlle Chapron, this Majesty represents a unique opportunity to acquire a Chapron masterpiece with a direct connection to the renowned French coachbuilder. French registered and offered with extensive documentation, this one-of-a-kind car affords an unparalleled combination of exclusivity, design heritage and historical significance: a rare opportunity for discerning collectors of French automotive art.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1956 DESCRIPTION:
• One of only 843 XK140 fixed-head coupés made with right-hand drive
• Delivered new to Switzerland
• Strinati family ownership from new
• Believed genuine 3,150 kilometres from new
• Requires recommissioning

Launched in 1954, the Jaguar XK140 was broadly similar to, though more refined than, its sensational XK120 predecessor, major engineering changes being confined to the repositioning of the engine 3" further forward and the adoption of rack-and-pinion steering as used on the racing C-Type. The suspension and brakes remained much as before, though with stiffer torsion bars at the front and telescopic shock absorbers at the rear, replacing the previous lever type. As before, three models were offered: roadster, coupé and drophead coupé, the latter two offering usefully increased cabin space and occasional rear seats. Outwardly the newcomer was distinguishable by its revised radiator grille, rear lights incorporating flashing indicators, and larger bumpers.

The power unit remained Jaguar's well-tried, 3.4-litre, twin-cam six, which now produced 190bhp in standard trim. A close-ratio gearbox enabled better use to be made of the increased performance, while Laycock-de Normanville overdrive became an option for the first time.

An original right-hand drive model, this XK140 coupé was despatched from the factory on 6th March 1956 to Jaguar agent Garage Claparède in Geneva, Switzerland, and on 6th April 1959 was sold by them to Madame Jeane Strinati, Pierre Strinati's mother, who is listed on the accompanying JDHT Certificate as first owner. The aforementioned heritage certificate records the original colour scheme as Cream with red interior, but Claparède's invoice states that the car was Grey (the colour it is today). A note written by Mr Strinati himself mentions that the car was Cream when imported (as attested by the swiss customs documents), so it must have been repainted upon its arrival in Geneva.

The odometer reading is 3,150 kilometres, which could very well be the distance covered from new given the car's remarkable state of preservation the car appears to have its fully original interior and exhaust manifold coating). Close inspection is recommended.

The car comes with instruction manuals; a wealth of Jaguar Drivers' Club correspondence (Mr Strinati was a life member having owned several examples including, among others, an SS100, an XK150S and an E-Type, the last two bought new. As with all the other cars in the collection, the Jaguar has been stored on axle stands for many years and will require recommissioning.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1971 DESCRIPTION:
• One of only 425 Ghibli SS 4.9 coupés built
• Delivered new in Italy
• Desirable manual transmission example
• Enthusiast ownership for 20 years (2004-2024)
• Well maintained

Unveiled at the 1966 Turin Auto Show, the Maserati Ghibli quickly distinguished itself as a formidable competitor in the Gran Turismo marketplace, standing alongside legends such as the Ferrari 365 GTB/4 'Daytona' and Lamborghini Miura. It was this competitive landscape that drove Maserati to introduce the Ghibli SS. The original Ghibli was equipped with a 4.7-litre V8 engine that produced around 306 horsepower. The Ghibli SS, however, came with a 4.9-litre V8 producing around 335bhp; its top speed of 280km/h (174mph) made it - at the time - the fastest Maserati road car ever produced.

Designed by Giorgetto Giugiaro at Carrozzeria Ghia, the Ghibli is celebrated for its striking looks, featuring a long hood, sleek lines and a low, elongated silhouette. This blend of elegance and aggressiveness typifies Italian sports cars of the 1960s and '70s. Beyond its thrilling performance, the Ghibli SS offers a refined level of accommodation for two passengers and their luggage, affording the perfect combination of luxury and speed. With around 425 examples produced, the Ghibli SS coupé is a rare and highly sought-after classic.

This Maserati Ghibli SS, chassis number 'AM115/49 1948', was manufactured on 25th November 1970. Delivered new in Italy, it was finished in elegant Oro Longchamps with a black leather interior, and is equipped with the 4.9-litre SS engine and the ZF five-speed manual transmission.

Acquired in 2004 by its previous (French) owners (members of the Club Maserati France), the Ghibli has been meticulously maintained over the past 20-or-so years. Accompanying documentation on file reveals a history of careful stewardship, including detailed service records from Landrin Sport et Collection in the Ardennes (2006-2016); Pierre Nallet's Garage du Trident in 2009; and Trident, a Maserati specialist in the Vendée in 2017. A 2016 expert appraisal on file confirms the car's outstanding condition, noting its nice paintwork, perfectly aligned bumpers, and original dashboard. There are also technical inspections from 2010, 2012 and 2017, and a French Carte Grise. Additionally, a repaint and major service were completed at the Ateliers des Légendes for €17,000, ensuring that this Ghibli SS not only looks stunning but is also thoroughly prepared and a delightful driving experience. More recently, the retractable headlights were overhauled and the battery replaced, and the car passed a French Contrôle Technique (technical inspection) in September 2024.

historical_significance: Related to Citroën's Croisière Jaune expedition
description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1934 DESCRIPTION:
• Similar to the vehicles used for Citroën's Croisière Jaune expedition
• Purchased for the collection in 1984
• Comes with extensive literature concerning the Croisière Jaune
• Requires recommissioning

The vehicle offered here is broadly similar to those used for André Citroën's audacious but ill-fated Central Asian Expedition of 1931/1932. Known popularly as the 'Croisière Jaune' (Yellow Cruise), this was the third such venture undertaken by Citroën using his autochenille half-tracks, which had been developed following his acquisition of the sole rights to an ingenious form of caterpillar-tracked drive system invented by engineer Adolphe Kégresse (chenille = caterpillar). The Central Asian crossing would be attempted by two separate groups: one travelling west-east from Beirut in Lebanon; the other east-west from Beijing in China, the plan being to meet at Kashgar on the ancient Silk Road. Despite many setbacks, the west-east group completed its mission and reached Beijing, although, sadly, expedition leader Georges-Marie Haardt would die later in Hong Kong.

Pierre Strinati purchased this autochenille on the 15th March 1984 from Oldtimer Gallery in Toffen, Switzerland; previously it had been in Belgium with one Yves Dumortier. One of the last additions to his collection, this vehicle was acquired because it reminded Pierre Strinati of his own expeditions to Africa and South America at a time when there were no maps of their unexplored territories. The history file contains an old Belgian registration document and extensive literature concerning the Croisière Jaune'. Recommissioning will be required following a lengthy period out of use.

THE MASERATI INDY

Maserati followed up its stunning, Ghia-styled Ghibli two-seater with the equally elegant Indy 2+2. Though the latter, announced in 1968 and noteworthy as the first unitary construction Maserati, was the work of Carrozzeria Vignale. The Indy first appeared publicly on Vignale's stand at the 1968 Turin Motor Show and was officially launched by Maserati at the Geneva Salon in 1969. Running gear was conventional, with independent front suspension, live rear axle and four-wheel disc brakes, while the power unit was—initially—the Modena firm's well-tried, 4.1-liter, four-cam V8, with 4.7- and 4.9-liter versions following. A ZF five-speed manual gearbox was standard, with a three-speed Borg Warner automatic available to special order. With 260bhp on tap, the top speed of Maserati's luxury four-seater was in the region of 150mph, a figure the subsequent larger-engined versions improved upon. The sleek Vignale coachwork was so effective that the Indy was able to carry four people in relative comfort without impairing its performance as a sports car. In 4.9-liter form, the Indy's claimed maximum increased to 320bhp, which pushed its top speed to 165mph (266km/h). Power steering and air conditioning were standard on the "4900" model, 300 of which were made between 1972 and 1975.

Autocar magazine's summary was one of almost unalloyed praise, "Classic touring car with vee-8 engine and 160mph potential. Beautifully smooth power unit, silky gearbox and light, power assisted steering. Good brakes, balanced handling, comfortable ride, superb stability. High price but few disappointments."


THE CAR OFFERED

Bonhams|Cars is pleased to offer this outstanding 1970 Maserati Indy 4700. The car is one of only 364 Indy 4700s produced. Adding to its rarity, this specimen is fitted with the highly desirable ZF 5-speed manual transmission. The car was originally delivered new to Mexico City and eventually made its way to the United States. The grand tourer is fitted with air conditioning, power steering, alloy wheels, power windows, and an AM/FM radio.

This Indy was part of the respected collection of the Riverside International Automotive Museum for many years. Prior to joining that collection, the Indy received an upgraded 4.9-liter Maserati power plant for an even more exceptional driving experience. This example was the recipient of prior restoration work, likely while it was in the museum collection. The exterior received new paint and was finished in its original color combination of Azzurro Hyperion over Black leather interior, still presenting well today.

The Indy is often praised as one of Maserati's great road cars of the era. The classic Vignale coachwork perfectly emphasized the cars outstanding performance yet gives the car enough elegance to make it worthy of the trident on the hood. With its 4.9-liter engine, ZF 5-speed manual transmission, and desirable livery, this particular example is undoubtedly one of the finest. An excellent car for high-speed rallies such as the Copperstate 1000, this stylish Indy is ready for its next caretaker.

THE PONTIAC GTO

For many enthusiasts the '64 and '65 GTO remains the only 'Muscle Car' that matters. The originator of the concept, the GTO was a special car at a special time and became an instant legend. All GTOs are collectors' items but none more so than the original '64, and at the time there were hardly enough to go around. Borrowed from the competition version of Ferrari's famous 250-series sports car, the initials stand for 'Gran Turismo Omologato' – homologated Grand Touring. The GTO started out as a high-performance options package for the 'intermediate' sized Pontiac Tempest Le Mans and came in sports coupé, hardtop coupé and convertible variants distinguished by those all-important 'GTO' badges. At the GTO's heart was a 389ci (6.4-liter) V8 engine available in two states of tune: standard 325bhp with a single, four-barrel carburetor or optional 348bhp (in '65, 360bhp) equipped with the Tri-Power set-up of three, twin-choke instruments. Transmission options included the (stock) heavy-duty three-speed manual gearbox, three-speed Hydra-Matic auto and Muncie close-ratio manual four-speeder with Hurst shifter, while there was a lengthy list of special performance-enhancing GTO accessories. Big-car power in a medium sized package made for exhilarating performance, Car & Driver magazine achieving a 0-60mph time of 4.6 seconds and the standing quarter mile in 13.1s/115.0mph with a 348bhp, manual transmission example, figures that put many a more exalted - and more expensive - purpose-built sports car to shame.


THE CAR OFFERED

To many enthusiasts, the Genesis of the Muscle Car starts with the Pontiac GTO. Combining the mild-mannered, mid-sized Tempest with the powerful 389 cubic inch V8 from the full-sized Grand Prix, Pontiac set off a firestorm of competition both within GM, and among the Big Three and all their respective divisions. This 1965 GTO hails from the second year for Pontiac's groundbreaking muscle car. This is an original 'triple black' car, and the build tags denote it as having the all-important 5N GTO option, paired with the code 2L 4-Speed floor shift option. It also features tri-power carburetors and power brakes. The black paintwork is particularly attractive, while signature slash-cut tailpipes and period Cragar SS wheels with redline tires complete the fantastic aesthetic. Swing open the door, and you'll find the black interior is authentically finished in the proper black vinyl, with details including an original steering wheel, Hurst 4-speed shifter with cue-ball shift knob, original Delco radio, and console-mounted vacuum gauge. No muscle car collection is complete without a great Pontiac GTO, and this excellent 1965 convertible is sure to find a place of pride in your stable.

THE 1975 PORSCHE 911 CARRERA

By the mid-1970s, the Porsche 911 had already etched its formidable reputation into the annals of automotive history. Having first dazzled enthusiasts and the public alike at its 1963 debut, the iconic rear-engine coupe had evolved measurably by 1975. Porsche's singular focus on continuous technical refinement led to the arrival of the Carrera 2.7—a model inherited directly from the legendary Carrera RS and bearing much of its high-performance DNA.

At its core, the 911 Carrera distinguished itself through its 2.7-liter flat-six engine, the very heart that beat within the revered Carrera RS. Fed by Bosch K-Jetronic fuel injection, this engine was celebrated for its lively throttle response, robust midrange torque, and reliable performance, producing 175bhp for U.S. specification cars—substantial for its era and delivering a crisp, invigorating driving experience. Coupled to the durable and precise Type 915 5-speed gearbox, the Carrera provided both sporting potential and usability, attracting dedicated drivers and discerning collectors.

Performance, however, was only part of the 911 Carrera's allure. The model's chassis, with its fully independent suspension, enabled deft handling, poise, and composure on both open highways and winding canyon roads. The sophisticated four-wheel disc brakes set a high benchmark for safety and stopping power among its contemporaries. Meanwhile, Porsche's renowned build quality and rigorous engineering imbued each 911 Carrera with unmistakable solidity and reliability.

Aesthetically, the Carrera's lines remained unmistakably 911: purposeful, athletic, and timelessly elegant. Flared rear fenders, bold Carrera script, and—on many examples—front and rear spoilers hinted at the car's formidable potential while offering improved aerodynamic performance. For 1975, bold new color options and high levels of trim customization became available, ensuring that each Carrera was as individual as its owner; Paint-to-Sample orders, in particular, encapsulated Porsche's commitment to bespoke exclusivity.

Collectors prize the 1975 Carrera for its rarity and direct lineage to Porsche motorsport icons. Just 395 examples were produced for the U.S. market, each offering a blend of mechanical sophistication and evocative style, made even rarer by early adoption of advanced fuel injection. Today, well-preserved or unrestored examples—particularly those in exceptional colors with extensive documentation—command strong global demand.

Inside, the Carrera delivered on the promise of everyday sporting comfort. The signature Germanic ergonomics, deeply bolstered seats, and precision-crafted switchgear ensured both driver focus and passenger delight. Optional luxuries, such as power windows, sunroof, leather upholstery, and upgraded audio, brought a touch of opulence to this purposeful sports coupe.

Beyond its technical credentials, the Carrera 2.7 embodies a spirit of lasting legacy. Its robust mechanicals, distinctive period features, and glorious flat-six soundtrack evoke a golden era of analog driving—one that continues to captivate a new generation of classic Porsche enthusiasts. Ownership marks entry into a storied tradition: a celebration of form, function, and the relentless pursuit of excellence that defines the Porsche marque.


THE CAR OFFERED

Offered here is a rare and highly original example of the 1975 Porsche 911 Carrera Sunroof Coupe, chassis 9115400287, engine no. 6451956. Delivered new as a US-specification Carrera to the southern United States, this car is immediately distinguished by its extraordinary Paint-to-Sample Green (257) livery—an audacious and seldom-seen hue that captivates in every light. The vibrant exterior is tastefully paired with its highly original Cinnamon leather interior, a combination specified from new and documented by the factory certificate; One of the most spirited and elegant 911 color palettes of the era.

As one of just 395 U.S.-market Carrera coupes built that year, and confirmed as production number 287, the car's numbers-matching engine and gearbox remain intact.

Refreshed over a decade ago, this 911 has since been preserved in highly original form, benefitting from both the patina and freshness that define a properly kept classic. The paintwork, executed in its original factory-ordered shade of Paint-to-Sample Green, remains true and resplendent, presenting with depth and luster. The Cinnamon leather interior, likewise, retains its period-correct character, with original materials and subtle evidence of gentle use.

The Carrera's specification is both desirable and correct, comprising the renowned 2.7-liter Bosch K-Jetronic injected flat-six, mated to the robust 915 five-speed manual transmission. Important original features include the factory sunroof, VDO instrumentation, rear spoiler, distinctive Fuchs-style wheels, Bosch fog lamps, and period Blaupunkt radio. Driver conveniences—such as power windows, 2+2 rear seating, door pockets, and analog clock—complete the package, marrying sporting intent with comfort.

The odometer reads just 61,830 miles at the time of cataloguing, an especially low total for a nearly 50-year-old 911 Carrera and highly indicative of long-term preservation and limited use.

Presented as a striking and one-of-one collector's example, this Paint-to-Sample Green over Cinnamon 911 Carrera Sunroof Coupe holds a coveted position among mid-1970s Porsche collectibles. Its matching-numbers integrity, documented provenance, singular color specification, outstanding condition, and carefully preserved originality render it an unmissable offering for the discerning Porsche aficionado or astute collector seeking one of the marque's most celebrated models from the golden era.

THE FORD MUSTANG

Ford created a new class of car almost overnight with the introduction of the Mustang Sports Coupe part way through the 1964 season, catching the rest of the US auto industry off guard. The brainchild of Lee Iacocca - subsequent savior of the Chrysler Corporation – the Mustang is one of the most remarkable automotive success stories of modern times and arguably the pinnacle of his long career with Ford. Aimed at the affluent young, for whom a car was as much a lifestyle statement as means of transport, the Mustang succeeded brilliantly, achieving sales in excess of a quarter million by the end of '64. This remarkable debut was followed by a staggering 524,791 sales in 1965, earning Ford a fortune.

PORSCHE 911 CARRERA

Porsche revived the evocative Carrera name—previously reserved for the competition-oriented versions of the 356—for its luxuriously equipped, top-of-the-range 911 in 1973. By the start of the 1984 model year, the Carrera title was applied across all 911 variants, coinciding with the introduction of the 3.2-liter engine. This revival marked a major update to the long-running 911, which was now selling better than ever after development had slowed while Porsche focused on meeting rising demand.

While retaining the classic air-cooled flat-six layout, the 3.2-liter engine was some 80% new, featuring an effective cam chain tensioner and improved lubrication system—finally addressing a longstanding 911 weakness. For the first time, an ECU controlled both fuel and ignition, making the engine more powerful, efficient, and responsive. Producing 207 bhp, a 27-horsepower increase over its predecessor, the Carrera's performance approached that of the original 1974 911 Turbo. This translated to a 0-60 mph time of just 6.1 seconds and a top speed of 150 mph (241 km/h), with 100 mph (160 km/h) reached in an exhilarating 14.0 seconds.

THE 2CV

Few automobiles can claim to have altered the course of motoring history as profoundly as the Citroën 2CV. Conceived in the pre-war years and launched to the public in 1948, the modest "deux chevaux" or "two horsepower" quickly became an enduring icon of postwar ingenuity, utility, and distinctly Gallic charm. The 2CV emerged as a response to the spiritual and practical needs of rural France; its mission was simple, yet revolutionary: to produce a car capable of carrying four adults and fifty kilograms of farm goods at speed across untreated roads, with an emphasis on economy, comfort, and robust simplicity.

Citroën's courageous engineering spirit shone in every aspect of the 2CV's production. Its featherweight construction, advanced long-travel suspension, and air-cooled engine made it uniquely suited to both urban and rural environments across the world. More than a utilitarian workhorse, the 2CV also became a symbol of egalitarian mobility and post-war renewal. Despite—or perhaps because of—its eccentric, unmistakable silhouette and minimalistic appointments, the 2CV endeared itself to motorists and collectors alike.

Throughout its production run, Citroën continued to refine the 2CV, introducing mechanical and aesthetic changes that heightened reliability without diluting the model's original spirit. The installation of the 425cc engine brought improved power and drivability, reinforcing the model's legend as nimble and almost unburstable. Its utterly engaging driving experience is enhanced by the car's renowned supple ride, razor-sharp economy, and communicative controls, ensuring that every journey is as memorable as it is practical.

International acceptance followed quickly, with the 2CV finding markets far beyond France. Production for export to the United States emerged in the 1960s, where the model's unconventional style and frugal engineering found loyal adherents seeking character as well as efficiency. Today, well-preserved 2CVs—especially genuine US-specification examples—are rare and keenly pursued by enthusiasts who appreciate their historical significance and unpretentious joy.

The 2CV's irresistibly straightforward design, paired with a uniquely French sensibility, has rendered it a pop culture ambassador, appearing in films, artwork, and the garages of the discerning for over half a century. The whimsical but purposeful two-tone combinations available in the late 1960s, together with delightful period accessories and a robust appetite for adventure, have made the later 2CVs particularly coveted in the collector community.

From student runabout to countryside mainstay, the enduring utility of the 2CV has been matched only by its role as a fashionable symbol of freedom and adventure. Its reliability, ease of maintenance, and irrepressible spirit continue to endear it to generations of motoring enthusiasts.

In the classic car world, provenance, originality, and a compelling story are as important as mechanical condition. Combination of period-correct finishes, low mileage, and celebrity history elevates this example as both an entertaining motoring companion and a testament to the 2CV's universal appeal.


THE CAR OFFERED

Presented here is a delightfully distinctive 1967 Citroën 2CV, chassis 7080428, in a its vibrant two-tone yellow and blue livery, colorfully complemented by the iconic blue retractable vinyl roof and gray-cloth-and-vinyl cabin, but by its compelling provenance, having passed through the hands of supermodel and entrepreneur Christie Brinkley, who received the car as a personal gift from her then-husband, singer-songwriter Billy Joel.

Purchased by its current owner in the mid-1990s directly from Ms. Brinkley, the car has since remained in careful, enthusiast stewardship for nearly three decades. Throughout this period, it served as both a beloved driver and a cherished conversation piece.

The car's two-tone exterior, a lively blend of yellow panels offset by blue wings and roof, brings exuberance to its famously minimalist lines. While the current vinyl roof displays some light tears, this honest cosmetic patina documents the authenticity of its years on the road and encourages either preservation or modest refurbishment in the next custodian's hands. The 15-inch steel wheels, mounted with well-worn Michelin tires, and the fitment of mud flaps at the front, both speak to the car's strong period-correct character and French-market heritage.

Mechanically, this 2CV's 425cc air-cooled twin-cylinder engine is reported to run and drive well, having benefited from recent preparation for sale, including a new battery, comprehensive ignition service, and fuel system flush. Paired with the famed four-speed manual transaxle, the powertrain provides the feather-light agility and surprising comfort for which these Citroëns are beloved; power is sent to the front wheels through supple, independent suspension.

Celebrities have long been drawn to the 2CV's unpretentious joie de vivre, and the connection to Christie Brinkley and Billy Joel endows this car with narrative value few collector cars can match. Records accompanying the sale (including service and registration history) testify to the stewardship of its present owner and ensure a reassuring history.

A rare opportunity to acquire a celebrity-owned 2CV with lasting provenance, this example represents the ideal intersection of eccentric charm, simplicity, and star-studded history. It stands poised to captivate its next caretaker—as it has for each of its fortunate custodians before.

THE ALPINA BMW

Founded in 1965 by Burkard Bovensiepen in Kaufbeuren, Bavaria, Alpina began producing tuned BMW models in the 1960s—well before BMW's own Motorsport division introduced its now-legendary "M" cars. A close collaborator with BMW from the outset, Alpina was granted official manufacturer status in Germany and played a pivotal role in shaping BMW's high-performance reputation through both its road cars and numerous motorsport successes.

At the time, the BMW 5 Series provided the ideal foundation for Alpina's engineering expertise. Renowned for its build quality and dynamic balance, the E28 platform offered a wide range of engines and transmissions, allowing Alpina to transform this refined German sedan into a genuine supercar contender.

Introduced in 1984, the M535i sat at the top of the E28 range with 218 bhp—impressive, yet insufficient for certain clients. Until the arrival of the 286bhp M5 in 1985, Alpina's B7 Turbo was the only alternative. Equipped with a KKK K27 turbocharger, the Alpina-developed M535i produced an astonishing 300bhp at the wheels—outperforming even the M5. In 1986, the B7 Turbo received a catalytic converter, yet Alpina succeeded in making it even faster and more powerful than its predecessor. With 320bhp, 375 lb-ft of torque, a 0–60mph time of under five seconds, and a top speed of approximately 170mph, the figures speak for themselves.

Priced significantly higher than both the M535i and the M5, the B7 Turbo was produced in limited numbers—approximately 236 examples in total. Of these, only 42 were built in "Katalysator" specification, and just four are believed to have been equipped with the ZF dogleg five-speed manual transmission.


THE CAR OFFERED

This B7 Turbo/3 Katalysator was delivered new on September 16, 1986, to Nicole Racing Japan, Alpina's official importer in Japan. Designated as a press car, it was specified with a high level of equipment, including Schwartzblau Metallic paint with signature Alpina stripes, heated Alpina seats and upholstery, air conditioning, electric sunroof, power windows, headlamp washers, and a special audio system. First registered in 1987, the car remained with Nicole Racing Japan for much of its life and was meticulously maintained. It was imported to the United States in 2015 when purchased from Japan by Mr. Fox of Canyon Country, California. Extensive service documentation is available from this period, including work carried out by 2002 AD in Pomona and Eurasian Automotive in Pasadena.

With fewer than 60,000 miles recorded and documented maintenance history from its home market, the car was already in highly original condition when acquired by its current owner in 2022. In addition, $14,442 was spent in 2019 on significant maintenance, including a complete brake overhaul, replacement of the head gasket, numerous oil and fuel lines, and suspension bushings throughout. The car has also been fitted with a modern Blaupunkt Bremen head unit, faithfully replicating the design of period-correct 1980s radios. As one of the rarest road-going Alpinas ever produced, this B7 Turbo/3 Katalysator represents a true collector-grade automobile. Offered with a comprehensive history file—including a copy of its original purchase invoice, Japanese and U.S. service records, and a U.S. title—this exceptional Alpina is the missing cornerstone of any serious 1980s performance car collection.

THE BUICK SKYLARK

Three special convertible models graced General Motors' 1953 catalogs. Cadillac's Eldorado featured standard chrome wire wheels and a top hidden, when lowered, by a body-color metal cover. The Oldsmobile 98 Fiesta came with every conceivable factory option except air conditioning. Both cars presaged the wraparound windshields that GM would usher in on the upscale marques for 1954. A model apart from the two was Buick's 1953 Skylark.

While the Eldorado and Fiesta were based on standard convertible bodies, the Skylark was something completely different. Although on the Roadmaster chassis, it had its own distinctive fender lines, and unlike the sibling specials retained a simple curved windshield. Called the "Anniversary Convertible," it commemorated Buick's 50th birthday and came standard with virtually all options, including Kelsey Hayes chrome wire wheels. With 1,690 built, the Skylark outsold the Eldorado and Fiesta by nearly three to one.

For 1954, the Skylark became a series unto itself, and the body was substantially redesigned. Rear fenders were bobbed, sloping gently down, and large chrome taillight nacelles were added. Finally, there was a wraparound windshield, as on all '54 Buicks, and the wheel cutouts were enlarged and elongated, their contrasting color providing a visual accent. At $4,355 it was the most expensive Buick, priced more than $800 above the most expensive Roadmaster.


THE CAR OFFERED

The 1954 Buick Skylark Convertible offered here is finished in Titian Red over matching red interior along with a white convertible soft top. This example received a complete restoration done to a very high caliber. The acres of brightwork shine beautifully and appear in terrific shape. The interior shows very little wear, while the paint is presented in overall great condition. Known as being the flagship of all Buick's of that era, the Skylark had distinct styling cues to set it apart from other luxury cars of its time, including the white painted inner fenders that adorns this convertible, something rarely seen in other vehicles.

Due to its rarity when compared to other Buick models, today Skylarks seem to be available much less often. Rarely seen in the first place, they are even more rare and desirable in this wonderful combination of arresting colors and excellent preparation and presentation. This example has been well cared for during its current ownership and drives as smooth as it looks. Surely a wonderful example of a Skylark as well as a terrific addition to any car collection.

THE R107 SERIES SL ROADSTERS

When Mercedes-Benz redesigned its famed SL in 1971, there was a lot of equity behind it. After all, when the incomparable 300 SL Coupe and Roadster were built fewer than 20 years before, they set the automotive world alight. The R113-series 230/250/280SL redefined the luxury roadster market with its unrivaled levels of refinement, luxury, and quality. For its latest iteration of the SL, Mercedes started with the chassis of the mid-size W114/115 model and sourced engines from the large W116 S-Class. The result was a luxurious V8 Convertible with continent-crushing performance wrapped in a timeless, crisp design that went on to become the longest-running passenger car series ever produced by Mercedes-Benz to date. With its combination of elegant styling and superb engineering, the R107 remains a cornerstone collector car, cherished by enthusiasts the world over.

THE 993 TURBO

The introduction of the last air-cooled Porsche 911 Turbo, internally coded as the 993 Turbo, marked the final flourish of the air-cooled era—a moment in sports car history revered by collectors and enthusiast purists alike. Unveiled for the 1996 model year, this flagship variant was a technical and aesthetic tour de force, refined from three decades of relentless Stuttgart innovation. For many, it represents the ultimate evolution of the original 911 silhouette, encapsulating heritage, performance, and enduring desirability in a single, exhilarating package.

At the heart of the 993 Turbo lay the legendary 3.6-liter "Mezger" flat six—freshly enhanced with twin KKK turbochargers and sophisticated Bosch Motronic electronic engine management. This arrangement delivered an explosive 408 horsepower, making the 993 Turbo the fastest production Porsche of its day and propelling it into the rarified company of genuine supercars. Indeed, 0–60 mph arrived in scarcely four seconds, while the 180 mph top speed was claimed with both authority and grace.

Yet, the 993 Turbo distinguished itself not by brute force alone. The introduction of all-wheel drive—the first ever on a production 911 Turbo—ushered in a new era of composure and stability, countering the model's reputation for rear-engined unpredictability. Power was delivered to the road via a compact viscous coupling, accentuating both safety and accessible performance, and fundamentally transforming the Turbo from a challenging sports car into a perfectly balanced, all-weather grand tourer.

Design, too, found new heights in the 993 Turbo: its wider haunches, elegantly integrated bi-plane rear spoiler, unique front and rear bumpers, and 18-inch hollow-spoke alloys all contributed to a form that is as muscular as it is timeless. These flourishes, underpinned by a reengineered multi-link rear suspension, set the 993 apart as arguably the most accomplished and attractive air-cooled 911 ever produced.

Production volumes for the 993 Turbo were limited, as Porsche's attention soon shifted to water-cooled engineering. As a result, well-preserved original examples are scarce and fiercely sought-after, particularly those boasting correct, coveted color combinations and meticulously chronicled provenance.

The cockpit paid homage to Porsche tradition while embracing a new era of luxury. Black leather, supportive adjustable seats, and climate control system melded with the unmistakable dash arrangement pioneered in the late 1960s. Every control and flourish reminded the driver of the 911's storied lineage, while subtle cosmetic and safety upgrades pointed to a new horizon of user-friendly performance.

The 911 Turbo's driving experience remains intoxicatingly analog, and the visceral nature of its flat-six soundtrack—unmuffled by forced induction—underscores its position as a collector's cornerstone. From the moment its ignition key turns, the car transforms the mundane into the memorable.

It is this blend of tradition, innovation, and raw emotional appeal that ensures the 993 Turbo is not simply the end of an era, but a zenith of the air-cooled Porsche's evolution: a last hurrah that remains—now and always—among the marque's most collectible and exhilarating creations.


THE CAR OFFERED

This 1997 Porsche 911 Turbo, VIN. WP0AC2993VS375644, represents a rare and highly desirable opportunity: an authentically preserved, U.S.-specification 993 Turbo in factory-correct Black (Schwarz, code A1) over Black leather, presented in time-capsule condition with a well-documented, continuous service record.

According to the included CARFAX Vehicle History Report, this Turbo was delivered new to the United States and has enjoyed a verifiable chain of just four private owners—each accounting for careful stewardship over the course of nearly three decades. The car has resided variously in Illinois, Florida, Ontario, Minnesota, and most recently Kentucky, as reflected in successive registration entries and service documentation. Throughout, it has consistently retained its original coachwork and interior.

The factory livery remains unaltered: black paintwork, exhibiting a depth of finish associated as a garage-kept examples, is affird as exceedingly original by multiple records and visual inspections. The cockpit, likewise, remains preserved with original Black leather upholstery showing only the slightest signs of conscientious use.

Service provenance is a highlight. A total of 28 documented service and maintenance records accompany the car, with leading Porsche dealers and marquee specialists carrying out maintenance at well-chosen intervals. THE 911 CARRERA 4S

Few sports cars in history have achieved the singular legacy of the Porsche 911. Launched in 1964, the model quickly established itself as the benchmark for rear-engined performance motoring, combining race-bred engineering with distinctive design and daily-drivable civility. By the 1990s, the model had undergone several evolutions, culminating in the air-cooled "993" generation—a widely celebrated final chapter in the revered lineage of air-cooled Porsches.

Introduced for the 1995 model year, the Type 993 brought forth a transformative blend of modern design and heritage cues. It introduced an entirely reimagined chassis, the ingenious Weissach rear suspension, and refined aerodynamics—all while retaining the unmistakable 911 silhouette. Power came from an alloy 3.6-liter flat-six with DOHC cylinder heads, its voice and flexibility earning it high praise from both press and privateers alike.

Within the 993 range, the Carrera 4S variant occupies a place of discrete distinction. Arriving for 1996, it married the visceral engagement of the naturally aspirated Carrera engine with the robust all-wheel-drive running gear, brakes, and the dramatically flared bodywork of the flagship Turbo. This formula yielded a grand touring 911 of singular stature—supercar presence without the forced induction, offering all-weather confidence, uncanny balance, and luxury appointments as standard.

The 4S's wide haunches, red brake calipers, and 18-inch alloy wheels instantly identified it as a serious road car. Inside, semi-aniline leather and advanced sound insulation complemented advanced option packages, including sport seats and premium hi-fi stereos. The resulting cockpit was at once driver-focused and luxuriously appointed. Its deeply sculpted front bumper and lowered stance underscored its performance pedigree.

Under the skin, the Carrera 4S featured Porsche's revered viscous-coupled all-wheel-drive system. This ensured composure and traction in any driving condition, further endearing the model to drivers seeking a year-round sports car. Acceleration to 60 mph was dispatched in under six seconds, with braking and cornering limits far above the era's norm for GT cars.

Production of the 993 generation concluded in 1998, marking the end of air-cooled engine architecture—a watershed for the Stuttgart marque and its intent on moving forward technologically. As such, the 993 Carrera 4S is widely regarded as a keystone collector's Porsche, prized for its monumental road presence, usability, and irreplaceable air-cooled character.

Today, the Carrera 4S remains an icon within an icon. Coveted by collectors for its rarity, robust engineering, and timeless design, it endures as the ultimate "do-it-all" 911 of the air-cooled era. It is no exaggeration to suggest that the 993 Carrera 4S captures the very essence of Porsche's golden era in sports car production.

THE FERRARI 365GT 2+2

By the mid-1960s, fifty percent of all Ferraris produced were being built with four seats. Following on from the success of its first such model, the 250GTE of 1960, Ferrari introduced the 330GT 2+2 in January 1964. Its replacement, the 365GT 2+2, was launched at the Paris Auto Show in October 1967. Sleekly styled in the manner of the limited edition 500 Superfast, the 365GT 2+2 was the most refined Ferrari to date.

Based on that of the contemporary 330GTC, the chassis was made up of Ferrari's familiar combination of oval and round steel tubing, and in addition to featuring independent suspension all round (for the first time on a Ferrari 2+2) the car boasted Koni's hydro-pneumatic self-leveling system at the rear. Further refinements included mounting the engine and drivetrain in rubber bushes to insulate the car's occupants from noise and vibration and providing ZF power-assisted steering and air conditioning as standard equipment.

Developing 320bhp in its 365GT incarnation, the well-proven 4.4-liter V12 engine was coupled to a five-speed gearbox. The car's blistering performance - top speed 150mph, 0-60mph in 7.0 seconds - was restrained by Girling ventilated discs all around. Endowed with that unusual combination of fine handling and a supple ride, the 365GT 2+2 was rated by Car magazine as 'the most civilized Ferrari yet.'

Finished in elegant Azzurro Blue, the color highlights the Pininfarina coachwork's subtle contour. The Cream interior, presenting with a pleasing patina, offers a glimpse into the car's well-cared-for past.

This EU-specification 365 GT 2+2 was originally delivered new to Italy. Documented in Ferrari Serial Numbers Part I by H. Raab, the car's early provenance is brilliantly mapped, with assembly sequence number 388 and body number 387/A.

In the early 1990s, the car was offered by Jim Carpenter Enterprises in Phoenix, Arizona, described at the time as being in good original order with 69,400 miles displayed. By 1995, the 365 GT 2+2 had migrated to California, where Scott Melnick presented it in Beverly Hills as an outstandingly original and unmolested example. From there, the car passed into the hands of discerning American custodians who prioritized sympathetic preservation and careful, thorough maintenance.

Mechanically, the Ferrari benefited from refurbishment by Hamilton Restorations of Fort Payne, Alabama in 1995 and 1996. Notable work included repairs to the factory-fitted rear self-leveling shocks, renewed thermostatic controls, and an overhaul of the exhaust system—supported by original invoices from both Hamilton Restorations and London Stainless Steel Exhaust Centre Ltd. in the United Kingdom. Maintenance continued over the ensuing years with Bo's Auto Service in Rainsville, Alabama addressing the fuel supply, air conditioning, and cooling systems during 2004 and 2009, all carefully documented through detailed receipts. The odometer presently indicates 80,358 miles.

Ownership prior to the 1990s remains to be discovered, but from that period onward, the car's voyage through notable Ferrari specialists and collectors is comprehensively attested.

Chassis no. 12215 offers a rare opportunity to secure a documented EU-market Ferrari 365 GT 2+2, uniting matching-numbers mechanical integrity with a compelling provenance. A distinguished addition to any collection, this grand tourer invites its next owner to relish in the balance of elegant design, V-12 performance, and remarkable usability that defines the very best of classic Ferrari motoring.

THE FERRARI 550 MARANELLO

With the introduction of the 550 Maranello in 1997, Ferrari returned to its tradition of building front-engined V12 sports cars, resurrecting a line that had remained dormant since the demise of the 365GTB/4 'Daytona' in 1974. The heart of any Ferrari is its engine, and the 550 Maranello's 48-valve, 5.5-liter V12 developed 485bhp at 7,000rpm, some 100-or-so horsepower more than the Daytona's. Ferrari had discovered long ago that providing optimum balance in a front-engined sports car necessitated the use of a rear transaxle, and the Maranello's came with six speeds. The power train was housed in a tubular steel chassis, to which was attached aluminum coachwork, while the all-independent suspension incorporated dual-mode (normal/sports) damping, switch-selectable by the driver, which was complemented by speed-sensitive power-assisted steering.

Styled by Pininfarina like its illustrious 'Daytona' predecessor, the 550 Maranello was similarly proportioned, adopting the classical combination of long bonnet, small cabin and truncated tail. The body's aerodynamics were developed in the wind tunnel, where hours of testing ensured that the minimum of drag was combined with constant downforce regardless of set up, an important consideration in a 200mph road car. Styling details such as the bonnet air scoop and hot air outlets behind the front wheelarches recalled the great competizione Ferraris of the past, in particular the immortal 250GTO, while the tail incorporated Ferrari's characteristic twin circular lights.

In 2004, Evo magazine published a 'Greatest Driver's Cars' feature that pitted the 550 Maranello against the Porsche 911 GT3, Honda NSX-R and Pagani Zonda C12S. The Ferrari won. "As with all great cars, there's no one facet that dominates the experience," declared the respected British motoring journal. "Yes, the engine is mighty, but the chassis is its equal. There's never been a supercar that's so exploitable and so rounded in its capabilities."


THE CAR OFFERED  

Presented here is a superb and highly original example of Ferrari's landmark front-engine V12 grand tourer: a 2001 Ferrari 550 Maranello, chassis number ZFFZS49A510125146. Delivered new as a U.S.-specification model, this Maranello was first registered in Florida before later relocating to California, where it has remained under long-term ownership. According to CARFAX, the car has had just two private owners from new and has covered a remarkably low 11,581 miles since 2001.

Finished in classic Rosso Corsa over black leather upholstery, the car presents as a well-kept, unmodified example. The paint retains a deep, lustrous finish, while the interior remains notably original, with factory leather trim across the seats, dashboard, and door panels showing minimal wear consistent with careful use and low mileage.

Power comes from Ferrari's naturally aspirated 5.5-liter V12, paired with the highly desirable factory six-speed manual transmission—an increasingly rare and defining attribute of the 550 Maranello. This combination represents one of the last great analog Ferrari grand tourers, blending traditional proportions, long-bonnet design, and exceptional mechanical engagement.

The CARFAX report documents consistent, responsible servicing from new. Early maintenance was carried out by authorized Ferrari dealers in Florida, including oil and filter changes, brake fluid service, and coolant replacement. Notable entries include brake fluid and oil service in May 2003, additional oil services in 2005 and 2011, and more comprehensive maintenance in November 2006 that included coolant service, replacement of the engine/powertrain control module, and new tires.

Following acquisition by its second owner in 2012, further servicing was recorded, including an oil and filter change and general inspection in March 2012, along with regular California emissions inspections through 2022; all passed successfully.

Importantly, the CARFAX confirms no accidents, no structural damage, no airbag deployment, and no title issues, further reinforcing the integrity of this example.

With its low mileage, documented ownership history, and well-preserved originality, this 2001 Ferrari 550 Maranello stands as a compelling opportunity for the collector seeking a refined yet visceral V12 Ferrari—one that represents the pinnacle of Ferrari's modern grand touring philosophy before the advent of paddle-shifted automation.

THE LAND ROVER DEFENDER

During the 1970s, experiments began to develop a 'next-generation' Land Rover using the Range Rover's coil-sprung chassis, and a new model debuted at the 1983 Geneva International Motor Show in 110" wheelbase configuration. While the familiar (and beloved) Land Rover body shape remained, coil springs replaced the venerable leaf spring suspension, and the four-cylinder engines were now backed with an all-synchromesh five speed gearbox. In 1984 the coil spring Ninety (with a wheelbase just short of 93 inches) fitted with a four-cylinder engine was introduced, and in 1990, the Ninety and One-Ten range was renamed Defender 90, 110 and 130 with a new range of engines including a V8 petrol and several diesel options. While the looks remained generally unchanged through the years, engines, gearboxes, and underpinnings were continually improved to ensure the Land Rover Defender remained The Best 4x4xFar.

THE BENTLEY AZURE

As owners of Bentley Motors since 1998, Volkswagen kept the existing Continental R-based Azure convertible in production until 2003 but delayed introducing its successor for a further three years. Production of the new Azure thus began for the 2006 model year and was based on the more modern Arnage platform. The latter had been built in two forms: Green Label (with BMW power) and Red Label with the long-running Rolls-Royce/Bentley 6.75-liter pushrod V8. A legacy of the Rolls-Royce/Bentley takeover battle with BMW, Volkswagen's use of its German rival's engines could only be a temporary measure, so the 'old' Bentley V8 was called up for duty, suitably up rated with twin turbochargers for the new Azure convertible. As well as the twin turbochargers, replacing the single unit used previously, this venerable engine was extensively reworked, Bentley claiming that more than half the parts were new. In this form it produced 450bhp and a mighty 645lb/ft of torque, while a new ZF six-speed automatic transmission fed this abundance of power to the rear wheels. Bentley claimed a 0-60mph (0-97km/h) acceleration time of 5.6 seconds and a top speed of 168mph (270 km/h), slightly faster than the previous model and still incredible for a vehicle of its ample size and weight. "In a word, wonderful," was how Autocar magazine greeted the new Azure, which was also reckoned "notably better for the new gearbox. Overall, it's amazing how much difference a decent auto 'box can make."

But Bentley was not done with the Azure yet. In 2009, the Azure T debuted with an additional 50hp on tap bringing total output to 500bhp, while torque rose to an even 1,000Nm (738 ft-lbs), capable of propelling the massive four-seat convertible to an astonishing 180mph. The 2010 model year marked the end of the line for Bentley's flagship Azure, and with no true successor, it remains a glorious monument to the incredible longevity of the mighty pushrod V8 engine.

THE PORSCHE 356 A 1500 SPEEDSTER

Few automobiles encapsulate the philosophy of focused driving pleasure and minimalist design quite as purely as the Porsche 356 Speedster. Introduced in 1954 at the urging of the celebrated U.S. importer Max Hoffman, the Speedster rapidly became an icon, coveted for its elemental appeal, lightweight architecture, and competition-bred engineering. Its debut represented a pivotal chapter in the evolution of the 356, integrating both the early 1500 "pre-A" mechanical purity and the emerging refinements of the forthcoming "A" series, resulting in a car that resonates among connoisseurs for both its rarity and panache.

With its dramatically raked windscreen—removable for racing—cut-downside glass, sleek bodywork and signature low-profile top, the 356 Speedster represented an aesthetic masterstroke from Erwin Komenda's studio in Stuttgart. The direct simplicity extended inside: minimalist bucket seats, a no-frills dashboard, and the evocative wheat-hued basket weave Acella Bast upholstery, reminiscent of race-proven 550 Spyders. Every detail was in deliberate pursuit of driving purity.

Engineering advancements were equally notable. The robust 1,488cc engine, equipped with Solex carburetors, provided eager torque and crisp response, its horizontally opposed layout delivering a low center of gravity and exceptional handling. The independent suspension and lightweight drum brakes combined agility and security, while the straightforward four-speed transmission affirmed the car's sporting intent. The result was not just a paragon of postwar German engineering, but an agile companion for track and public road alike.

Production numbers for early Speedsters were modest, especially in the rare Speedster Blue livery—fewer than 180 are believed to have left the factory finished in this evocative shade, amplifying the appeal for dedicated Porsche collectors. As a "normal" 1500, these very early examples bridge the transition between the earlier pre-A and later A-series refinements, endowing them with particular technical and historic resonance among marque purists.

Within the Porsche firmament, the Speedster is among the most mythic and widely celebrated models. Period advertisements extolled it as "born for the Pacific Coast," and legendary racing drivers such as James Dean famously favored the minimalist, elemental configuration. Today, these rare survivors represent a pinnacle of collectible Porsche quality, their commanding presence honored on concours lawns and in the most discriminating private collections worldwide.

Its durable construction and strong international following have cemented the Speedster as a favorite in historic motorsports competition and touring events, with original, well-documented and expertly restored examples especially coveted. The car's light weight and sporting balance have aged gracefully, endearing it both to passionate drivers and theorists of design purity.

The allure of a fully authentic, numbers-matching Speedster cannot be overstated. Fewer still have the benefit of accompanying documentary heritage and concours-level preparation, combining provenance, technical integrity, and visual distinction in one cohesive masterpiece. The seamless fusion of timeless styling, unimpeachable character, and a captivating backstory elevates such an example to the apex of the collectible Porsche hierarchy.

The car's recent restoration, performed to an uncompromising concours standard, comprised a complete body-off process with the highest regard for period-correct integrity. The interior and convertible top were entrusted to the leading experts at Autos International, renowned for their expertise in period Porsche cabins, while the restoration of critical trim components was executed by Victor Miles. Instrumentation was meticulously restored by Palo Alto Speedometer, and a new wiring harness fabricated and fitted by Y & Z, assuring the car's electrical reliability and safety. The car presents today as a model of specialist craftsmanship, with little more than 62 miles accrued since the completion of its restoration—effectively as-new and displaying the crispness and integrity of a freshly completed project. The entire exterior is protected by an expertly applied paint protection film (PPF), ensuring preservation of its pristine finish.

Accompanying documentation further attests to the car's authenticity. Supplied with its Certificate of Authenticity, correct toolkit and spare, and original owner's manual.
Service records establish its early life in the United States, with maintenance in New York through 1965, and a more recent workshop order from Porsche Palm Springs recording a technical inspection in November 2025.

Owing to its quality, the car has been selected for display at the prestigious Quail Motorsports Gathering, underscoring its eligibility for blue-chip concours events and international exhibitions. In terms of mechanical authenticity, it retains its matching factory engine and transaxle, both painstakingly rebuilt to original specifications. All major assemblies are reported to be correct to the 1955 build, with the interior retrim reflecting its factory configuration in both color and materials.

This singular Speedster sits at the crossroads of rarity, restoration excellence, and documented authenticity. For the discerning collector seeking a centerpiece for a world-class Porsche or postwar sports car collection, chassis 80341 presents a rare opportunity. As one of the earliest and most correct Speedsters—and with its extraordinary provenance, color, and restoration—this car is an unrepeatable offering and one of the true blue-chip icons of the Porsche marque.

THE CHRYSLER CI

Chryslers of the late 1920s and 1930s were not only very strong and robust touring cars, they were actually quite fast for their day. Between 1925 and 1931, Chryslers competed internationally at events such as the Mille Miglia, the Le Mans 24 Hours, and the Spa 24 Hours racking up impressive results amidst world-class competition that included Bugatti, Mercedes, and Alfa Romeo.

The Series CM was introduced in January 1931 and was offered in six body styles. It was updated in July of that year and was offered as a first-series 1932 model, the CI, with an updated narrow-profile radiator surround and cowl lamps relocated to the body.


THE CAR OFFERED

From a Los Angeles enthusiast, this 1932 CI-6 Chrysler has been frequently seen for the last 8 years around their home turf of Santa Monica and Malibu, often used as an errand-runabout. Under previous ownership the car was repainted in a primrose yellow with brown fenders and striping. Accented with orange spoked wire wheels with whitewall tires, and a tan soft top, the striking car shows well with excellent proportions and lots of charm. A brown interior accented with wood veneer dash, the dickie seat, dual side-mounted spare wheels and the trunk at the rear complete the charismatic package. It certainly offers its new owner a substantive pre-war motorcar, with driving ability that belies its more genteel looks.

BMW 850 Ci

The BMW 850Ci is the V12 powered grand touring flagship coupé from BMW's first generation 8 Series (E31), introduced in the early 1990s. With its long nose silhouette, elegant proportions and 2 door, 4 seat layout, the car was conceived not as a cramped sports car but as a high-end GT — a refined, powerful and exclusive grand tourer designed to deliver both performance and comfort. Early 850Ci models carried BMW's 5.0 liter naturally aspirated V12 engine, producing roughly 296–300 horsepower, accelerating from 0–60 mph in about 6.6–6.8 seconds, and reaching a top speed of 155 mph.

In autumn 1994 the 850Ci was significantly upgraded. BMW replaced the engine with a larger 5.4 liter V12 (the M73), boosting output to around 323–326 horsepower and raising torque to about 490 Nm — which sharpened its performance, with a 0 100 km/h (0–62 mph) time around 6.0–6.3 seconds, while still capping top speed at its electronically governed 250 km/h.

Beyond straight line performance, the 850Ci offered a blend of luxury and GT comfort that was rare for its time. The E31 chassis was built from the ground up for this model, rather than being derived from BMW's 3, 5 or 7 Series platforms — giving it bespoke proportions and a sense of exclusivity that underscored its flagship status. Inside, leather seating and a well-appointed cabin became standard, pushing it firmly into the "luxury coupé" realm rather than pure performance car.

In short, the BMW 850Ci was BMW's statement of capability in the early 1990s: a flagship grand touring coupé combining V12 muscle with luxury GT sensibilities. Even today it stands out as one of BMW's most ambitious and stylish coupes of its era — a car that didn't just aim to go fast, but to carry you there in comfort and elegance.


THE CAR OFFERED

This 1997 BMW 850Ci represents the final year of E31 production for North America and is one of just 1,218 examples produced worldwide. With only 363 officially delivered to the region, it was originally sold new in California. This example shows just over 52,000 miles and has been retained by only four owners from new.

Finished in Cosmos Schwartz Metallic (Black Metallic) over Light Grey Leather, the cabin offers a spacious 2+2 seating arrangement with supportive, electrically adjustable front seats and comfortable rear seating for occasional passengers. Amenities include automatic climate control, power sunroof, period correct mobile telephone, BMW factory audio system with cassette player, and trunk mounted CD changer.

The vehicle includes original tool kit, owners' manuals, and OEM wheels.

THE MOTORCYCLE OFFERED

Without question one of the most handsome and readily recognizable motorcycle power units of all time, the Harley-Davidson 61ci (1,000cc) overhead-valve v-twin - known as the 'Knucklehead' after its distinctively shaped rocker boxes - arrived powering a stylish all-new motorcycle in 1936. The last engine Bill Harley would design and oversee the completion of. Its design being one that would endure for 11 years, while DNA from this engine would persist until the early 2000's. An all new "wish-bone" frame was totally revolutionary with updated body work to really bring Harley Davidson into a modern era after the Depression. The overhead valve cylinder head arrangement, which previously had been reserved for Harley- Davidson race bikes, increased power to 37hp in 'E' trim and 40bhp in high-compression 'EL' trim. Truly a super bike of its day and the defining model of the brand.

This 1947 Knucklehead EL was the beneficiary of a restoration in which many of the bikes original components were retained. It wears a stunning shade of red similar to Harleys in-period "Flight Red". Power is driven through the rear wheel by a 'rachet top' 4 speed gearbox, with fuel atomized by a Linkert M-74. A decoding of its casting numbers confirms the presence of matching 'Belly' numbers, (47-4904), and a casting date of 'E7' on the transmission case, denoting May 1947.

For a period after its restoration, this 'Knucklehead' has been on static display, and it is offered without a key and will need some work undertaken to return it to running condition and the road. Other works could also be completed to further increase the restoration and originality of the machine.

THE PLYMOUTH BARRACUDA

In early 1963 Chrysler engineers put a Hemi head on a modified raised-block 426 wedge to create a competitive NASCAR engine, the 426 Hemi. It was shaped by all the experience gained in years of competition, and best of all for Mopar enthusiasts, to be eligible for NASCAR competition it had to be available in a regular production street configuration. The Street Hemi incorporated many of the race version's performance components, including the crankshaft, connecting rods and cross-bolted main bearing caps. The milder grind camshaft used hydraulic lifters and lower rate springs, in an attempt to limit rpm and keep to the 425-limit imposed by management. With dual Carter AFB carburetors, it was the most awesome engine of a period when awesome engines were the rule. History has passed judgment on the Street Hemi, making it the most sought and valuable power plant of the Muscle Car era.

The new for 1970 'Cuda was now built to accommodate the legendary 426 cubic inch Hemi. At a 70 percent premium over Plymouths largest powertrain, the 440-cid 390-hp Six Barrel, the Hemi was only for serious race minded individuals. In addition to the enormous price tag, the race spec Hemi-powered 'Cudas were only built for two model years, 1970 and 1971 adding to the rarity and allure.


THE CAR OFFERED

This rare and nicely restored 1970 Plymouth Hemi 'Cuda Hard Top was ordered with a raft of options. A relatively early production example built on November 10, 1969, according to the fender tag it was finished new in the current shade of Lime Light with a Black vinyl roof over Black vinyl interior. Fitted with the line-topping 426ci Hemi V8 mated to a A727 Torqueflite automatic, among the options boxes ticked where the Light Package (A01), Elastomeric Bumper Front (A21) -- which included body-colored racing mirrors, Super Performance Axle Package (A32) that added 9¾ Dana Axle with sure grip and a taller 4.10 gear ratio, a seven blade torque drive fan, 26 inch radiator with shroud, Hemi Suspension Handling Package, power front disc brakes, and Rallye Instrument Cluster (A62).

The early history of this 'Cuda is not recorded at the time of cataloging. By the late 1990s it was in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area, including being shown at the Car Craft Magazine Nationals in St. Paul in 1999 and 2003. In the early 2000s it entered the collection of the late enthusiast and stunt aviator Scott Romuld of St. Paul, Minnesota. When not flying for the North American Flight Team 'T-6 Thunder', piloting a WWII-era T-6 Texan fighter plane, he piloted the next best thing—this Hemi-powered land rocket. The current owner acquired the car for his expansive collection in February of 2011and has retained the 'Cuda since.

Subject of an older restoration prior to the current ownership, it has been maintained as part of a large collection for the past 14 years. The engine number stamped on the bottom of the engine corresponds with the chassis number, indicating has retained its original engine. Documented by copy of its 1970 Fender Tag Decoder Report, it is a rare opportunity to acquire one of these earth-shaking machines. If you are in search of arguably the ultimate American muscle car for show or go, this is the Hemi 'Cuda for you.
